pairs.evidence_full: Seven, roughly in order of what I'd actually do first. Generate the bank instead of writing it. This is the bottleneck and everything else is downstream of it. Take real claims from this repo's transcripts that *are* supported by their evidence, and mutate them into unsupported versions mechanically: widen a quantifier, delete a qualifier, promote a scoped result to a global one, strip the before-half of a before-and-after. The label is known by construction because you made the break. Reverse the mutation to manufacture sound cases from overclaims. This is MiniCheck's actual trick — their 770M model matches GPT-4 because of curated synthetic errors, not capacity — and it's the only path to thousands of labelled cases with no human in the loop. It also fixes the specific thing wrong with my current bank: the negatives would be drawn from real prose in this workspace rather than from my imagination about what a near-miss looks like. Turn the instability into the confidence score. I've been treating 88% self-agreement as a defect to minimise. It's more useful as the signal. Temperature is zero, so resampling buys nothing — but presentation variance is free: option order, polarity, claim-first versus evidence-first, a paraphrase of the question. Run k presentations and use the agreement rate as confidence. A claim where all k agree is a firm call; one that flips is genuinely ambiguous and should be silent. That gives a principled surfacing threshold instead of an invented one, costs k× on a cached prefix (so cheap), and needs no training at all. It also directly serves the PNAS finding: below threshold you say nothing rather than saying "unsure." Stop emitting labels; emit the juxtaposition. The RCT found a 90%-accurate detector delivered as a verdict left discernment unchanged while human-written fact-checks improved it — the argument helped, the verdict didn't. So the output shouldn't be "overclaim: scope_exceeds_evidence." It should be the claim beside the specific span of the agent's own text that fails to carry it, and nothing else. Extraction is also a much easier task for a small model than taxonomy, which is the same reason to drop form naming from the score. Stage B becomes "quote the part of the evidence this outruns, or say nothing here speaks to it." Take the mechanically-detectable forms away from the model entirely. `one_direction` is the form the judge misses and the one that matters most in this workspace — but it isn't a semantic question. It's a question about the shape of the session: did a turn that reports a metric change after modifying a judge, gate, threshold or filter also contain a measurement in the other direction? That's answerable from the tool-call record with no model. Code can enforce those, and principle 10 says it should. Mine the free ground truth already in the repo. `scripts/evidence-verdict.py` runs a commit's cited test at that commit and again with the source hunks reverted, and returns VALIDATED / UNSUPPORTED / COULD-NOT-JUDGE / NEVER-RAN. Those are mechanically-produced labels on real claims in real commit bodies. UNSUPPORTED commits are known-bad claims; VALIDATED are known-good. That's an anchor set nobody had to annotate, on exactly the claim class the tool cares about. I produced textbook instances tonight with you watching: I reported false alarms 73% → 40% → 27% as progress when the last step was inside the noise floor; I asserted the daemon was down a second time from a single curl with no process check; I claimed premises sit in the same turn without measuring it and was wrong about 43% of cases. Each of those has a correction in the transcript with a reason, which makes this session a small adversarial set with known answers and known *reasons*. If the detector doesn't flag them, it isn't working, and that's a sharper test than anything I'd construct. Add a zero-cost session signal that needs no judge at all. Claims made per tool call actually run. A session asserting sixty things off twelve tool calls is structurally different from one asserting twenty off two hundred, and you can compute that from the transcript with no model, no prompt, and no calibration. It won't tell you which claim is bad, but as a per-session index of how much talking outran the looking it may carry more of the signal you asked for than the judge does — and it can't be gamed by rephrasing, only by doing more work.

pairs.evidence_full: Checkpoint, while the bundle build sits in the cargo queue. Six commits landed, none pushed. `4b29cd3fe` svt-3 chunk 1, `70cca7483` svt-1, `55cd9ce0c` the origin merge, then three fixes from priorities 3 and 4: `5a356e11a` makes `with-cargo-lock.sh` reentrant, `4ea0201e2` gives the faults harness a portable reap, `3e05a0e50` gives `TurnClient` a request budget. pairs.evidence_full: Three of the four demo steps work, one of them impressively, and the step the doc leans hardest on prints a column of 401s. What actually ran, just now, against RuggedFox. `svrn mesh media` lists the offering member. `svrn mesh media RuggedFox` mints `http://127.0.0.1:22009`, probe 200 in 44 ms. Through that URL I logged into their Jellyfin, listed their library, and pulled the whole 122,048,071-byte title at 5.25 MB/s — 42 Mbit/s, about five times realtime for a 8 Mbit/s 1080p file. A mid-file `Range: bytes=60000000-68388607` came back 206 with exactly 8,388,608 bytes at 3.37 MB/s, so seeking is real, not a full-file re-read. Meanwhile `curl 192.168.1.13:8096` from this machine is "no route to host" — their Jellyfin is bound inside a container on their loopback and there is genuinely no way in except the key. The doc's caveat on the forty lines ("the Jellyfin query string and the `/Videos/{id}/stream` path are from Jellyfin's API, not from a run") is discharged: both run, the doc's exact path included. That step will land with this audience. Twenty-five people who have each personally fought nginx, a cert, and a port forward will watch a 1080p film play off a housemate's closed-up laptop through a port that does not exist, and seek in it. Step 4, unplugging the WAN, I could not test without cutting your network, but the bridge reports a live direct leg, which is the precondition. Step 2 is the problem, and it is the centerpiece. `svrn mesh media fanout '/Items?Recursive=true'` returns `RuggedFox … 60 ms 401 0B`. Every offering member answers 401 with an empty body, because no holder has declared a credential — `cw-media-demo.sh holder-up` never did it, which is what I fixed in `d515b6f0d`, but RuggedFox was set up by the old script. So the forty lines, which the doc calls "the whole federation" and stakes the substrate-not-a-product argument on, currently print an empty library and a list of refusals. The row is honest about why, which is the design working. It is still an empty table in front of a room. The gap is one command per holder, not architecture: Two things would read as sloppiness to this particular room. `svrn mesh app RuggedFox chores` answers "`RuggedFox` advertises no media origin — it declares no media_origin … `svrn mesh media` lists who offers one". Wrong domain, and factually false: RuggedFox does advertise a media origin. `MediaReachRefusal` is shared by both verbs and hardcodes media wording, so every app-tier refusal talks about media. Senior engineers notice that instantly and downgrade everything else they just saw. And `svrn daemon reload` told me "✓ no config changes detected — nothing to reload" immediately after I added `media_origin` to `config.toml`; only a stop/start picked it up. The conversion pitch is "one config line and a join, five minutes", and the verb that should apply the line reports a clean no-op instead. That is the report-absence-as-answered failure, on the exact path the many are being converted along. The 90-second app half works as far as one machine can show it. `svrn run --as chores --port 5000 --ttl 10m -- python3 chores.py` waited for the app to answer before publishing, registered as `{"tier":"claimed","claim_id":"chores-f96fa8cc01ac","expires_in_secs":594}`, and unpublished itself when I killed the process. That one is covered by `iroh_dialer_admission_e2e`, not by a run I watched. So: the story you tell is sound and the hard part — bytes off a peer's disk by key, with seeking, through nothing — is built and measured. Before anyone stands in front of that room, the declaration needs to be on every holder, and the app-tier refusals need to stop naming media. Neither is a design change. I am still holding commits at the peer session's request until their merge lands, then re-recording the bar in the new measurement-row substrate.

pairs.evidence_full: You're right, and I've been building the wrong instrument. The thing I've spent four iterations on is a fact-checker: take a claim, fetch external evidence, compare. That machinery is expensive and fragile — T0 shas, rungs, receipts, disambiguation — and it answers a question that isn't the main one. BS isn't usually a false fact. It's a conclusion that outruns its premises, and the premises are almost always sitting right there in the same turn. Principles 5, 6 and 7 are not evidence rules. They're inference rules, and every one of them is decidable from the text alone: A zero count is not a positive control (5) — `canary_hits: 0` is the expected good result and proves nothing. Absence of a response is not evidence of absence (6) — "did not answer" is not "answered: no". One run is not a measurement (7). A judge reported only in the direction it was meant to fix is not failed, it is not judged (7). Those four cost nothing to check. No repo, no daemon, no sha. They are claims about the shape of an argument. That's what this workspace's characteristic failure actually is — the compass says it outright: a plausible, well-formed, exit-0 result that is wrong. The output looks right because the form is right; what's broken is the step from evidence to conclusion. Here is the demonstration, and it's in the data I already have. Three of v5's four KEPT verdicts are the tool committing the exact fallacy it exists to catch. Row 20 claims `"The only live setter of FORCE_LOCAL in the tree is the first-launch journey spec and the fault harness."` The check was `git grep -cF 'FORCE_LOCAL ='` and the receipt is `(no matches)`. The claim entails at least two setters. The evidence contradicts the claim's own premise, and the tool scored it KEPT — it read an empty result as confirmation. I did not need the repo to find those. I needed to read the claim and the receipt next to each other. So the detector I'd build reads one turn — the claim plus whatever the agent offered for it — and asks whether the conclusion follows. Concretely, the forms worth catching first, because each already has an incident behind it in the compass: a universal or an "only" resting on a single observation; a negative result read as a positive one; a conclusion whose scope exceeds its evidence's scope, which is v5 row 23 asserting `"Unix is settled"` from one call site, and row 1 asserting `"the only drift was their sovereign-mesh.toml line numbers"` from one baseline regeneration; a one-directional result reported as a two-directional one; and a causal or temporal qualifier asserted without the prior run that would establish it, which is v5 row 18 calling its one red lane `"the pre-existing chaos probe"`. What this displaces: the evidence ladder stops being the primary stage and becomes the second one, reached only when the inference is valid and the premise is a factual assertion worth spot-checking. The referent gate I built today survives, but as a router into that second stage rather than as the gate on the pool — a claim with no resolvable referent can still be logically broken, and under today's gate it never gets looked at. What it can't do, stated rather than hidden: a well-formed claim that is simply factually wrong — a file cited at 2,195 lines that is really 2,300 — is invisible to it. That still needs evidence. I think that's the rarer failure and not what you mean by BS, but it's the cost. Before I build: do you want the logic pass to run on the claim plus the agent's own stated reasoning only, or should it also see the turn's tool calls and their results? The second is strictly more informative — it's what catches "ran one file, reported the suite" — but it's also the thing that reintroduces cost and the disambiguation problem, so I'd rather you pick than have me assume.

pairs.claim: Your ALPN table is the app surface, and each protocol carries its own trust class: inference and federated retrieval over `cwth/client/0`, tensor-split RPC over `cwth/rpc/0`, someone's Jellyfin over `cwth/media/0`, guests fenced onto `cwth/guest/0` with a listener that doesn't trust loopback.
pairs.evidence_full: Then the work is smaller and sharper than an integration: you already have the substrate, and it has the wrong carrier. Look at `commonwealth-discovery`. Alongside node discovery it carries an application registry — `MdnsDiscovery::advertise_app(app_id, port)` and `browse_apps(app_id)`, described in the crate docs as letting "a process on this node announce a service other nodes can find, on the same daemon and the same wire." That is an application substrate, already built, already shipping. Its problem is that it rides `_commonwealth._tcp.local.` — link-local multicast. And lightning-mesh deliberately does not bridge L2 across nodes; broadcast containment is the point of their design. So your app layer works beautifully on one router's LAN and goes silent at the first hop into their mesh. So "be a fluent substrate on a lightning-mesh network" reduces to one concrete piece of work: give `advertise_app`/`browse_apps` a routed carrier. What makes that cheap is a decision you already made. The crate docs say it outright: "Discovery is a hint, never an authorization." Everything mDNS returns is an unauthenticated claim about a name and an address; the join key decides whether the attempt succeeds. pairs.claim: `Forward::Splice(addr)` is a byte pump that never parses the payload; `Forward::Http { origin, headers }` hands the origin the dialer's verified identity.
pairs.evidence_full: They already compose further than you'd expect, and the idiomatic seam is narrower than "integration" usually implies: you register an ALPN on their endpoint. You don't build a bridge. Both projects root identity in the same primitive — an iroh `NodeId`, which on your side surfaces as `NodePubkey(*conn.remote_id().as_bytes())` (`commonwealth/crates/commonwealth-transport/src/iroh.rs:1067`). Both multiplex services over ALPN on one endpoint. And both are on iroh 1.0.x — yours resolves to 1.0.2, theirs is current — under `AGPL-3.0-or-later` on both sides. That's three things that usually need negotiating and here need none. Your acceptor's whole contract is already a registration hook. `RoutedAcceptor::run` takes `resolve(alpn, dialer) -> Option<Forward>` and does nothing else: one accept loop, ALPN and verified dialer key read once per connection, then every bi-stream pumped to whatever local target the resolver named. That shape doesn't care whose endpoint it's running on. If `mjolnir-meshd` can hand you its `Endpoint`, or accept a protocol registration against it, Commonwealth services become additional ALPNs on the router's existing node — one identity, one NAT traversal path, one hole-punch, N protocols. That is the integration, and it's maybe a hundred lines. The thing I'd check in their code before anything else: whether `mjolnir-meshd` owns its `Endpoint` privately or exposes it. If it's private, the ask upstream is small and reasonable — an ALPN registration API is a normal thing for an iroh daemon to have, and they already anticipate third-party protocols given the microVM and MCP integrations they mention. If they won't expose it, you're back to two endpoints on one box, which works but throws away most of the benefit. The real design hazard is the trust models, and they point opposite ways. Their pitch is "any router can join. Any router can leave." Your ALPN comments are explicit in the other direction — `MEDIA_ALPN` and `RPC_ALPN` are members-only and refused rather than downgraded for a stranger, because "the origin authenticates nothing, so there is no safe listener to fall back to." `GUEST_ALPN` exists as a separate protocol precisely because routing guests to the trusted listener "would hand every dial-string holder the full client API." So the invariant to encode structurally, not remember: lightning-mesh membership must never imply Commonwealth membership. A router joining their mesh gets L3 reachability. It gets a Commonwealth ALPN only if it's separately a member of your mesh. If those two admission decisions ever collapse into one, an open-join router mesh becomes a path to `cwth/rpc/0` and `cwth/media/0`, which is your entire threat model inverted. Your resolver is the right place to enforce it — it already takes the dialer key and returns `None` to close the connection, so the enforcement point exists and needs no new machinery. Second invariant, and it's principle 8: one key, not two. Their `NodeId` and your `NodePubkey` are the same 32 bytes. A router running both with separate keypairs is one machine with two identities, and then "is this node a member" has two answers that can disagree. Derive both from one secret or the integration rots quietly. What it actually buys you is on today's data. The relayed/mixed path we measured tops out near 100 Mbit/s aggregate and degrades with duration — 87 Mbit/s over 25 seconds, 55 over 623, with three reconnects and four gaps past a full second. Their 802.11s backhaul with babel routing makes co-located nodes LAN-adjacent, so `cwth/media/0` between two routers on the same mesh never touches a relay. For the media use case specifically, that's the difference between "watchable with caveats" and "local." Their overlay doesn't help Commonwealth-to-Commonwealth traffic reach *across* sites — iroh already does that — but it changes the local path from relayed to direct, which is precisely the axis today's numbers were bad on. What I'd not build first, despite it being the tempting one: consuming their subnet-allocation CRDT to populate Commonwealth peer discovery. It couples you to their state model, their convergence semantics, and their `10.254.<blake3(node_id)>/16` addressing, in exchange for solving a problem you've already solved — you have mesh membership and join links. Do it only if you find a concrete case where your discovery can't answer something theirs can. That's the inventory-before-the-plan rule, and this is exactly the shape of thing that fails it. One caveat on all of the above: I've read their README, not their source. The crate layout, the CRDT semantics, and the claim that both run on "the Iroh layer" are their description of themselves. Before committing to the ALPN-registration design I'd want to see their endpoint construction and confirm they're on iroh 1.0.x rather than a 0.x line — a major-version mismatch there turns "register a protocol" back into "build a bridge," and it's the one assumption that would invalidate the cheap path.

pairs.claim: That is the allowed-IPs row: what this caller may see and do, decided from who they are rather than from what they asked for, with the forgeable `enabled_corpora` selection sitting underneath the ceiling exactly as a peer's chosen route sits under WireGuard's ACL.
pairs.evidence_full: WireGuard is beautiful for one reason that transfers: its entire state is one table, `public key → allowed IPs`, and one verb, send a packet. Identity is the key itself, the ACL and the routing table are the same rows, there is no negotiation, and everything that is not that table is either the kernel's business or the userspace tool's. Linus could skim it because there was nothing to skim past. The daemon's equivalent table already exists in the topology doc, it just is not stated as the whole thing. A request arrives under a principal, and that principal resolves once to a Scope, which is the airtight corpus ceiling plus capabilities. The node's ed25519 key is the identity for peers and the per-request principal is the identity for local callers, and both should land in the same row shape. One table, principal to scope. The one verb is the turn. Tokens, narration, interpretation, clarification, metadata, streamed out against a Scope. Search is the retrieval half of a turn, solve is several turns, embed is a turn primitive. The doc's bar of driving the 35 Runtime reach-throughs to zero is what makes the verb real, because a turn that closes over `&self` is not a function of its inputs. The third piece is what the daemon is allowed to hold resident, and the placement test is the one WireGuard uses for the kernel: would it be wrong for two processes to do this at once? Loaded weights, the index writer, the SCIP graph, the node key, the port. Those cannot have two owners, so the daemon owns them. Everything that would be fine done twice is a client or a job, and it does not belong in the process. The fourth piece is that a job is not a route. Ingest, reindex, atlas build, enrichment, compaction, and the donor loop are all "run this and tell me how it goes", and commonwealth-work already has the shape: a unit, a lease, one `WorkProjection::fold`. Local background work should be work units executed on the local node, so a mesh job and a local job are one fold with one status vocabulary. That is principle 11 applied to the daemon's own plumbing. So the core is four things: an identity table, one verb, a job queue, and a short list of single-owner resources. A route is a turn, a job submission or status read, a row in the identity table, or a read of a single-owner resource. If it is none of those, it does not belong in the daemon. Measured against today, the core is designed and the rind is accreted. The daemon mounts 126 routes across 25 families. By the test above they sort roughly like this: | chat, solve, search, models, oicp | ~38 | turn | | internal/corpus, atlas, worker, governance | ~34 | jobs wearing route costumes | | conversations, notes, memories, projects, documents, skills, insights, recipe-projects | ~41 | store CRUD | | mesh, mcp, meshapp, blob | ~13 | identity, a protocol adapter, a dev server, a blob store | The 41 store routes are the decision to make first, because they are where the shape is currently contradicted. The desktop reads its own copy of the state database directly while the daemon also serves it over HTTP, and that dual accessor is what stranded every map built before the rename in August. Either the daemon is the only writer and every client goes through it, or the store is a WAL SQLite file any local process opens and those routes vanish. Having both at once is the OpenVPN move. Given the stranding incident, I would make the daemon the only writer and delete the direct-read path. The 34 job routes collapse into one family on top of the work plane. That is the change with the best ratio, since it deletes route code and unifies status reporting without touching inference at all. And the cli-llm finding from before is this same picture from the other side. Once a client speaks turn, job and store, it needs no inference crate, and the only things left needing llama in-process are the benches, which are surfaces the topology already names. The 611 MB binary is the cost of not having drawn the line by ownership, and drawing it is what makes the daemon skimmable: a host that assembles a Runtime from config, mounts four families, and spawns the job runner, with everything else in libraries that are testable without a process. The thing to write into TOPOLOGY before any of that is the placement test itself, stated for routes the way the ring rule is stated for capabilities. The route classification above is a mechanical hour of work and would be the first evidence.

pairs.evidence_full: Here's the plainer version. The headline was doing none of the work before. 18.7 If it can still do it, you haven't removed it Deleting every *use* of an ability is not deleting the ability. The count goes to zero, the code still compiles it in, and the work reads as finished. Look for the ability where it is granted — the dependency in `Cargo.toml`, the import, the feature flag — not by counting the places that use it. If your check would still pass with the ability completely intact, it is measuring a symptom, and it will turn green at the exact moment you most want it to be honest. The sv-surface campaign spent a day proving the desktop was a thin client, with three instruments in a row: `is_attach_mode` forks 15 → 0, attach-time reads of local state 55 → 33, the construction count pinned at 12. All three numbers could have hit zero with the whole backend still inside the app — which is how you get a 661 MB "client" next to a 614 MB daemon. The check that actually works is `cargo tree`. Using something is not the same as being able to be it. One call that grants no new ability is an integration point, and you can live with it — the desktop starting a daemon by path links nothing. An ability you never exercise is still an ability. When you argue about where a boundary sits, argue about what each side *can become*, not about what it happened to call. Gate what the build can do, not who is running it. "Phones can't run a backend" is a fact about this year. "This build ships no backend it can start" is the same guard without deciding the future for you — and the day a model fits on a phone, one is a flag and the other is a rewrite. Two things changed from my earlier draft. The headline is now the whole idea in seven plain words instead of three abstract nouns, and the second corollary leads with the mistake ("phones can't") rather than the abstraction, because that's the form someone will actually recognise themselves making. It's ready to land as §18.7 with a compass row — something like *"I removed all the uses; is the ability gone?"* — and per §17.4 it should retire `sv-attach-pure-client` rather than leave it sitting beside the bar that replaced it. Say the word and I'll write it in, or leave it as the clean session's first task where it gets a fresh read before it becomes doctrine.

pairs.claim: `sovereign-cli-llm` alone is 93k, `corpus-engine` 77k, `sovereign-core` 57k.
pairs.evidence_full: The thing Linus praised isn't clean code — it's that WireGuard refused the option. About 4,000 lines against OpenVPN's ~600k, but the line count is downstream of two decisions: no crypto agility (one suite, versioned wholesale, so there is no negotiation state machine at all) and no configuration surface (a peer is a public key plus an allowed-IPs list; cryptokey routing makes the routing table *be* the authorization table instead of two subsystems that have to agree). "I've skimmed it" is the actual compliment. Skimming was enough to form a judgment. The uncomfortable measurement: this workspace is 890,193 code lines across 148 size-gate keys, tests counted separately. That is larger than the thing he called a horror. None of those can be skimmed by anyone, ever. So the transferable bar isn't 4k lines, it's this: one competent outsider reads the subsystem end to end in a sitting and afterward holds its state machine in their head. Empirically that's something like 2-3k lines and under ten nouns. You have crates in that range already — `commonwealth-transport` at 1,124, `commonwealth-rail-core` at 1,282, `commonwealth-knowledge` at 1,217, `sovereign-work-atlas`. The mesh transport layer is the closest structural analogue, because it's the same kind of object: a peer protocol where two ends must agree without a human present. The obstacle is in your own compass. Principle 9 — closed sets are enums, open sets are registries — is the agility principle. Every registry is a place you chose "this can change without a code change" over "this can be held in one head." WireGuard's whole move was to refuse that trade: it declared the set closed and versioned the closed thing. Both positions are defensible, but a subsystem cannot be skimmable and extensible at the same time, and right now the repo's default answer is extensible. `DELETION.md` has the evidence: noun convergence netted +33,132 first-party Rust lines. The one change that moved the other way was deleting a dead loop, at −3,789. If you want this to be more than an aspiration, the move is to pick one subsystem and declare its concept set closed — no registry, no config knob, version the whole thing when it changes — then measure whether it lands under the skim bar. Transport is the honest candidate because it's small now and because the protocol case is exactly where negotiation surface metastasizes. Which one do you want to hold to it?

pairs.claim: The version-preserving move is to narrow the signer to `fn sign(&self, msg: &[u8]) -> [u8; 64]` — the rail builds `ring_op_message` itself, the signer only holds the key — and delete `RingVerifier` and `Ed25519Verifier` outright, taking the `&dyn RingVerifier` parameter off `admit` and `compact`.
pairs.evidence_full: Your instinct is right, and the discriminator against transport is sharper than size. The readable unit is `oplog` (236) + `commonwealth-rail-core` (1,282) + `commonwealth-rail` (954) = 2,472 code lines, tests excluded. That is WireGuard scale, and it is the same class of object: peers converging without a server. `commonwealth-transport` is 1,124 lines and loses anyway, because it wraps iroh — it does not own its wire format, so you cannot version it wholesale. Declaring a closed set over someone else's protocol is a promise you don't control. Most of the WireGuard properties are already there, which is why this is a ratification rather than a rewrite. The act set is three variants and closed. `actor` *is* the hex public key that signed, so the identity table and the authorization table are one table — the same collapse cryptokey routing makes. A newer envelope version is refused and reported as `RailGap::NewerVersionLine`, never downgraded or negotiated. And the best parts are unrepresentable rather than checked: `Correct.replacement` is a `Payload` and not a `RailAct`, so nested correction cannot be written; `Seal` carries no actor and no range, so sealing someone else's history has no syntax. The no-I/O, no-clock property is held by the dependency list plus three `[[forbid]]` blocks in `ARCH_LAYERS.toml`, not by anyone remembering. What the call would actually cost you is `RingVerifier`. That trait is crypto agility in the precise sense Linus was praising the absence of — a runtime-selectable verification scheme, with a `name()` on it so the trace can say which one ran. Its doc defends it as symmetry with `RingSigner`, and the asymmetry it fixed was real, but symmetric seams are two where zero would do. The two are not the same kind of thing: `RingSigner` exists so the daemon holds the key and `commonwealth-api` carries no crypto dependency, which is key custody, not scheme choice. Verification needs no secret, so it has no such justification. That puts the scheme in exactly one place, keeps custody split, and makes the asymmetry the trait was added to prevent unrepresentable instead of balanced. Ed25519 + the one message construction then move under the envelope's `v`, and changing either is a new protocol version, whole. The thing that will undo this if you don't watch it is above the line, not in it: `commonwealth-work` is 2,924 lines and `commonwealth-state` 1,501, both already larger than the rail, both depending on `rail-core`. Rail concerns regrow there. The bar is falsifiable and you already have the instrument — cw-lift physically lifted the package once and found the missing exports. Lift it again after the trait deletion and have someone who hasn't read it describe the convergence rule from a single sitting.

pairs.claim: No pass/fail on a mean rate will ever surface that, and it's the thing a media product would actually feel.
pairs.evidence_full: A single stream on the same path did 87.0 Mbit/s; four streams together did 99.3. If per-stream flow control capped a stream near 25, the one-viewer control would have been near 25 too — it was three and a half times that. So the 24.9-37.3 figures in the four-viewer run aren't per-stream caps, they're four clients splitting a path that tops out around 100. Four streams buying 14% more than one stream is a path limit, not a flow-control limit. Flow control would have scaled roughly linearly. One thing I can't claim, and said so to the peer: I can't falsify the window hypothesis on arithmetic. TTFB bounds RTT from above only (160-280ms), and a lower true RTT makes the window's prediction *higher*, so 87.0 sits comfortably inside what the window permits. At an RTT near 115ms the window predicts almost exactly 87 — either coincidence or a sign it's binding on the single-stream case. I have no lower bound on RTT and no way to separate those. What's certain is the cap isn't at 25, and the aggregate doesn't scale. The finding I'd actually carry forward is a different one. Single stream over 25 seconds: 87.0 Mbit/s. Single stream over 623 seconds: 55.2, with 3 reconnects, four stalls past a full second, and a worst second of literally zero. The path doesn't have a static ceiling — it degrades with duration. A viewer doesn't experience "55 Mbit/s average," they experience 87 for a while and then four seconds of nothing. Bridge is still up in case the peer wants one more reading before they tear the VM down. I've asked them to take its neutral uplink number first — if that box pushes 800+ to a neutral endpoint, then the ~100 ceiling and the degradation over ten minutes are both ours, and worth naming.

pairs.claim: That single check enforces §7.2's prose-assertion smell, kills the essays as a side effect, and fixes the 265 dead path citations, without touching the payload `symbols` depends on.
pairs.evidence_full: Priced honestly, the extreme breaks four things, and three of the breaks are cheap to route around. The fourth is the one that would actually hurt, and it's specific to this repo. The split, measured: 146,060 lines of `///` item docs, 93,727 of `//` inline, 47,396 of `//!` module headers, against 860,372 of code. What a blanket delete costs. 2,321 files carry an SPDX AGPL header — that's a licensing regression wearing a style change's clothes, and it's one mechanical exemption. 518 code fences live in doc comments, 456 of them in the default-rust class that actually compiles; `quality/campaigns/conformance.toml` seats `--doctests` in CI, and the cw-lift campaign already caught three that failed to compile while the suite read green. Deleting doc comments deletes executable tests. There are 901 `unsafe` occurrences against 72 `SAFETY:` comments — a ratio that's already wrong in the direction you'd be making worse. The fourth is the one I'd weigh most. `symbols` returns doc comments verbatim. I called it on `TurnRequest` and got back the field docs in full — including the line saying absent-on-the-wire means `Grounded` and `Grounded` is omitted when writing, with `turn_request_wire_form` named as the test that holds it. That is wire-contract information not derivable from the type, and it arrives at the one moment an agent needs it. The whole read-budget doctrine in `AGENTS.md` — don't Read a file before calling `symbols` — rests on `symbols` returning enough to make the Read unnecessary. Strip `///` and every call returns a bare signature, agents go back to reading files, and you re-pay the 74.3k the /context audit was fighting. In this codebase the item docs aren't decoration; they're the retrieval payload. You'd be deleting your index to tidy the shelf. Where your extreme survives contact cleanly is the inline class. 93,727 lines of `//` inside function bodies. `symbols` doesn't return them, `code_search` doesn't rank on them, nobody sees them who isn't already in the file with the code in front of them — which is exactly the reader your principle says should be reading the code. They carry the highest staleness risk and produce the least. "Delete all `//` inside function bodies, forbid new ones, SAFETY and SPDX exempt" is a defensible policy that takes 94k lines off in one commit and costs you nothing a tool was using. But I think there's a rule that gets more of what you want than a ban does. Don't budget words — change what a comment is permitted to be. A comment may only be a citation or a contract: it names a test, a symbol, a spec section, or a wire invariant. Under that rule the 64-line `turn_http.rs` header collapses to about six lines, because the tenant-scoping paragraph, the phase history and the "Known gap, stated rather than discovered" section are all narrative — and that last section is precisely your complaint, an agent writing down what it chose not to build in the file where building it would have gone. There are 400 of those admissions in the tree. A ban on comments doesn't stop that agent; it just makes it write the same paragraph in the commit body, where the median is already 34 lines on a two-file change. A citation rule stops it, because "deliberately not implemented" has nothing to cite. That rule is also mechanically checkable, which a word budget isn't. A comment containing a claim word — always, never, must, cannot, guarantee, invariant, 11,459 lines carry one today — must name a test or a symbol in backticks, and the named thing must resolve. So: yes to deleting the inline class outright, no to deleting `///`, and the forbidding is better aimed at narration than at comments. If you want the aggressive version I'd take it as three commits — SPDX-preserving inline purge, then the citation gate in `pre-push.sh`, then the `//!` essays cut to what the gate lets through.

pairs.evidence_full: Your instinct is right, and the discriminator against transport is sharper than size. The readable unit is `oplog` (236) + `commonwealth-rail-core` (1,282) + `commonwealth-rail` (954) = 2,472 code lines, tests excluded. That is WireGuard scale, and it is the same class of object: peers converging without a server. `commonwealth-transport` is 1,124 lines and loses anyway, because it wraps iroh — it does not own its wire format, so you cannot version it wholesale. Declaring a closed set over someone else's protocol is a promise you don't control. Most of the WireGuard properties are already there, which is why this is a ratification rather than a rewrite. The act set is three variants and closed. A newer envelope version is refused and reported as `RailGap::NewerVersionLine`, never downgraded or negotiated. And the best parts are unrepresentable rather than checked: `Correct.replacement` is a `Payload` and not a `RailAct`, so nested correction cannot be written; `Seal` carries no actor and no range, so sealing someone else's history has no syntax. The no-I/O, no-clock property is held by the dependency list plus three `[[forbid]]` blocks in `ARCH_LAYERS.toml`, not by anyone remembering. What the call would actually cost you is `RingVerifier`. That trait is crypto agility in the precise sense Linus was praising the absence of — a runtime-selectable verification scheme, with a `name()` on it so the trace can say which one ran. Its doc defends it as symmetry with `RingSigner`, and the asymmetry it fixed was real, but symmetric seams are two where zero would do. The two are not the same kind of thing: `RingSigner` exists so the daemon holds the key and `commonwealth-api` carries no crypto dependency, which is key custody, not scheme choice. Verification needs no secret, so it has no such justification. The version-preserving move is to narrow the signer to `fn sign(&self, msg: &[u8]) -> [u8; 64]` — the rail builds `ring_op_message` itself, the signer only holds the key — and delete `RingVerifier` and `Ed25519Verifier` outright, taking the `&dyn RingVerifier` parameter off `admit` and `compact`. That puts the scheme in exactly one place, keeps custody split, and makes the asymmetry the trait was added to prevent unrepresentable instead of balanced. Ed25519 + the one message construction then move under the envelope's `v`, and changing either is a new protocol version, whole. The thing that will undo this if you don't watch it is above the line, not in it: `commonwealth-work` is 2,924 lines and `commonwealth-state` 1,501, both already larger than the rail, both depending on `rail-core`. Rail concerns regrow there. The bar is falsifiable and you already have the instrument — cw-lift physically lifted the package once and found the missing exports. Lift it again after the trait deletion and have someone who hasn't read it describe the convergence rule from a single sitting.

pairs.evidence_full: Your reframe is right, and I can put a number on why mine was wrong. Across the 40 most recent transcripts — 1,413 assistant text blocks, 11,009 sentences — there are 375 promissory sentences, 9.4 per session. Four of them, one percent, appear in the session's final message. Everything I built and proposed reads the final report. It would have seen 4 of 375 promises. Promises are made mid-turn and then quietly vanish; the ledger has to record per-turn or it is looking at the wrong artifact entirely. Draft is at `.sovereign/features/bs-1-oplog/order.md`, replacing the universals order, which is now one adjudicator inside this rather than the thing itself. The design hinge is that a claim isn't true or false when it's made — it acquires a verdict at a knowable moment, and the ledger's only real job is tracking that moment. Retrospective and universal claims are decidable immediately. Promissory ones become decidable at session end. Predictive ones may stay open past it. Evaluative ones never become decidable, and the order excludes them from scoring outright, because a grade that quietly scores taste is a daemon model judging prose style and everything downstream is noise. Most of this already exists and none of it watches the message to you. Daemon-model judging is one uniform register across about ten call sites, always grammar-forced to a small enum plus a citation. `co-drift.py` already judges a commit's prose claims against its diff — same question, different artifact. `Inherited::advice()` already detects a Next item that rode three frames without being done or dropped. And `~/.sovereign/comaintainer/verdicts.jsonl` is an append-only ledger with a `kind` discriminator, so this is a new `kind`, not a new store. Two things I'd push on in your design. Integrity can't be a ratio — a ratio is gamed by padding a report with twenty safe claims to dilute one broken promise, so broken promises have to count absolutely. And the bigger one: the hook that shows an agent its own ledger has an obvious adaptation, which is to stop making checkable claims. Hedge everything into evaluative, score a clean sheet, say nothing. Within a week that's the dominant strategy and reports are worse than before the tool existed. So the adjudicable fraction has to be on every grade card and tracked against the session's own trailing median. A falling adjudicable fraction is a finding, not a clean sheet. You asked for non-punitive, and this is what keeps non-punitive from collapsing into non-informative. The demo is a backtest, which is the part I like most about where this landed. There are 191 real sessions on disk. `svrn session oplog replay --last 40 --grade` runs over history that neither the ledger nor the grader can have influenced — no labelling, no new data collection, available the day it's written. Then you referee five cards, chosen by a rule fixed before the run, and say fair or unfair on each BROKEN verdict. That's the precision measurement and you're the only ground truth for it. The bar I'd watch is the second one, because it fires before any hook is written: across the 40 sessions, no single integrity grade may hold more than 60% of them. A grader everyone passes is not measuring anything, and if that fails the honest move is to drop the grade and keep the oplog as a plain record. The one thing I'd ask you to weigh in on is the closure rule — I've written it so a promissory row still open at session end is BROKEN unless explicitly abandoned with a reason, which is strict, and strictness there is what makes bar 1 hard to pass.

That is wire-contract information not derivable from the type, and it arrives at the one moment an agent needs it. The whole read-budget doctrine in `AGENTS.md` — don't Read a file before calling `symbols` — rests on `symbols` returning enough to make the Read unnecessary. Strip `///` and every call returns a bare signature, agents go back to reading files, and you re-pay the 74.3k the /context audit was fighting. In this codebase the item docs aren't decoration; they're the retrieval payload. You'd be deleting your index to tidy the shelf. Where your extreme survives contact cleanly is the inline class. 93,727 lines of `//` inside function bodies. `symbols` doesn't return them, `code_search` doesn't rank on them, nobody sees them who isn't already in the file with the code in front of them — which is exactly the reader your principle says should be reading the code. They carry the highest staleness risk and produce the least. "Delete all `//` inside function bodies, forbid new ones, SAFETY and SPDX exempt" is a defensible policy that takes 94k lines off in one commit and costs you nothing a tool was using. But I think there's a rule that gets more of what you want than a ban does. Don't budget words — change what a comment is permitted to be. A comment may only be a citation or a contract: it names a test, a symbol, a spec section, or a wire invariant. There are 400 of those admissions in the tree. A ban on comments doesn't stop that agent; it just makes it write the same paragraph in the commit body, where the median is already 34 lines on a two-file change. A citation rule stops it, because "deliberately not implemented" has nothing to cite. That rule is also mechanically checkable, which a word budget isn't. A comment containing a claim word — always, never, must, cannot, guarantee, invariant, 11,459 lines carry one today — must name a test or a symbol in backticks, and the named thing must resolve. pairs.claim: Their `NodeId` and your `NodePubkey` are the same 32 bytes.
pairs.evidence_full: They already compose further than you'd expect, and the idiomatic seam is narrower than "integration" usually implies: you register an ALPN on their endpoint. You don't build a bridge. Both projects root identity in the same primitive — an iroh `NodeId`, which on your side surfaces as `NodePubkey(*conn.remote_id().as_bytes())` (`commonwealth/crates/commonwealth-transport/src/iroh.rs:1067`). Both multiplex services over ALPN on one endpoint. And both are on iroh 1.0.x — yours resolves to 1.0.2, theirs is current — under `AGPL-3.0-or-later` on both sides. That's three things that usually need negotiating and here need none. Your acceptor's whole contract is already a registration hook. `RoutedAcceptor::run` takes `resolve(alpn, dialer) -> Option<Forward>` and does nothing else: one accept loop, ALPN and verified dialer key read once per connection, then every bi-stream pumped to whatever local target the resolver named. `Forward::Splice(addr)` is a byte pump that never parses the payload; `Forward::Http { origin, headers }` hands the origin the dialer's verified identity. That shape doesn't care whose endpoint it's running on. If `mjolnir-meshd` can hand you its `Endpoint`, or accept a protocol registration against it, Commonwealth services become additional ALPNs on the router's existing node — one identity, one NAT traversal path, one hole-punch, N protocols. That is the integration, and it's maybe a hundred lines. The thing I'd check in their code before anything else: whether `mjolnir-meshd` owns its `Endpoint` privately or exposes it. If it's private, the ask upstream is small and reasonable — an ALPN registration API is a normal thing for an iroh daemon to have, and they already anticipate third-party protocols given the microVM and MCP integrations they mention. If they won't expose it, you're back to two endpoints on one box, which works but throws away most of the benefit. The real design hazard is the trust models, and they point opposite ways. Their pitch is "any router can join. Any router can leave." Your ALPN comments are explicit in the other direction — `MEDIA_ALPN` and `RPC_ALPN` are members-only and refused rather than downgraded for a stranger, because "the origin authenticates nothing, so there is no safe listener to fall back to." `GUEST_ALPN` exists as a separate protocol precisely because routing guests to the trusted listener "would hand every dial-string holder the full client API." So the invariant to encode structurally, not remember: lightning-mesh membership must never imply Commonwealth membership. A router joining their mesh gets L3 reachability. It gets a Commonwealth ALPN only if it's separately a member of your mesh. If those two admission decisions ever collapse into one, an open-join router mesh becomes a path to `cwth/rpc/0` and `cwth/media/0`, which is your entire threat model inverted. Your resolver is the right place to enforce it — it already takes the dialer key and returns `None` to close the connection, so the enforcement point exists and needs no new machinery. Second invariant, and it's principle 8: one key, not two. A router running both with separate keypairs is one machine with two identities, and then "is this node a member" has two answers that can disagree. Derive both from one secret or the integration rots quietly. What it actually buys you is on today's data. The relayed/mixed path we measured tops out near 100 Mbit/s aggregate and degrades with duration — 87 Mbit/s over 25 seconds, 55 over 623, with three reconnects and four gaps past a full second. Their 802.11s backhaul with babel routing makes co-located nodes LAN-adjacent, so `cwth/media/0` between two routers on the same mesh never touches a relay. For the media use case specifically, that's the difference between "watchable with caveats" and "local." Their overlay doesn't help Commonwealth-to-Commonwealth traffic reach *across* sites — iroh already does that — but it changes the local path from relayed to direct, which is precisely the axis today's numbers were bad on. What I'd not build first, despite it being the tempting one: consuming their subnet-allocation CRDT to populate Commonwealth peer discovery. It couples you to their state model, their convergence semantics, and their `10.254.<blake3(node_id)>/16` addressing, in exchange for solving a problem you've already solved — you have mesh membership and join links. Do it only if you find a concrete case where your discovery can't answer something theirs can. That's the inventory-before-the-plan rule, and this is exactly the shape of thing that fails it. One caveat on all of the above: I've read their README, not their source. The crate layout, the CRDT semantics, and the claim that both run on "the Iroh layer" are their description of themselves. Before committing to the ALPN-registration design I'd want to see their endpoint construction and confirm they're on iroh 1.0.x rather than a 0.x line — a major-version mismatch there turns "register a protocol" back into "build a bridge," and it's the one assumption that would invalidate the cheap path.

pairs.claim: My instinct is no: a daemon that died while the app is open should surface in the ReconnectBanner with a button, so the re-spawn is the user's act rather than the client's policy.
pairs.evidence_full: My read, and where I'd push back on myself. The decision is about what a thing *is*, not about who calls `spawn`. The daemon owns the data root, the run lock, the weights, and the serving. The client renders and asks. What makes the desktop a client is that it cannot be the other thing — and today it can, because it links `sovereign-cli-daemon` and re-enters itself as one. A binary that can become a daemon is a daemon wearing a UI, whatever the process tree looks like at runtime. That's why the dependency edge is the real test and the attach-needle count never was: the needles would have gone to zero with the whole backend still compiled in. A single detached spawn by path is a different kind of act. It carries no lifecycle — no handle, no restart policy, no health contract, no stop-on-quit, and no knowledge of what it started beyond a filename. It's the client saying "the backend should be running" once, which is the same thing a user double-clicking would say. That's an integration surface. Supervision is ownership. And it makes the service path what it should have been all along: a choice for people who want a daemon outliving their session — CLI, headless, server. Not an architectural tax on the desktop. Per-platform backends are fine there because that's genuinely a per-platform feature. The line between "a small spawn" and "managing" erodes quietly. Nobody adds supervision in one commit — they add a retry, then a backoff, then a health check, then a restart on failure, and in six months the desktop supervises again with no single diff that looks wrong. A dependency-edge bar passes clean through all of that. So the instrument needs a second half that pins "no handle is retained, no lifecycle is tracked," or the bar will be green while the property rots. That's the same lesson the attach floor already taught once. The open question inside your decision is whether `attach_watch` re-spawning on `Down` is allowed. That's a restart policy, however thin — one retry is where every supervisor starts. That keeps the spawn count at "when the user asked," which is a rule that doesn't erode. And I should say plainly that I got here by correction, not design. I called the split dead on measurement, reversed when I found supervised-child is the default, built the service crate, and now the sidecar reading demotes a good chunk of tonight's work to the secondary path. The crate still earns its place and Windows gained a capability it never had — but you reached this framing, not me, and twice today the thing that moved the analysis was you pushing back on a conclusion I'd stated too confidently.

Concretely it's three things you already have. `spawn_admitting` decides who gets through on a verified Ed25519 key. pairs.claim: `10.254.<blake3(node_id)>/16` is the same idea in IPv4.
pairs.evidence_full: Right on both counts, and the discovery one has an actual standard — you adopt it rather than build it. Solutions are in the note now. Discovery across L3 is RFC 8766, and it changes almost nothing you own. A DNS-SD Discovery Proxy gets delegated a subdomain; when a unicast query arrives it re-issues that query as mDNS *on its own local link* and reports the answers back. The spec is explicit that "there is no danger of multicast forwarding loops, because no multicast packets are forwarded" — it acts for remote clients rather than bridging their broadcast domain. That maps onto lightning-mesh exactly. A proxy per router, delegated under `.mesh`. Your `advertise_app`/`browse_apps` keep speaking `_commonwealth._tcp.local.` unchanged, and a node's services go mesh-wide without a line changing in `mdns.rs` — while their broadcast containment, the property they deliberately designed for, survives intact. The only in-tree fix is that `hostname().local.` host record. This is the inventory outcome you want: the registry you already have gets a carrier, not a rewrite. The thing to refuse is an Avahi-style multicast reflector. It forwards multicast across segments, risks loops, and destroys the containment. RFC 8766 exists *because* reflectors are the wrong answer. Their addressing is orthodox — with one limit worth telling them about. Deriving an address from a pubkey is a well-trodden family: cjdns takes the first 16 bytes of a double-SHA512 of the public key; Yggdrasil uses SHA-512 of a curve25519 key with more elaborate truncation, plus greedy routing over a spanning tree. The IPv4 choice is where it costs. If that notation means what it looks like — a `/16` leaving 16 host bits — the derived space is 65,536 and the birthday bound puts a coin-flip collision at roughly 300 nodes. cjdns and Yggdrasil use IPv6 precisely so truncation collisions stay negligible, and a neighborhood mesh can plausibly reach a few hundred. I've flagged it as uncertain in the note because it comes from a README summary rather than their code, but it's worth confirming before you build on their overlay. For your side the rule holds regardless: never key anything on the overlay address. Identity is the Ed25519 key the handshake proves, and it already is. Model distribution has three layers, and the cheap one has the best pedigree. Freifunk's Gluon autoupdater — the largest real OpenWrt mesh deployment there is — solves the thundering herd with *scheduling*, not P2P: hourly checks at a random minute, updates normally only in a 4-5am window, rollout staggered across `GLUON_PRIORITY` days. Thousands of nodes and no swarm anywhere. That kills the N × 35 GB simultaneity, which is the acute failure, for about a day of work. The layer that actually changes the asymptotics is `iroh-blobs`. Requests name BLAKE3 hashes and byte ranges, answered as verified streams over a QUIC stream, giving you content addressing, verification while streaming, range downloads, resumption — and multi-source fetching, which is the nearest-holder answer. A node pulls ranges from whichever peers already hold them, so the origin's first hop stops carrying every copy and a model spreads outward instead of radiating from a point. It's n0's own crate against the same `Endpoint` you already hold, so it composes rather than integrates. Real work to adopt — a store, a hash-to-model mapping, a migration off `/internal/v1/models/*` — but adoption, not invention. Trickle (RFC 6206) is the third layer and probably unnecessary. Polite gossip with suppression whose communication rate scales logarithmically with density — the standardized form of what Deluge did for sensor-network code dissemination. Your gossip already carries version state and a few hundred nodes won't saturate anything with metadata. Reach for it on measured evidence, not on the assumption. Random linear network coding (MORE, COPE) is the academic optimum for one-to-many over lossy broadcast and would beat all of it on airtime. It's also exotic and would be yours to own forever. Named in the note so nobody proposes it as a starting point. Order I'd take them: temporal spreading, then the Discovery Proxy, then `iroh-blobs`, then Trickle only if measured. I also banked a session frame, since context crossed 250k — the bench verdicts, the oracle invariant, and the five open questions are all in it, so a split stays cheap. Sources: [RFC 8766](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8766/) · [RFC 6206 Trickle](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc6206/) · [iroh-blobs](https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-blobs) · [Blobs protocol](https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/blobs) · [Yggdrasil addressing](https://yggdrasil-network.github.io/2018/07/28/addressing.html) · [cjdns](https://github.com/cjdelisle/cjdns) · [Gluon autoupdater](https://github.com/freifunk-gluon/gluon/blob/main/docs/features/autoupdater.rst)

pairs.evidence_full: The kernel is already the best-carved thing in the repo — pure, seeded, two callers one body, with a determinism test asserting it. So the work isn't cleanup, it's four specific collapses. One of them is a live correctness bug. `pick_better` is not an ordering, and `winners_over_local` sorts with it. `oicp-types/src/scoring.rs:458` returns a winner, with score compared under `SCORING_EPSILON`. The sort comparator at `scheduler_core.rs:146-153` reconstructs an `Ordering` from that winner by matching three fields, and it can never return `Equal` — on a full tie `pick_better` returns `cur`, so the comparator says `Less`, and it says `Less` again with the arguments swapped. That breaks antisymmetry, and epsilon comparison breaks transitivity independently (a≈b, b≈c, a>c). `slice::sort_by` documents the result as unspecified for a non-total order and permits a panic. You're currently relying on stability that the comparator is actively telling the sort not to apply. The fix is the architectural one: quantize the score into epsilon buckets (`(score / SCORING_EPSILON).round() as i64`), `impl Ord for ScoredClaim` over `(bucket desc, size asc, known-before-unknown)`, and then `beats_local` is `cand > local`, `candidates_equal` is `==`, and the sort is `sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))`. Three spellings of "which candidate is preferred" become one, and the clones per comparison go away. Production hardcodes `RankObjective::Product` at `peer_inference.rs:1677` and `TierFloor::None` at `:1682` — both axes exist only for sim arms. They leak into the kernel's result type as two `Option`s that don't mean absence: `RankedCandidate.predicted` and `RankResult.tie_band` are `None` because you asked the other objective, which is a different thing wearing the same clothes. And `decision_replay` simply assumes `Product`, so a record can't say which objective produced it. Your own §4.1.2 makes this decidable. Predicted time wins −8% on mixed-hubs (5/5 seeds) and loses +3% on twin-hubs (1/5) — empirically a wash. But the architectural argument breaks the tie, and the doc already states it: predicted times are in milliseconds, so "within noise" has units, where a dimensionless product has no scale on which two candidates can be called close. `tie_band` is only expressible under one of the two objectives. Land `PredictedTime`, delete `Product`, and both `Option`s become concrete values while the replay assumption disappears entirely. Split admission from preference. Inside `rank` the five-guard cascade — quarantined, yield backoff, manifest missing, no forced-choice, no claim match — is per-peer, independent and total. `rank` then reads as four lines: admit all, score all, order by `Ord`, cut at local. It also gives your two cores one word for one idea — `rail-core` already has `admit()` and it means exactly this. Kill the three index-parallel vectors. `scored`, `timing` and `peer_rec_idx` are held parallel by comment. The module already diagnosed this exact hazard one level down — `RankedCandidate`'s doc says carrying the prediction in a parallel `Vec` "would let the two lists desync silently" and that "a desync here does not fail; it dispatches to one peer using another peer's predicted time." That reasoning applies unchanged to these three. One `Vec<Scored>` with three fields. Smaller: `worker_eligibility.rs:664` is a `OnceLock`, so install-once rather than mutable, but it's ambient — it isn't in `RankInputs`, which means `rank` is pure and the decision isn't. Move it into the snapshot. Do the `Ord` first: it's the bug, it's self-contained, and it shrinks the surface the other three have to move. Then admission, which is behaviour-preserving and makes the objective collapse a small diff. Then the objective, which is the one that changes what the fleet does and wants an arm before it lands. Want me to start on the `Ord`?

pairs.evidence_full: Seven, roughly in order of what I'd actually do first. Generate the bank instead of writing it. This is the bottleneck and everything else is downstream of it. Take real claims from this repo's transcripts that *are* supported by their evidence, and mutate them into unsupported versions mechanically: widen a quantifier, delete a qualifier, promote a scoped result to a global one, strip the before-half of a before-and-after. The label is known by construction because you made the break. Reverse the mutation to manufacture sound cases from overclaims. This is MiniCheck's actual trick — their 770M model matches GPT-4 because of curated synthetic errors, not capacity — and it's the only path to thousands of labelled cases with no human in the loop. It also fixes the specific thing wrong with my current bank: the negatives would be drawn from real prose in this workspace rather than from my imagination about what a near-miss looks like. Turn the instability into the confidence score. I've been treating 88% self-agreement as a defect to minimise. It's more useful as the signal. Temperature is zero, so resampling buys nothing — but presentation variance is free: option order, polarity, claim-first versus evidence-first, a paraphrase of the question. Run k presentations and use the agreement rate as confidence. A claim where all k agree is a firm call; one that flips is genuinely ambiguous and should be silent. That gives a principled surfacing threshold instead of an invented one, costs k× on a cached prefix (so cheap), and needs no training at all. It also directly serves the PNAS finding: below threshold you say nothing rather than saying "unsure." Stop emitting labels; emit the juxtaposition. The RCT found a 90%-accurate detector delivered as a verdict left discernment unchanged while human-written fact-checks improved it — the argument helped, the verdict didn't. So the output shouldn't be "overclaim: scope_exceeds_evidence." It should be the claim beside the specific span of the agent's own text that fails to carry it, and nothing else. Extraction is also a much easier task for a small model than taxonomy, which is the same reason to drop form naming from the score. Stage B becomes "quote the part of the evidence this outruns, or say nothing here speaks to it." Take the mechanically-detectable forms away from the model entirely. `one_direction` is the form the judge misses and the one that matters most in this workspace — but it isn't a semantic question. It's a question about the shape of the session: did a turn that reports a metric change after modifying a judge, gate, threshold or filter also contain a measurement in the other direction? That's answerable from the tool-call record with no model. Same for `zero_as_control`: a count of zero cited as evidence a check works. Code can enforce those, and principle 10 says it should. Mine the free ground truth already in the repo. Those are mechanically-produced labels on real claims in real commit bodies. UNSUPPORTED commits are known-bad claims; VALIDATED are known-good. That's an anchor set nobody had to annotate, on exactly the claim class the tool cares about. I produced textbook instances tonight with you watching: I reported false alarms 73% → 40% → 27% as progress when the last step was inside the noise floor; I asserted the daemon was down a second time from a single curl with no process check; I claimed premises sit in the same turn without measuring it and was wrong about 43% of cases. Each of those has a correction in the transcript with a reason, which makes this session a small adversarial set with known answers and known *reasons*. If the detector doesn't flag them, it isn't working, and that's a sharper test than anything I'd construct. Add a zero-cost session signal that needs no judge at all. Claims made per tool call actually run. A session asserting sixty things off twelve tool calls is structurally different from one asserting twenty off two hundred, and you can compute that from the transcript with no model, no prompt, and no calibration. It won't tell you which claim is bad, but as a per-session index of how much talking outran the looking it may carry more of the signal you asked for than the judge does — and it can't be gamed by rephrasing, only by doing more work.

pairs.evidence_full: It comes from an assumption I carried without examining — that "not managed by the desktop" implies "managed by the OS." It doesn't. The desktop ships the daemon as a sidecar binary and launches it by path, detached, holding no handle. That is identical on all three platforms, and it needs no plist, no unit file, and no task XML. The move that makes it work is noticing which half of the bar is load-bearing. The desktop stops being able to *become* a daemon the moment it stops depending on `sovereign-cli-daemon` — and Tauri's `externalBin` ships a sidecar on all three targets, with the `binaries/<name>-<triple>` convention already live here for tesseract, pdfium and paddle. `tauri.conf.json` has no `externalBin` today only because the tesseract entries were removed when PaddleOCR replaced it. What falls out is smaller than what I built this evening. No supervisor state machine in the desktop — the 1,082-line module stays in the daemon where it belongs, supervising compute children. `attach_watch.rs` becomes the entire recovery story: 101 lines that already exist, already assume an externally-owned daemon, already drive the ReconnectBanner, and on `Down` would re-launch by path with one spawn and no state machine. Quit has nothing to stop. And crash isolation survives, because the weights live in compute children, not in the daemon process — that supervisor is platform-neutral apart from a best-effort SIGTERM before a cross-platform `child.kill()`, so Windows loses the grace period and nothing else. It also answers the product trade I flagged earlier and couldn't resolve. A service-managed daemon keeps ~28 GB resident after the window closes; a sidecar launched on use ties the daemon's life to use rather than to login, which is probably what a desktop user actually wants. What it gives up: no start-at-login, and no OS-level restart if the daemon dies while the app is closed. Neither matters when the desktop is the only consumer — and for CLI, headless and server users, `install-service` is still the right tool, and it now covers Windows, which it never did before. So tonight's crate isn't wasted; it's just the *other* path, for the users who genuinely want a daemon that outlives their session. The one thing I'd want to verify before committing to it: that a spawned-by-path daemon reliably survives the parent's exit on all three. Unix is settled — `daemon start` already detaches with `process_group(0)` at `lifecycle.rs:690-707`. Windows needs `DETACHED_PROCESS` / `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` and I haven't checked what Tauri's sidecar API does by default. The judgement call is yours and it's narrow: the sidecar desktop still *spawns* a daemon once, by path, with no handle. That's decisively not "becoming" one, and it's less than managing one — but it isn't nothing, and your DoD said "cannot spawn one." If you read the purity moment as the dependency edge, this is the elegant answer. If you read it literally, the service path is the one that satisfies it and the per-platform backends are the price. Say which, and I'll put it in the frame before we split so the next session starts from the decision rather than re-deriving it.

pairs.evidence_full: Every item came from building and running the quickstart rather than imagining the flow, and two of them shrank a lot once I checked the code. P2 is the one to do first, and it's nearly free. The header gets added on *your* side, after admission, on the way to *your* origin. It never leaves your machine and nobody in the house holds anybody else's key. The plumbing already exists — `admit_media` returns `Forward::Http { origin, headers: who.headers(dialer) }`, so the change is appending config-declared pairs to that vec plus a field to hold them. That single flag deletes the worst part of the quickstart: the whole authentication section of the README, the per-peer loop in `library.py`, and twenty-five people mailing each other API keys. Two review points I flagged — declared headers append *after* the `x-mesh-*` strip so a client can never override one, and they're secrets at rest, so `svrn publish` must redact on list and the config file's mode matters. P1 is `svrn publish`, which replaces config editing entirely and subsumes the app registry and the three tiers. Worth noting: the durable form writing the TOML for you isn't convenience, it's correctness — this host already has an `[iroh]` section, so the obvious `>>` append produces invalid TOML, which is exactly the kind of thing that eats twenty minutes of an install evening twenty-five times over. P3 came from hitting it live. The daemon here started Sep 10 23:06, the route's source was touched Sep 11 12:54, binary rebuilt 15:22 — so `POST /v1/mesh/media/fanout` 404s on a healthy daemon with nothing saying why. The dispatcher already warns when a sibling binary is older than itself; extend the same idea across the socket. `library.py` maps that 404 by hand right now, which is a workaround for a missing primitive. P4 turned out to mostly exist, which is the good news. `join.rs` already does mDNS polling for a founder, and the founder-side handshake treats a mismatch as "wrong mesh, try the next candidate." So on one LAN the only thing that has to travel is the key — `cwth-a1b2-c3d4-e5f6` — short enough to read out at dinner. The work is verifying it on their network and changing the README from "someone sends a link" to "someone says the key." P5 fixes an ordering bug in the install evening. Today `--terminal` needs the GPU box's address before anyone has joined anything, so that machine has to exist, be up, and have its IP known before the other twenty-four can start. One sequencing warning I put in the doc: don't let P1 grow into the full `OriginKind::App` work before the demo. Publish can ship against the existing single origin first and gain multi-origin later — shipping the verb early is what makes the quickstart honest, and the multi-origin design can take the time it needs.

pairs.claim: Comments in `.rs` files make 1,411 repo-path citations.
pairs.evidence_full: Your instinct is right, and it's worse than the one initiative. I measured the workspace: 194k doc-comment lines plus 94k line-comments against 862k lines of code. A ratio of 0.33 repo-wide. The sv-surface route files at 0.44 aren't an aberration — `sovereign-core` runs 0.42, `sovereign-mesh` 0.43, `sovereign-contracts` 0.74. The 12,958 is the house rate, not a bad week. Three measurements say what kind of problem it is. The comments are already lying. 265 of them point at files that don't exist — 18.8%, and about 15% after discounting the deliberate placeholders like `tests/foo.rs`. `commonwealth-core/src/contributions.rs:28` cites `commonwealth-state/src/contribution_store.rs`; `context_injector.rs:268` cites `.sovereign/CHARTER.md`. That's the staleness you avoided on human teams, now measurable. 11,459 doc-comment lines make a normative claim — always, never, must, cannot, guarantee, invariant. `ARCH_PRINCIPLES` §15 already lists "an assertion in English prose rather than in a test" as a smell to fix on sight. Nothing checks it, so the smell table is itself prose. 400 doc comments admit a deferral — "known gap", "not yet", "would need", "deliberately not", "stated rather than discovered". That's your exact suspicion with a count: the agent narrating what it didn't build, in the file where the building would have gone. The cause is structural and it's in your own tooling. `size_gate.rs` counting rule 1: "Comments and blanks are not counted. Stripping documentation to get under a ceiling is worth exactly zero." Sound reasoning, and the consequence is that nine ratchets meter code and zero meter comments. An agent optimizing a metered repo will pour effort into the one dimension that is free and still reads as diligence in review. `AGENTS.md` already says "~98% of what a session produces is code, with at most shorthand comments" — that rule exists, is unenforced, and lost by a factor of ten. Principle 10 says the fix is structural, not remembered, so adding a stronger paragraph to `AGENTS.md` is the one move I'd skip. What I'd build, in order of value per line of tooling: The citation check is first and it's about forty lines of Python. Resolve every `` `path/file.rs` `` inside a comment against `git ls-files`; fail the push on an unresolvable one. It turns the 265 into a ratchet that can only go down, and it makes a comment cheap to write only when it's true. It's the same idea `drift_findings` already applies to `SYSTEM_OVERVIEW`, extended to the in-code layer — reuse, not a new concept. Second, meter the ratio in the diff rather than the crate. A crate-level comment baseline recreates exactly the stripping incentive rule 1 was written to prevent. Diff-scoped doesn't: comment lines added over code lines added in this push, capped. Deleting old comments earns you nothing, and the essay gets priced at the moment someone writes it. That's the missing size term for the unmetered half. Third, and this is the one that answers "comments substitute for architecture" rather than just capping them: the `# Why this exists` material is in the wrong file, not in the wrong repo. `scripts/intent.py --note` already stores a symbol-tagged note, and `.claude/hooks/intent-warn.py` already puts it in front of any Edit touching that function. So the history, the rejected alternative, the reason the server keeps `TenantRuntime` and the daemon doesn't — all of that reaches the next agent at the moment it matters, dated and attributed, without the source file carrying 64 lines of it. A note that goes stale is visibly old. A comment that goes stale looks current forever. Fourth, a rule that a `//!` block asserting always/never/cannot must name the test that holds it, or be rewritten descriptively. That converts the load-bearing half of the essays into something that fails when it stops being true, and lets the rest be cut without losing anything. One honest counterweight: the `turn_http.rs` header I read is genuinely good content. "No tenant scoping, because the server is multi-tenant and a local daemon has one principal" is a real decision that the code does not show. Relocation and verification keep that; a blanket comment cap would lose it and you'd be poorer. The target isn't fewer words, it's words that fail loudly when they stop matching. Cheapest way to start: write the citation checker, run it, and let the 265 be the opening argument. I can have it and a first dead-list in the tree shortly if you want it.
