The watcher stays an observer, and recovery attaches to the next thing the user actually does — `ensure_reachable` as a precondition of a turn — with the existing button as the explicit path. Write it into the bar as: the client may bring a backend up at a moment a user action asks for one, and may never do so on a timer or a health signal. The case for auto-restart is real and worth stating. In the sidecar topology there is no service manager, so a crash leaves a dead backend and a user looking at a banner; "down" is never a user goal, and the app already knows the path. Principle 12 even says calling something is not owning it, so one more call looks free. It is not free, for four reasons that the principles name directly. The trigger is unfit for the job. `attach_watch` declares `Down` after three missed probes at five-second intervals — about fifteen seconds. The daemon's own readiness budget is 120 seconds (`parse_ready_timeout`, `lifecycle.rs:883`), launchd and systemd wait ten before relaunching, Task Scheduler sixty. So `Down` routinely means "starting", not "dead". Spawning on it either loses the `RunLock` race and exits as noise, or races a start that was already underway. Principle 6 closes on exactly this: absence of a response is not evidence of absence — distinguish "answered: no" from "did not answer". Making the signal fit would mean teaching the client about pids, locks and load phases, which is principle 12's "hand a component's gap to a neighbour and that neighbour knows its internals forever". It creates a second restarter. Where a service is registered, the OS already does this: launchd `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false` throttled at ten seconds, systemd `Restart=on-failure` with `StartLimitBurst=5` per 600s, Task Scheduler `RestartOnFailure` five times at one-minute intervals. Two implementations of "when does the daemon come back", with different thresholds, is principle 8. The sharper cost is that an app-driven kickstart routes around systemd's burst brake, so the one platform with a crash-loop limiter loses it. Principle 6's whole subject is that degrading quietly spends the caller's trust instead of their attention. A backend that died four times in two minutes is information the user needs; an auto-respawn renders it as a flickering banner. And it is step one of the sequence the bar already predicts — "a dependency-edge gate passes clean through someone adding a retry, then a backoff, then a health check, then a restart policy; nobody re-supervises in one commit." Shipping the retry deliberately means the census half of the instrument opens with a finding we chose, and the bar loses standing to refuse the second and third. Principle 12 is explicit that a retry is the ownership side of the line, not the calling side. There is also nothing to watch it fail with. Principle 5 asks for the input that makes a check red before it lands; an auto-restart policy needs a crash-loop harness to have ever been observed behaving, and there isn't one. What the middle path costs, named: in a sidecar topology with no service registered, a backend that dies while the app idles stays dead until the user does something, and that user pays one bring-up plus readiness on their next turn. Attach bootstrap measured 1,008/490/322 ms; a cold load is longer. That is the price of not owning it and it is small. Three things follow if you take it. `attach_restart_daemon` should stop erroring when no service is registered and fall back to `ensure_reachable`, so the button works in both topologies. And the fifteen-second threshold wants raising above the OS's own recovery window regardless of this decision; today it cries wolf during every normal restart. One interaction worth weighing before you answer: if the desktop installs the service at setup on all three platforms, the no-service topology barely exists and this question mostly dissolves. That is a product call about whether a user who never wants a background daemon can opt out.

pairs.claim: The client's bring-up spawns detached — `process_group(0)` on unix, `DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` on Windows — so a daemon it starts survives the app quitting.
pairs.evidence_full: Two things are true here, and one of them is a mistake I made. The factual half first: the Windows blocker you're remembering was real, and it closed yesterday. `install_service` no longer hard-errors on Windows — `fe5a85cc3` added `install_schtasks` and the Scheduled Task XML, so there are three backends now. But it is cross-compile verified only. `cargo xwin check` proves it builds; nobody has run it on a Windows host to confirm Task Scheduler accepts the XML. So the platform blocker is closed in code and open in evidence, and I made a default rest on the open half. That is the thing you're smelling. The concession that matters more: I under-weighted the OS-agnostic path when I wrote that amendment, and I conflated two requirements that deserve separating. "Available to the mesh after you close the window" is already covered by the OS-agnostic mechanism, one code path, all three platforms. What the service actually adds is narrower than I implied: availability across reboot and logout, without anyone opening the app. I wrote the amendment as though the service were the only way to honour what you said, and it isn't — it's the way to honour the last mile of it. And there's a real hit inside my commit, not just in the framing. The silent-daemon branch calls `stop_service()`. My reason is that it rolls back a registration made seconds earlier to avoid a port race — but the bar says a desktop that stops a service is managing a daemon again, and a reason is not an exemption. That branch shouldn't exist. So the mechanism isn't wrong, the ordering and the default are. The sidecar plus client bring-up is what lets the 1,990 lines die, it's OS-agnostic, and it's one mechanism to verify on Windows instead of two. The service is the reboot-persistence upgrade on top, and it should not be a silent default while its Windows leg has never been run. What I'd do: drop the automatic registration from `maybe_restart_into_supervised` and the `stop_service` rollback with it, keep `service_adoption.rs` — the resolution order is tested and it's the right code — behind an explicit call, and add a `DEFAULTS_LEDGER` row whose flip condition is a real Windows host confirming the task registers and the daemon comes back at logon. Then the sidecar work proceeds as the thing that actually removes the supervision. The one call that's yours: with the service off by default until Windows is verified, a desktop-only user contributes to the mesh until they reboot, not across it. Acceptable as the interim, or do you want the service default-on now and the Windows verification treated as a release blocker instead?

pairs.claim: `config_setup.rs:256-299` shells `launchctl kickstart -k gui/<uid>/com.svrnmesh.daemon` and `systemctl --user restart svrnmesh` today.
pairs.evidence_full: Assessment, with one trace still running. `sovereign-desktop` links no crate that can assemble or host a daemon. Checkable by `cargo tree`, enforceable by the layer ratchet already in the repo, and it goes red structurally rather than by a count that lags. The four `Launch` variants that drag `sovereign-cli-daemon` into the desktop binary — `Daemon`, `Worker`, `ComputeChild`, `RpcWorker` — all exist only because the desktop can *become* a daemon. `ComputeChild`'s own doc says "ANY binary that can be `current_exe` must handle this variant"; a desktop that never spawns compute children is not such a binary. 1,990 production Rust lines of daemon lifecycle in the desktop crate, of which about 271 survive. The survivors are exactly the right ones: `attach_watch.rs` (101 lines, already assumes the daemon is externally owned), `kickstart_daemon` (46), `request_daemon_reload` (43), the readiness probe (69), `attach_restart_daemon` (12). The in-process `EmbeddedDaemon` + `RunLock` ownership in `state.rs` is 365 lines; child supervision is 645; the mobile-host supervisor another 90; `smoketest`'s crash-isolation subprocess 302, which belongs in the daemon since the daemon is what loads models. The replacement is already written. `install-service` writes a launchd LaunchAgent with `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false` and a systemd user unit with `Restart=on-failure` plus `StartLimitBurst=5`. `ReconnectBanner.svelte` already renders an attach-down state driven by `attach_watch`. The OS-managed topology isn't new code — it's the path the desktop already takes when it finds a daemon running, which is how I ran every measurement today. One risk retires immediately: the supervisor state machine doesn't need deleting. `sovereign_compute::supervisor` is consumed by `sovereign-cli-daemon` at `daemon_cmd/bootstrap.rs:592` and `discovery_policy.rs:24` for its own compute children. The desktop is a caller, not the owner — a daemon supervising its compute children is correct; a desktop supervising a daemon is not. *Windows is the hard blocker.* There is no service backend at all — no unit template, no `contrib/windows/`, no prebuilt Windows CLI, and `install_service` hard-errors on the platform. The desktop *does* ship Windows (NSIS installer, `scripts/build-desktop-windows.sh`). And the supervisor is platform-neutral — one `cfg(unix)` in 1,082 lines — so supervised-child is currently the only way a Windows user gets a daemon at all. Delete it without a Windows story and the platform breaks outright. The mitigation that keeps the bar honest is `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]` for the daemon crate: green on macOS and Linux, Windows a declared exception with a `DEFAULTS_LEDGER` row and a review-by date, then the Windows backend as its own rung. *Nothing installs the service.* Not the DMG, not the NSIS installer, not `install.sh`, not the app — it's a manual `svrn install-service` from a shell whose `PATH` gets baked into the unit. A desktop that no longer spawns a daemon must install the service itself or refuse to start with a remedy. The first is the product answer and it's cheap: both units are per-user (`~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `~/.config/systemd/user`), so no elevation. That's the one place the desktop *should* touch the daemon — once, at setup, not every launch. *No socket activation anywhere.* "Client connects, daemon starts" doesn't exist on any platform, and cold model load budgets 120s. Under a resident LaunchAgent this is better than today, where quitting kills the child and the next launch reloads the model — but it's a product decision you should make deliberately: a resident daemon holds GB of RAM after the window closes. *Smaller gaps that become user-visible once the service is the only daemon:* `daemon status` never consults the service manager, so it can't say whether the daemon is supervised or why it's down; `uninstall-service` is documented in two places and does not exist; neither platform survives a reboot before login (LaunchAgent, no systemd linger). Whether anything in first-launch genuinely requires the desktop process to hold the models, the store, or a Runtime rather than ask a daemon — that trace is still running, and it decides whether macOS and Linux can go pure or need a first-run exception. The journey test setting `SOVEREIGN_FORCE_LOCAL=1` is the tell I want explained before I'd commit to a sequence. Sequencing I'd propose, subject to that: finish the correctness waves (each removes a reader either way), have the desktop install the service at setup, delete supervision and the in-process path on Unix, move the deps behind `cfg(windows)` and mint the layer bar, then build the Windows backend and take the bar green everywhere.

pairs.evidence_full: The audit was worth running — two findings contradicted decisions already made in this tree, and I'd have shipped both. The secrets convention was already litigated, against us. But `mcp/auth.rs:3-9` says flatly "never from the on-disk `config.toml` (ARCH §7)", and `secret_store.rs:3-16` keeps MCP tokens 0600 under `~/.svrnmesh/secrets/` — after full keychain due-diligence across mac, Linux, Windows and headless — specifically "so the secret never rides along with anything the app shares, syncs, backs up, or gossips to a mesh peer." Which in a house of twenty-five gossiping peers is exactly the failure that would have found us. The good news is it makes both rungs *cheaper*, not more expensive. Config declares only the header name, shaped like the existing `McpAuthConfig`; the value lives 0600 in the secrets dir. And hm-2's whole shape already exists: `PUT /v1/mcp/servers/{name}/token` is "set a secret over the loopback socket instead of hand-editing TOML." Both rungs are now copies rather than designs. hm-3 cited a mechanism whose own doc rejects the thing I proposed. I said "extend the dispatcher's stale-sibling warning across the socket." That warning compares artifact mtimes *within one directory* and explicitly bails when binaries sit in different locations — every socket case. And `sibling.rs:22-27` is a written rejection of the socket version: SHA stamping "flaps in exactly the loop that matters — dirty trees stamp `-dirty` on both sides while their code differs." I cited it as a model without reading its rationale. Committed as `10b549b05`. The campaign still has four rungs and the ladder order didn't change — hm-1 first, because it deletes a practice rather than typing.

pairs.claim: The readable unit is `oplog` (236) + `commonwealth-rail-core` (1,282) + `commonwealth-rail` (954) = 2,472 code lines, tests excluded.
pairs.evidence_full: Your instinct is right, and the discriminator against transport is sharper than size. That is WireGuard scale, and it is the same class of object: peers converging without a server. `commonwealth-transport` is 1,124 lines and loses anyway, because it wraps iroh — it does not own its wire format, so you cannot version it wholesale. Declaring a closed set over someone else's protocol is a promise you don't control. Most of the WireGuard properties are already there, which is why this is a ratification rather than a rewrite. The act set is three variants and closed. `actor` *is* the hex public key that signed, so the identity table and the authorization table are one table — the same collapse cryptokey routing makes. A newer envelope version is refused and reported as `RailGap::NewerVersionLine`, never downgraded or negotiated. And the best parts are unrepresentable rather than checked: `Correct.replacement` is a `Payload` and not a `RailAct`, so nested correction cannot be written; `Seal` carries no actor and no range, so sealing someone else's history has no syntax. The no-I/O, no-clock property is held by the dependency list plus three `[[forbid]]` blocks in `ARCH_LAYERS.toml`, not by anyone remembering. What the call would actually cost you is `RingVerifier`. That trait is crypto agility in the precise sense Linus was praising the absence of — a runtime-selectable verification scheme, with a `name()` on it so the trace can say which one ran. Its doc defends it as symmetry with `RingSigner`, and the asymmetry it fixed was real, but symmetric seams are two where zero would do. The two are not the same kind of thing: `RingSigner` exists so the daemon holds the key and `commonwealth-api` carries no crypto dependency, which is key custody, not scheme choice. Verification needs no secret, so it has no such justification. The version-preserving move is to narrow the signer to `fn sign(&self, msg: &[u8]) -> [u8; 64]` — the rail builds `ring_op_message` itself, the signer only holds the key — and delete `RingVerifier` and `Ed25519Verifier` outright, taking the `&dyn RingVerifier` parameter off `admit` and `compact`. That puts the scheme in exactly one place, keeps custody split, and makes the asymmetry the trait was added to prevent unrepresentable instead of balanced. Ed25519 + the one message construction then move under the envelope's `v`, and changing either is a new protocol version, whole. The thing that will undo this if you don't watch it is above the line, not in it: `commonwealth-work` is 2,924 lines and `commonwealth-state` 1,501, both already larger than the rail, both depending on `rail-core`. Rail concerns regrow there. The bar is falsifiable and you already have the instrument — cw-lift physically lifted the package once and found the missing exports. Lift it again after the trait deletion and have someone who hasn't read it describe the convergence rule from a single sitting.

pairs.claim: And here's the one that'll actually land with a coliving community, which I didn't expect to find in your code: `RevocationProposal` collects votes and `has_majority` decides — a single node cannot evict a peer on its own.
pairs.evidence_full: That audience diagnosis is the most useful thing you've said, because it rules out the obvious answer. They'll nod, agree it's cool, and build the home server anyway, because the home server is legible and the mesh is a lecture. Whatever you extract has to beat nginx-plus-Tailscale-plus-Caddy on *effort*, not on virtue. Virtue gets you two weeks. The layer I'd extract is the authenticated service bus, and its pitch is one sentence: you never write a login page again. Concretely it's three things you already have. `HttpBridge` mints a localhost port that reaches someone else's service. `spawn_admitting` decides who gets through on a verified Ed25519 key. And `Forward::Http` carries that verified identity into the origin as `X-Mesh-Member`, `X-Mesh-Node`, `X-Mesh-Pubkey` — with any client-supplied `x-mesh-*` header stripped first, so a forged one can't reach the app. Think about what that does for a dilettante. They write a twenty-line Flask app. Normally it lives on `localhost:5000` and dies there, because sharing it means a box, a domain, a cert, and accounts — and accounts are where every house project dies. The chore rotation needs to know who you are. The grocery list needs to know who added the oat milk. The door camera needs to know who's asking. Every one of those hits the auth wall and gets abandoned. With this, their app reads a header. No OAuth, no passwords, no user table, no session cookies, no Auth0 free tier. And because it's HTTP headers over a byte splice, it works in Flask, Express, a Go binary, or a shell script with `netcat`. That's what makes it a substrate rather than a framework — it's language-agnostic because it refuses to be clever. The sleeper feature is that your laptop is a server. For dilettantes, "deploy" is where projects go to die. If `python app.py` on the machine where you wrote it is already reachable by the whole house, the loop from idea to multiplayer is one command and zero infrastructure. That's the thing that'll get five of them building in the first week. Removing someone is a proposal, not a command. That's not a feature, it's a *political stance*, and it's the same one the house already runs on. A home server has an admin; someone owns it, someone pays for it, someone's the asshole when it's down, and everything breaks when they move out. That's not a technical problem, it's a social one, and it's why coliving infrastructure rots. Your membership model dissolves it. For a house of cool people who are suspicious of centralization but keep accidentally building it, "no admin, and eviction is a vote" is the thing they'll repeat to each other. What not to extract, since you asked for the layer specifically. Not corpora, not enrichment, not RAPTOR — too much surface, and none of it is why they'd start. Not the mesh join ceremony as a concept they have to learn; someone sends a link, you click it, you're in. Not the ALPN table — `expose` should mint the protocol and never mention it. The test I'd hold it to: can someone build their first house app without learning a single new noun beyond "the house" and "expose"? If they have to know what a node or a peer or an endpoint is, you've extracted too much. Don't lead with the model server, even though it's your strongest technology. With one GPU the mesh version is identical to their plan with extra steps, and they'll notice. It becomes compelling the moment there are two, and the honest wedge isn't "decentralized" — it's the queue. Twenty-five people sharing one 4090 is a waiting room. The other half is social: someone can contribute their gaming PC while they're asleep without handing anyone root on it. Let that arrive in month two, after the service bus has already made five of them productive. The five-minute demo I'd build, because this audience buys with their hands: someone writes a stupid app — who's home, what's in the fridge, whose turn for dishes — types one command, and everyone's phone opens it at a stable name and it already knows who they are. Then unplug the WAN and show it still works. That last beat is the whole argument, made in four seconds, with no slide. Two traps worth naming before you pitch it. The membership question has real teeth in a house: if anyone can invite anyone, someone's ex has a key, and the revocation vote is the answer but only if it's actually wired and they know about it — lead with it rather than discovering it later. And their instinct will be to run one always-on box anyway, for the things that must be up when laptops are closed. That's fine and you shouldn't fight it. Just make sure it joins as a peer rather than a hub, because the moment it becomes the place everything lives, you've built their home server with extra steps and the mesh is decoration. Want me to fold this into the design note as its own section? It's a different audience than the lightning-mesh engineering piece, so it might deserve a separate file — something like a house-substrate brief you could actually hand to the collaboration.

The daemon publishes on `GET /status` under `process.build` the tuple its startup banner already computed and discarded. `exe_mtime` is what decides, because every crate here is `version.workspace = true` and both sides of the incident read `0.6.0`. I went with the fuller design rather than the cheaper one I'd floated, and reading the acceptor changed where the real constraint sits: `resolve()` runs once per connection, but each *bi-stream* opens its own TCP, so per-request demux across a connection is free. pairs.claim: And `App` gets its own trust class, so admitting a housemate to your chore app isn't the same decision as admitting them to your tensor RPC.
pairs.evidence_full: Both are in `docs/internal/DILETTANTE_MESH_DEMO.md`. The work item came out cleaner than I expected because the inventory answered most of the design. Three things already exist that shape it. `MemberCapabilities.origins` is already a *set*, not a scalar — `candidate_of` reads `origins.contains(&OriginKind::Media)`, so the gossip model anticipated more than one origin from the start. `fan_out` is already generic over its row payload with two in-tree consumers, media and federated knowledge search, so the primitive isn't media-shaped — only its exposed route is. And `iroh_identity_forward` already parses request heads and rewrites `x-mesh-*` headers, so per-request routing has machinery. The constraint that decides the shape is `OriginKind`'s own doc comment: a closed set, where "every kind has one ALPN and one acceptor route, so a new kind is a new variant beside a new route, never a string." Which forces the real question — are house apps a closed set? Someone writing a chore app at 1am can't add an enum variant, an ALPN, and a route and recompile. By your own rule, open sets are registries. So the resolution keeps both halves honest: one new closed-set variant `OriginKind::App`, on one new ALPN `cwth/app/0`, whose route demultiplexes by name against a registry in config. The closed set stays closed — one variant, one ALPN, one route. App names become config data that changes without a code change. The genuinely hard part is that `resolve(alpn, dialer)` is called once per *connection*, before any request is read — so the app name isn't available when the forward target gets decided. I laid out three ways out and recommended a third `Forward::HttpByName` variant that demuxes per request using the head-parsing that already exists, stripping a client-supplied app header exactly as forged `x-mesh-*` headers are stripped today. Its cost needs stating in the doc comment or someone will misread it later: an app connection's *target* becomes a per-request decision, which is a weaker statement than the acceptor makes today. The admission decision — is this dialer allowed the App class at all — still happens once per connection on the verified key. Only the which-app demux moves. I also carried forward the test that matters, tied back to the oracle problem in the other doc: a dialer admitted to `cwth/app/0` must still be refused `cwth/rpc/0` and `cwth/media/0`. Separate trust classes are only real if there's a failing input that proves it. One thing worth knowing before you build it — the hack works today. Point `media_origin` at your Flask app instead of Jellyfin and `/v1/mesh/media/fanout` becomes a generic house-wide fanout, since it takes an arbitrary path, method, headers and body. Mislabeled but functional, and useful for proving the stories out before committing to the design.

pairs.evidence_full: Landed in `01831c013`, report-only. The trend is the finding, and it's worse than the sv-surface snapshot suggested. Aggregate comment lines per code line on *added* lines, by window: 0.27 on 2026-06-10, 0.40 on 08-09, 0.44 on 09-03, 0.49 on 09-08. Up 81% in three months, monotone across every window I sampled, against a stock of 0.33 — so new code is landing at half again the existing density and pulling the stock up behind it. Commits carrying at least one file where added comments exceed twice the added code went 23% to 39% over the same span. The median commit's worst file sits at 1.83 comment lines per code line; p90 is 15.0, and the worst in the range is 46. The sweep over the last 200 commits, 171 of which touch `.rs`: `comment-ratio` above 0.5 fires on 78%, `inline-comment` above ten lines per file on 62%, `dead-citation` on 2%. Two of those can't become gates in the shape I proposed. Raising the comment-ratio bar doesn't rescue it — 0.75 gives 67%, 1.0 gives 60%, and even 3.0 still fires on 35%. There is no threshold that separates the pathological from the normal, because the pathological *is* the normal here. A gate firing on four commits in five gets `--no-verify`'d inside a week, which your own `pre-push.sh` header already names as how gates die. So comment-ratio and inline-comment belong in `size-gate`'s shape — a per-crate baseline that may only fall, starting wherever you are — not as a threshold. Inline-comment is the one exception worth a hard bar: above 50 added `//` lines in a single file it fires on 6% of commits, and 50 body comments in one commit is defensible as "stop." `dead-citation` is the one I'd promote to blocking today, and the measurement inverted my reasoning about it. There are 170 dead cited paths in the tree — my first rough pass said 265 and over-counted, the engine's placeholder filter and ancestor resolution are stricter. I assumed they were rot from renames. They aren't: 86% name a path with no add-event anywhere in history. That's §11.1 violated inside a comment, which is precisely your "the agent spends its energy on the comment" — it writes a citation that looks checkable and never checks it. The diff gate catches them at 2 per 171 commits with no false positives in the sample, which is the birth rate; the standing 170 is a separate one-time burn-down, not something a ratchet reaches. On the build itself: two new decider kinds in `co-arch.py`, and `inline-comment` needed no new code at all — it's the existing `count` kind with a lookahead, which is the reuse §19 asks for. Seven planted cases, each rule with both a violation and a clean control. `--range A..B` runs deciders only, no model call, nothing persisted. One thing I found that isn't mine: the live profile's self-test fails on `uncited-symbol` — confirmed pre-existing by stashing my patch. §11.1 is currently unenforced at the commit hook, which is probably related to how 170 invented citations got in.

The rings, innermost first. | Ring | What runs | Cost per iteration | Data it needs | | 0 | the byte re-check plus every corruption class as pure Rust tests in sovereign-eval, generated from a banked harvest | seconds, cargo test with a filter, zero inference | a harvest file per corpus; the faithfulness obsidian seeds are already HarvestItem-shaped | | 1 | span-binding rescore over banked transcripts | seconds to a minute, zero inference | one chaos run per corpus whose harvest writes segments plus sealed-pool chunk ids and hashes | | 2 | chaos-monkey banks on both tiers, nightly | about an hour per bank per machine | the banks that exist plus one on uap-blue-book-scans for real OCR garble | | 3 | every fleet turn in normal use, continuously | free, it is dogfooding | the flip-soak telemetry journals already capture turns; add segments and pool identity to what they write | Ninety percent of iterations happen in ring 0. It validates the instrument against labels by construction and it never touches a model, so a change to the re-check is judged in the time a test takes. Ring 1 is where the timidity axis lives, because demotion is a model decision and only real transcripts have it. Ring 2 exists to refresh ring 1's bank when the generator changes. Ring 3 is what gets you to the large n. At roughly seven claims a turn and perhaps half admitted, a turn yields about three or four admitted spans. The 200-span rung is one nightly bank. The 2,000 rung is a week of fleet turns on two machines. The 20,000 rung is either months of dogfooding or a rented pod for a weekend, and it is never 20,000 chaos-monkey questions. Synthetic Stream B spans do not count toward the bound at all. They validate the instrument, and a bound computed on constructed cases would be the instrument grading itself. Heterogeneity, so the objective is not overtrained. The byte check cannot overfit, it is deterministic. What can overfit is the demotion path, tuned until the timidity axis looks good on the bank it was tuned on. Four guards, three of which cost nothing: Two generator tiers on two machines, never a single model's failure style. One corruption kind and one corpus held out entirely, under the same peek-budget ledger the mechanism-fidelity lane already keeps. Engineering, in order, with the ring each unblocks. Write the content hash at the three index sites. Carry corpus chunk id and hash on the resolved address, at the streaming site and in the display resolver's signature, which today takes bare chunk texts. Unblocks ring 0's address classes. The re-check function and five new witness variants in the adversarial generator. Bench harvest and flip-soak journal write segments plus sealed-pool identity. Span-binding rescore in the chaos-monkey rescore path. Stale revision waits on the watcher retaining prior revisions. That class is never-ran until then, and it says so. pairs.claim: The mitigation is the SEP pattern turned one notch further: the publisher replicates the atlas (`mesh_sharing = true` on the claim index, `false` on the text) so retrieval happens locally on the reader's node, and only the fetch of a cited paragraph hits the publisher.
pairs.evidence_full: Most of this moonshot is already on disk in the shape of custody flags, a watcher, and a ledger. The new part is one ledger row kind and a settlement layer on top of it. Here is how it would run. The outlet becomes a node, not a website. The FT runs a sovereign daemon with two corpora. The archive is the parent, shipped exactly the way SEP ships today: `query_sharing = true`, `mesh_sharing = false`. Peers can run federated searches and get cited snippets back, but the bytes never leave the newsroom's machine. The second corpus is the newsroom's own `wikipedia-newsworthy`: watcher-driven, event-bullet grain, a rolling tracked set that gets refreshed in place as a story develops and drops out of daily attention after the window closes. That recipe is 60 lines of TOML and the only thing that changes for the FT is the acquire block. The watcher is the thing print never had: a story is not a frozen artifact anymore, it is a tracked entity with revisions, and a correction is an in-place refresh with a ledger entry rather than a paragraph in italics on page A2 that nobody reads. Editorial rigor stops being a norm and becomes a data structure. The recipe is the subscription. `svrn meshapp install ft` resolves the registry entry, verifies the sha256, and pulls the recipe plus the FT's own meshapp bundle. The entitlement is not a paywall cookie. It is the grant mechanism that already exists for lending a corpus to peers: ephemeral, revocable, scoped to a set of nodes. The FT's daemon answers federated queries only from nodes holding a live grant. Revoking is one row, not a cookie invalidation cascade across CDNs. The ledger is the meter, and that is the token. The unit of value in an LLM is the token because it is fungible, metered at the point of use, and priced by whoever owns the weights. Journalism has never had that unit. Pageviews measure attention, not use. The turn-stage ledger already appends a row from the code that executes each stage, at the moment it executes, with residual rows always present so a mechanism that forgot to record itself shows up as unclaimed time. The retrieval ledger already accounts every chunk as considered, admitted, or dropped with a named reason. Add one row kind, custodian, and every answer carries an honest statement of whose evidence was admitted: | custodian | considered | admitted | cited in answer | dropped: reason | | ft.newsroom | 9 | 4 | 3 | 5: not_selected_by_objective | | nyt.newsroom | 6 | 2 | 2 | 4: below_noise_floor | | wikipedia-newsworthy | 12 | 1 | 0 | 11: superseded_by_primary | A cited row is the token. The publisher sets the price per cited claim, settlement happens in aggregate, and nobody needs to know who the reader was. The reader's own reading history stays `scope = local` and structurally never leaves the machine. The kind-vs-delta invariant that already fails the eval when a step's declared kind disagrees with the observed delta is the same invariant that stops a publisher billing for chunks that were considered and dropped. This is where it stops being a distribution channel and starts being a product print cannot make. Atlas atoms carry provenance: extractor, source document, signal kind. So the FT's claim about a central bank decision and the NYT's claim about the same decision are distinct atoms with distinct custody, and where they disagree the enrichment pipeline mints a tension atom. The reader asks what happened and gets a synthesis whose ledger says three claims from the FT, two from the NYT, one tension between them, and the tension is a first-class object they can open. The thing the outlets are competing on, sourced and verified claims, becomes the metered unit rather than the thing that gets scraped for free the moment it is published. Now the trade-offs, because the moonshot has three holes. Federated search leaks the query to the publisher node. Every question a reader asks the FT's daemon is visible to the FT. The publisher then sees which paragraphs were cited, which is exactly what it bills on, and nothing else. Settlement needs signed rows, and today the trust anchor is sha256 plus a reviewed PR. The registry file names ed25519 signing as the next step and it would have to land before any of this carries money. A ledger row that a node can forge is a pageview with extra steps. A grant holder re-serving to non-grant peers is the free-rider case and the answer is the same: signed rows and revocable grants, not DRM. The grounding gate is load-bearing in a way it is not for the SEP. A small local model hallucinating about Kant is embarrassing. Hallucinating a quote from a central banker under an FT custodian row is a libel with a receipt. The custodian row has to be admitted only for spans the segment verdict resolved to a chunk, never for the draft's paraphrase, and that is a stricter rule than the pipeline enforces today. What exists and what does not, in inventory order. Exists: the query/replicate split, scope, grantable plus the ephemeral grant store, the newsworthy watcher, the registry with corpus dependency, the turn-stage ledger with honest residuals, the retrieval ledger with drop reasons, atoms with provenance, tension atoms, the update manifest URL. Does not exist: the custodian row kind, signed ledger rows, any settlement, a relay that hides the asking node's identity, and an editorial revision ledger on the watcher's in-place refresh. Four of those five are small. Settlement is the one that is a company, not a commit.

pairs.evidence_full: The thing Linus praised isn't clean code — it's that WireGuard refused the option. About 4,000 lines against OpenVPN's ~600k, but the line count is downstream of two decisions: no crypto agility (one suite, versioned wholesale, so there is no negotiation state machine at all) and no configuration surface (a peer is a public key plus an allowed-IPs list; cryptokey routing makes the routing table *be* the authorization table instead of two subsystems that have to agree). "I've skimmed it" is the actual compliment. Skimming was enough to form a judgment. The uncomfortable measurement: this workspace is 890,193 code lines across 148 size-gate keys, tests counted separately. That is larger than the thing he called a horror. `sovereign-cli-llm` alone is 93k, `corpus-engine` 77k, `sovereign-core` 57k. None of those can be skimmed by anyone, ever. So the transferable bar isn't 4k lines, it's this: one competent outsider reads the subsystem end to end in a sitting and afterward holds its state machine in their head. You have crates in that range already — `commonwealth-transport` at 1,124, `commonwealth-rail-core` at 1,282, `commonwealth-knowledge` at 1,217, `sovereign-work-atlas`. The mesh transport layer is the closest structural analogue, because it's the same kind of object: a peer protocol where two ends must agree without a human present. The obstacle is in your own compass. Principle 9 — closed sets are enums, open sets are registries — is the agility principle. Every registry is a place you chose "this can change without a code change" over "this can be held in one head." WireGuard's whole move was to refuse that trade: it declared the set closed and versioned the closed thing. Both positions are defensible, but a subsystem cannot be skimmable and extensible at the same time, and right now the repo's default answer is extensible. `DELETION.md` has the evidence: noun convergence netted +33,132 first-party Rust lines. The one change that moved the other way was deleting a dead loop, at −3,789. If you want this to be more than an aspiration, the move is to pick one subsystem and declare its concept set closed — no registry, no config knob, version the whole thing when it changes — then measure whether it lands under the skim bar. Transport is the honest candidate because it's small now and because the protocol case is exactly where negotiation surface metastasizes. Which one do you want to hold to it?

Deleting doc comments deletes executable tests. There are 901 `unsafe` occurrences against 72 `SAFETY:` comments — a ratio that's already wrong in the direction you'd be making worse. The fourth is the one I'd weigh most. `symbols` returns doc comments verbatim. I called it on `TurnRequest` and got back the field docs in full — including the line saying absent-on-the-wire means `Grounded` and `Grounded` is omitted when writing, with `turn_request_wire_form` named as the test that holds it. That is wire-contract information not derivable from the type, and it arrives at the one moment an agent needs it. The whole read-budget doctrine in `AGENTS.md` — don't Read a file before calling `symbols` — rests on `symbols` returning enough to make the Read unnecessary. Strip `///` and every call returns a bare signature, agents go back to reading files, and you re-pay the 74.3k the /context audit was fighting. In this codebase the item docs aren't decoration; they're the retrieval payload. You'd be deleting your index to tidy the shelf. Where your extreme survives contact cleanly is the inline class. 93,727 lines of `//` inside function bodies. `symbols` doesn't return them, `code_search` doesn't rank on them, nobody sees them who isn't already in the file with the code in front of them — which is exactly the reader your principle says should be reading the code. A comment may only be a citation or a contract: it names a test, a symbol, a spec section, or a wire invariant. Under that rule the 64-line `turn_http.rs` header collapses to about six lines, because the tenant-scoping paragraph, the phase history and the "Known gap, stated rather than discovered" section are all narrative — and that last section is precisely your complaint, an agent writing down what it chose not to build in the file where building it would have gone. pairs.evidence_full: The kernel is already the best-carved thing in the repo — pure, seeded, two callers one body, with a determinism test asserting it. So the work isn't cleanup, it's four specific collapses. One of them is a live correctness bug. `pick_better` is not an ordering, and `winners_over_local` sorts with it. `oicp-types/src/scoring.rs:458` returns a winner, with score compared under `SCORING_EPSILON`. The sort comparator at `scheduler_core.rs:146-153` reconstructs an `Ordering` from that winner by matching three fields, and it can never return `Equal` — on a full tie `pick_better` returns `cur`, so the comparator says `Less`, and it says `Less` again with the arguments swapped. That breaks antisymmetry, and epsilon comparison breaks transitivity independently (a≈b, b≈c, a>c). `slice::sort_by` documents the result as unspecified for a non-total order and permits a panic. You're currently relying on stability that the comparator is actively telling the sort not to apply. The fix is the architectural one: quantize the score into epsilon buckets (`(score / SCORING_EPSILON).round() as i64`), `impl Ord for ScoredClaim` over `(bucket desc, size asc, known-before-unknown)`, and then `beats_local` is `cand > local`, `candidates_equal` is `==`, and the sort is `sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))`. Three spellings of "which candidate is preferred" become one, and the clones per comparison go away. Production hardcodes `RankObjective::Product` at `peer_inference.rs:1677` and `TierFloor::None` at `:1682` — both axes exist only for sim arms. They leak into the kernel's result type as two `Option`s that don't mean absence: `RankedCandidate.predicted` and `RankResult.tie_band` are `None` because you asked the other objective, which is a different thing wearing the same clothes. And `decision_replay` simply assumes `Product`, so a record can't say which objective produced it. Your own §4.1.2 makes this decidable. Predicted time wins −8% on mixed-hubs (5/5 seeds) and loses +3% on twin-hubs (1/5) — empirically a wash. But the architectural argument breaks the tie, and the doc already states it: predicted times are in milliseconds, so "within noise" has units, where a dimensionless product has no scale on which two candidates can be called close. `tie_band` is only expressible under one of the two objectives. Land `PredictedTime`, delete `Product`, and both `Option`s become concrete values while the replay assumption disappears entirely. Split admission from preference. Inside `rank` the five-guard cascade — quarantined, yield backoff, manifest missing, no forced-choice, no claim match — is per-peer, independent and total. That's `admit(peer, req, now) -> Result<Admitted, ExclusionReason>`, and pulling it out lets you test it exhaustively against the closed `ExclusionReason` enum instead of through a 200-line loop. `rank` then reads as four lines: admit all, score all, order by `Ord`, cut at local. It also gives your two cores one word for one idea — `rail-core` already has `admit()` and it means exactly this. Kill the three index-parallel vectors. `scored`, `timing` and `peer_rec_idx` are held parallel by comment. One `Vec<Scored>` with three fields. Smaller: `worker_eligibility.rs:664` is a `OnceLock`, so install-once rather than mutable, but it's ambient — it isn't in `RankInputs`, which means `rank` is pure and the decision isn't. Move it into the snapshot. Do the `Ord` first: it's the bug, it's self-contained, and it shrinks the surface the other three have to move. Then admission, which is behaviour-preserving and makes the objective collapse a small diff. Then the objective, which is the one that changes what the fleet does and wants an arm before it lands. Want me to start on the `Ord`?

Your reason is that availability is a property of the node, not a convenience for the app. A node that only exists while someone has a window open isn't a mesh member; it's a client that occasionally appears. It also reframes the opt-out correctly. "Don't run when I'm not using the app" is not a lifecycle preference, it's a membership one — the user is saying they don't want to contribute while away. That belongs in the contribution settings ("don't lend this machine"), where it's honest and reversible, not in a service checkbox where it looks like a startup-items preference and quietly removes the node from the mesh. And it kills the idle-exit knob I floated last turn: a daemon that exits when nobody is looking cannot answer a peer, so that mechanism is incompatible with the goal. It sharpens the re-spawn answer rather than complicating it. The scenario that most needs automatic recovery is a crash at 3am with nobody at the machine — and the app is closed, so an app-side retry covers exactly the case where a human is already present to press a button. pairs.claim: Its problem is that it rides `_commonwealth._tcp.local.` — link-local multicast.
pairs.evidence_full: Then the work is smaller and sharper than an integration: you already have the substrate, and it has the wrong carrier. Look at `commonwealth-discovery`. Alongside node discovery it carries an application registry — `MdnsDiscovery::advertise_app(app_id, port)` and `browse_apps(app_id)`, described in the crate docs as letting "a process on this node announce a service other nodes can find, on the same daemon and the same wire." That is an application substrate, already built, already shipping. And lightning-mesh deliberately does not bridge L2 across nodes; broadcast containment is the point of their design. So your app layer works beautifully on one router's LAN and goes silent at the first hop into their mesh. So "be a fluent substrate on a lightning-mesh network" reduces to one concrete piece of work: give `advertise_app`/`browse_apps` a routed carrier. What makes that cheap is a decision you already made. The crate docs say it outright: "Discovery is a hint, never an authorization." Everything mDNS returns is an unauthenticated claim about a name and an address; the join key decides whether the attempt succeeds. Because discovery carries no trust, you can swap its transport without touching the trust model. This is a plumbing change, not a security redesign — and that property is worth protecting deliberately, because the tempting shortcuts all erode it. Their `.mesh` DNS is the carrier I'd pick, over their CRDT or iroh's own pkarr discovery. It's routed, it's native to their world rather than something you impose, and it's the only option where a non-Commonwealth client benefits — a browser on the mesh can reach `jellyfin.nodename.mesh` without knowing what Commonwealth is. The CRDT would give you convergence and liveness for free but couples you to their state model to solve a problem you've already solved. Iroh's discovery sidesteps lightning-mesh entirely, which also means it gets none of the mesh's locality. One concrete bug you'll hit on the way: `advertise_app` builds its host as `format!("{}.local.", hostname())`. Carrying those TXT records over a routed namespace doesn't help if the address inside them is a `.local` name that doesn't resolve off-segment. The record needs their overlay address — `10.254.<blake3(node_id)>` — or the `.mesh` name, not the local hostname. Now the fluency test, which is your own bar. A known workflow should be three shell lines, and if it isn't, the friction is a bug in the CLI rather than something to wrap ceremony around. We spent a chunk of today pasting a base32 dial string between two machines by hand. On a network that already has a node registry and a DNS namespace, that ceremony *is* the friction bug. The fluent version is that a Sovereign daemon on a lightning-mesh router finds other Sovereign daemons by name, and admission is still the join key — discovery got easier, trust did not get weaker. That distinction is the whole design, and it's the thing to write down before any code so nobody later "simplifies" it into mesh-membership-implies-Commonwealth-membership. What you'd actually be offering that network. Your ALPN table is the app surface, and each protocol carries its own trust class: inference and federated retrieval over `cwth/client/0`, tensor-split RPC over `cwth/rpc/0`, someone's Jellyfin over `cwth/media/0`, guests fenced onto `cwth/guest/0` with a listener that doesn't trust loopback. One GPU box anywhere on the mesh serves every node — which you've already validated, at $0.08, when a pod holding zero corpora answered a query with five chunks served by RuggedFox at 0.73s. And today's numbers argue for this deployment shape specifically. The media path over a relay topped out near 100 Mbit/s aggregate and decayed from 87 to 55 over ten minutes with three reconnects. Over an 802.11s backhaul those peers are link-local. The substrate story and the performance story point the same direction for once. The overlap I'd chase first is MCP. They already name it — "MCP: AI agent control plane using mesh discovery for resource coordination" — and you have 33 MCP tools and a daemon that serves them. That's not two projects needing a bridge; that's the same idea arriving from two directions, and it's the cheapest place to find out whether their model of agent-plus-mesh matches yours before you commit to anything structural.

pairs.claim: If you want the aggressive version I'd take it as three commits — SPDX-preserving inline purge, then the citation gate in `pre-push.sh`, then the `//!` essays cut to what the gate lets through.
pairs.evidence_full: Priced honestly, the extreme breaks four things, and three of the breaks are cheap to route around. The fourth is the one that would actually hurt, and it's specific to this repo. The split, measured: 146,060 lines of `///` item docs, 93,727 of `//` inline, 47,396 of `//!` module headers, against 860,372 of code. What a blanket delete costs. 2,321 files carry an SPDX AGPL header — that's a licensing regression wearing a style change's clothes, and it's one mechanical exemption. 518 code fences live in doc comments, 456 of them in the default-rust class that actually compiles; `quality/campaigns/conformance.toml` seats `--doctests` in CI, and the cw-lift campaign already caught three that failed to compile while the suite read green. Deleting doc comments deletes executable tests. There are 901 `unsafe` occurrences against 72 `SAFETY:` comments — a ratio that's already wrong in the direction you'd be making worse. The fourth is the one I'd weigh most. `symbols` returns doc comments verbatim. I called it on `TurnRequest` and got back the field docs in full — including the line saying absent-on-the-wire means `Grounded` and `Grounded` is omitted when writing, with `turn_request_wire_form` named as the test that holds it. That is wire-contract information not derivable from the type, and it arrives at the one moment an agent needs it. The whole read-budget doctrine in `AGENTS.md` — don't Read a file before calling `symbols` — rests on `symbols` returning enough to make the Read unnecessary. Strip `///` and every call returns a bare signature, agents go back to reading files, and you re-pay the 74.3k the /context audit was fighting. In this codebase the item docs aren't decoration; they're the retrieval payload. You'd be deleting your index to tidy the shelf. Where your extreme survives contact cleanly is the inline class. 93,727 lines of `//` inside function bodies. `symbols` doesn't return them, `code_search` doesn't rank on them, nobody sees them who isn't already in the file with the code in front of them — which is exactly the reader your principle says should be reading the code. They carry the highest staleness risk and produce the least. "Delete all `//` inside function bodies, forbid new ones, SAFETY and SPDX exempt" is a defensible policy that takes 94k lines off in one commit and costs you nothing a tool was using. But I think there's a rule that gets more of what you want than a ban does. Don't budget words — change what a comment is permitted to be. A comment may only be a citation or a contract: it names a test, a symbol, a spec section, or a wire invariant. Under that rule the 64-line `turn_http.rs` header collapses to about six lines, because the tenant-scoping paragraph, the phase history and the "Known gap, stated rather than discovered" section are all narrative — and that last section is precisely your complaint, an agent writing down what it chose not to build in the file where building it would have gone. There are 400 of those admissions in the tree. A ban on comments doesn't stop that agent; it just makes it write the same paragraph in the commit body, where the median is already 34 lines on a two-file change. A citation rule stops it, because "deliberately not implemented" has nothing to cite. That rule is also mechanically checkable, which a word budget isn't. A comment containing a claim word — always, never, must, cannot, guarantee, invariant, 11,459 lines carry one today — must name a test or a symbol in backticks, and the named thing must resolve. That single check enforces §7.2's prose-assertion smell, kills the essays as a side effect, and fixes the 265 dead path citations, without touching the payload `symbols` depends on. So: yes to deleting the inline class outright, no to deleting `///`, and the forbidding is better aimed at narration than at comments.

A claim opens at the commit that was HEAD when it was made and closes at the commit when it came due. `git diff T0..T1` is the evidence, and for a promise that diff *is* the adjudication: "I'll wire the Stop hook next" becomes a bounded mechanical question over a bounded object. No retrieval, no judge, no model. I measured whether git has the resolution for that, because the idea is worthless if a session sits between two commits a day apart. Over the last 40 sessions: 1,031 commits landing inside session windows, mean 25.8 per session. The deeper thing this fixes is one I'd half-buried. I was treating the transcript's tool log as the golden for what the agent did, but the agent chooses which commands to run and which output to show. It sits outside the agent's narrative entirely, so it closes most of the `echo "test result: ok"` hole for anything about code state: an agent can lie about what it saw, but not about what the tree became. The gap, and it's real: 6 of those 40 sessions committed nothing at all. Investigation, review, and planning sessions land no commits, and for those git is silent. Then the harness's file snapshots, for work that never reached a commit. Then the session's own tool output, for claims about runs rather than code. Then you, for what none of the three can settle. Each rung is weaker and more forgeable than the one above, and the adjudicator should always take the highest rung that can answer. pairs.evidence_full: It comes from an assumption I carried without examining — that "not managed by the desktop" implies "managed by the OS." It doesn't. The desktop ships the daemon as a sidecar binary and launches it by path, detached, holding no handle. That is identical on all three platforms, and it needs no plist, no unit file, and no task XML. The move that makes it work is noticing which half of the bar is load-bearing. `Command::new(path).spawn()` links nothing. The desktop stops being able to *become* a daemon the moment it stops depending on `sovereign-cli-daemon` — and Tauri's `externalBin` ships a sidecar on all three targets, with the `binaries/<name>-<triple>` convention already live here for tesseract, pdfium and paddle. `tauri.conf.json` has no `externalBin` today only because the tesseract entries were removed when PaddleOCR replaced it. What falls out is smaller than what I built this evening. No supervisor state machine in the desktop — the 1,082-line module stays in the daemon where it belongs, supervising compute children. Quit has nothing to stop. And crash isolation survives, because the weights live in compute children, not in the daemon process — that supervisor is platform-neutral apart from a best-effort SIGTERM before a cross-platform `child.kill()`, so Windows loses the grace period and nothing else. It also answers the product trade I flagged earlier and couldn't resolve. A service-managed daemon keeps ~28 GB resident after the window closes; a sidecar launched on use ties the daemon's life to use rather than to login, which is probably what a desktop user actually wants. What it gives up: no start-at-login, and no OS-level restart if the daemon dies while the app is closed. Neither matters when the desktop is the only consumer — and for CLI, headless and server users, `install-service` is still the right tool, and it now covers Windows, which it never did before. So tonight's crate isn't wasted; it's just the *other* path, for the users who genuinely want a daemon that outlives their session. The one thing I'd want to verify before committing to it: that a spawned-by-path daemon reliably survives the parent's exit on all three. Unix is settled — `daemon start` already detaches with `process_group(0)` at `lifecycle.rs:690-707`. Windows needs `DETACHED_PROCESS` / `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` and I haven't checked what Tauri's sidecar API does by default. The judgement call is yours and it's narrow: the sidecar desktop still *spawns* a daemon once, by path, with no handle. That's decisively not "becoming" one, and it's less than managing one — but it isn't nothing, and your DoD said "cannot spawn one." If you read the purity moment as the dependency edge, this is the elegant answer. If you read it literally, the service path is the one that satisfies it and the per-platform backends are the price. Say which, and I'll put it in the frame before we split so the next session starts from the decision rather than re-deriving it.

pairs.claim: `rank` then reads as four lines: admit all, score all, order by `Ord`, cut at local.
pairs.evidence_full: The kernel is already the best-carved thing in the repo — pure, seeded, two callers one body, with a determinism test asserting it. So the work isn't cleanup, it's four specific collapses. One of them is a live correctness bug. `pick_better` is not an ordering, and `winners_over_local` sorts with it. `oicp-types/src/scoring.rs:458` returns a winner, with score compared under `SCORING_EPSILON`. The sort comparator at `scheduler_core.rs:146-153` reconstructs an `Ordering` from that winner by matching three fields, and it can never return `Equal` — on a full tie `pick_better` returns `cur`, so the comparator says `Less`, and it says `Less` again with the arguments swapped. That breaks antisymmetry, and epsilon comparison breaks transitivity independently (a≈b, b≈c, a>c). `slice::sort_by` documents the result as unspecified for a non-total order and permits a panic. You're currently relying on stability that the comparator is actively telling the sort not to apply. The fix is the architectural one: quantize the score into epsilon buckets (`(score / SCORING_EPSILON).round() as i64`), `impl Ord for ScoredClaim` over `(bucket desc, size asc, known-before-unknown)`, and then `beats_local` is `cand > local`, `candidates_equal` is `==`, and the sort is `sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))`. Three spellings of "which candidate is preferred" become one, and the clones per comparison go away. Production hardcodes `RankObjective::Product` at `peer_inference.rs:1677` and `TierFloor::None` at `:1682` — both axes exist only for sim arms. They leak into the kernel's result type as two `Option`s that don't mean absence: `RankedCandidate.predicted` and `RankResult.tie_band` are `None` because you asked the other objective, which is a different thing wearing the same clothes. And `decision_replay` simply assumes `Product`, so a record can't say which objective produced it. Your own §4.1.2 makes this decidable. Predicted time wins −8% on mixed-hubs (5/5 seeds) and loses +3% on twin-hubs (1/5) — empirically a wash. But the architectural argument breaks the tie, and the doc already states it: predicted times are in milliseconds, so "within noise" has units, where a dimensionless product has no scale on which two candidates can be called close. `tie_band` is only expressible under one of the two objectives. Land `PredictedTime`, delete `Product`, and both `Option`s become concrete values while the replay assumption disappears entirely. Split admission from preference. Inside `rank` the five-guard cascade — quarantined, yield backoff, manifest missing, no forced-choice, no claim match — is per-peer, independent and total. That's `admit(peer, req, now) -> Result<Admitted, ExclusionReason>`, and pulling it out lets you test it exhaustively against the closed `ExclusionReason` enum instead of through a 200-line loop. It also gives your two cores one word for one idea — `rail-core` already has `admit()` and it means exactly this. Kill the three index-parallel vectors. `scored`, `timing` and `peer_rec_idx` are held parallel by comment. The module already diagnosed this exact hazard one level down — `RankedCandidate`'s doc says carrying the prediction in a parallel `Vec` "would let the two lists desync silently" and that "a desync here does not fail; it dispatches to one peer using another peer's predicted time." That reasoning applies unchanged to these three. One `Vec<Scored>` with three fields. Smaller: `worker_eligibility.rs:664` is a `OnceLock`, so install-once rather than mutable, but it's ambient — it isn't in `RankInputs`, which means `rank` is pure and the decision isn't. Move it into the snapshot. Do the `Ord` first: it's the bug, it's self-contained, and it shrinks the surface the other three have to move. Then admission, which is behaviour-preserving and makes the objective collapse a small diff. Then the objective, which is the one that changes what the fleet does and wants an arm before it lands. Want me to start on the `Ord`?

pairs.claim: `svrn mesh media fanout /System/Info/Public` — one request to everyone, one attributed row each, and it needs no API key so it works before anyone has set one up.
pairs.evidence_full: A holder authenticates to its own media server, and nobody in the house ever holds anyone else's key. That's the whole change, and it's the one that made the demo viable. Jellyfin's API keys are per-server, so federating twenty-five libraries used to mean twenty-five people each holding twenty-four other people's credentials — which nobody sane does, and which would have killed the demo in the room. Now each person declares their own key on their own machine, and their daemon adds it after the caller is admitted as a member, on their side of the wire. The part that wasn't in the plan and mattered most: appending a header isn't enough to make it authoritative. Append-only leaves the viewer's copy *ahead* of the holder's in the request head, and origins disagree about which one wins on a duplicate name — so a viewer could have picked the credential their own request ran under. A declared name now displaces the client's. Stripped first, appended last, exactly one on the wire. It's proven rather than asserted: `house_mesh_publish_roundtrip` runs two daemons over real iroh against an origin that returns 200 only when exactly one token line arrives with the holder's value. Same viewer, sending its own token, refused before the declaration and served after. I broke it two ways to confirm the test can see both failures — removing the append, and removing only the displacement — and both go red. Plus `svrn mesh media declare`, which reads the value from stdin so it never lands in shell history, stores it 0600, and never prints it back. What you bring to the house. `curl -fsSL https://svrnme.sh/install.sh | sh` — three prebuilt binaries, no clone, no Rust. And `~/dev/house-mesh`, two files, about 280 lines: the quickstart and `library.py`. Push that somewhere public and it's the only thing anyone reads. Nobody touches the monorepo. Per person, five minutes: install, `svrn setup --terminal http://<the-gpu-box>:9741` which downloads *nothing*, `svrn mesh join <key>`, one line in config for `media_origin`, and `printf '%s' "$KEY" | svrn mesh media declare x-emby-token`. The demo in the room is four beats. `svrn mesh media` — the house appears. `svrn mesh media alex` — a localhost URL that streams off Alex's disk with seeking intact. Then unplug the WAN and do it again. The line to say while that's happening: *you already wanted one model server. Now everyone also gets everyone else's media, and nobody writes a login page.* One thing to do before you walk in. None of this has met an actual Jellyfin. The wire is proven; the `/Items` query string and the stream path come from Jellyfin's API docs, not from a run. Stand up one Jellyfin, declare a key, and run `library.py check` then `list`. That's an hour, and it's the difference between a demo and an apology. What's honestly not ready. Nothing is pushed — that's your call. One app per person, because `media_origin` is still singular; the multi-origin design is written up but unbuilt, and it's what turns this from a media feature into the substrate. pairs.evidence_full: It piggybacks, but on the deterministic half of the verifier work rather than the model half, and the reason is the verifier research's own refutation result. The grounding verifier crossed honesty at 0.82 and competence at 0.12 with no threshold passing both, and the named cause was that a critic reading the generator's chunks has errors correlated with the generator's. Every experiment in the verifier economy prereg is about breaking that correlation. For a billable unit there is a cheaper answer than decorrelating a model: never let a model admit anything. The attested-records spec already draws that line for `attest verify`, which re-runs the two deterministic strata and deliberately skips the model strata because a check that needs a GPU is a second opinion, not a check. The custodian row sits on the same line. A model can hand a span `Unverified` and that is all it can do. Only the byte check, span verbatim at range in the custodian's corpus at its signed content hash, can admit. The model's error correlation is out of the billing path by construction, and the bench's job shrinks to two provable things: the byte check is complete against every way a span can be wrong, and the demotion path is not buying that completeness with silence. What makes it rigorous, in order of what it borrows: Instrument validation before any result is read. Labels by construction, the Stream B pattern: every corruption is mechanically checkable at a known site. The re-check must catch 100% of each negative class as a separate row with its own interval, because a pooled zero hides a class with five samples. Then the gate is run once with the range check deliberately disabled and must go red on every class. That log ships with the baseline. Six new corruption classes the taxonomy does not have, because none of it was written for a row that bills. Misattribution, which is verbatim bytes from custodian A billed to custodian B. Right words at the wrong address, which is the pool-index trap already documented on the `Grounded` variant. Address None reaching a row. Stale revision, which the newsworthy watcher's in-place refresh generates for real, and which means corrections, the product itself, break bindings. Poisoned pool, a chunk in the reader's sealed pool that is not in the custodian's canonical corpus, which the runtime resolver cannot catch and only the hash re-check can. And phrase-shortcut leak, measuring what the two-word shortcut admits. Fabrication at zero with the Wilson bound stated, and timidity non-regressed against the first-run baseline. A bench that reports only fabrication is satisfied by a node that bills nothing, and a row worth nothing to the custodian is the failure the honesty number would hide. Frozen transcripts, rescored offline. The chaos-monkey rescore pattern and the faithfulness lane's rule that every number is replayable from the JSONL alone. Turns run once on the SEC filings corpus, which is custodian-shaped and needs no signature, plus a newsroom corpus through the watcher so stale revision has a generator. What zero actually buys, stated now. By the rule of three, zero of two hundred bounds the rate at about 1.5 percent at 95 percent confidence. Zero of twenty thousand bounds it at 0.015 percent. The spec's 200-turn bar is the first rung of the instrument. The liability floor a publisher's counsel signs against needs the twenty-thousand row, and that is a rescore over banked artifacts, not twenty thousand inference runs, which is why the substrate is frozen transcripts. Five kill bars, each with a consequence that is a design change rather than a tuning: a fabrication above zero with the instrument green means a span reached a row without passing the check, so there is a second decider on the admission path to find and remove, not a threshold to move. A timidity regression over five points to reach zero means the honesty was bought with silence and goes in the defaults ledger as rejected. And if the stale-revision class cannot be generated, Phase 3's revision ledger on the watcher is a prerequisite for billing, not a nicety.

pairs.claim: 518 code fences live in doc comments, 456 of them in the default-rust class that actually compiles; `quality/campaigns/conformance.toml` seats `--doctests` in CI, and the cw-lift campaign already caught three that failed to compile while the suite read green.
pairs.evidence_full: Priced honestly, the extreme breaks four things, and three of the breaks are cheap to route around. The fourth is the one that would actually hurt, and it's specific to this repo. The split, measured: 146,060 lines of `///` item docs, 93,727 of `//` inline, 47,396 of `//!` module headers, against 860,372 of code. What a blanket delete costs. 2,321 files carry an SPDX AGPL header — that's a licensing regression wearing a style change's clothes, and it's one mechanical exemption. Deleting doc comments deletes executable tests. There are 901 `unsafe` occurrences against 72 `SAFETY:` comments — a ratio that's already wrong in the direction you'd be making worse. The fourth is the one I'd weigh most. `symbols` returns doc comments verbatim. I called it on `TurnRequest` and got back the field docs in full — including the line saying absent-on-the-wire means `Grounded` and `Grounded` is omitted when writing, with `turn_request_wire_form` named as the test that holds it. That is wire-contract information not derivable from the type, and it arrives at the one moment an agent needs it. The whole read-budget doctrine in `AGENTS.md` — don't Read a file before calling `symbols` — rests on `symbols` returning enough to make the Read unnecessary. Strip `///` and every call returns a bare signature, agents go back to reading files, and you re-pay the 74.3k the /context audit was fighting. In this codebase the item docs aren't decoration; they're the retrieval payload. You'd be deleting your index to tidy the shelf. Where your extreme survives contact cleanly is the inline class. 93,727 lines of `//` inside function bodies. `symbols` doesn't return them, `code_search` doesn't rank on them, nobody sees them who isn't already in the file with the code in front of them — which is exactly the reader your principle says should be reading the code. They carry the highest staleness risk and produce the least. "Delete all `//` inside function bodies, forbid new ones, SAFETY and SPDX exempt" is a defensible policy that takes 94k lines off in one commit and costs you nothing a tool was using. But I think there's a rule that gets more of what you want than a ban does. Don't budget words — change what a comment is permitted to be. A comment may only be a citation or a contract: it names a test, a symbol, a spec section, or a wire invariant. Under that rule the 64-line `turn_http.rs` header collapses to about six lines, because the tenant-scoping paragraph, the phase history and the "Known gap, stated rather than discovered" section are all narrative — and that last section is precisely your complaint, an agent writing down what it chose not to build in the file where building it would have gone. There are 400 of those admissions in the tree. A ban on comments doesn't stop that agent; it just makes it write the same paragraph in the commit body, where the median is already 34 lines on a two-file change. A citation rule stops it, because "deliberately not implemented" has nothing to cite. That rule is also mechanically checkable, which a word budget isn't. A comment containing a claim word — always, never, must, cannot, guarantee, invariant, 11,459 lines carry one today — must name a test or a symbol in backticks, and the named thing must resolve. That single check enforces §7.2's prose-assertion smell, kills the essays as a side effect, and fixes the 265 dead path citations, without touching the payload `symbols` depends on. So: yes to deleting the inline class outright, no to deleting `///`, and the forbidding is better aimed at narration than at comments. If you want the aggressive version I'd take it as three commits — SPDX-preserving inline purge, then the citation gate in `pre-push.sh`, then the `//!` essays cut to what the gate lets through.

pairs.evidence_full: That audience diagnosis is the most useful thing you've said, because it rules out the obvious answer. They'll nod, agree it's cool, and build the home server anyway, because the home server is legible and the mesh is a lecture. Whatever you extract has to beat nginx-plus-Tailscale-plus-Caddy on *effort*, not on virtue. Virtue gets you two weeks. The layer I'd extract is the authenticated service bus, and its pitch is one sentence: you never write a login page again. Concretely it's three things you already have. `HttpBridge` mints a localhost port that reaches someone else's service. `spawn_admitting` decides who gets through on a verified Ed25519 key. And `Forward::Http` carries that verified identity into the origin as `X-Mesh-Member`, `X-Mesh-Node`, `X-Mesh-Pubkey` — with any client-supplied `x-mesh-*` header stripped first, so a forged one can't reach the app. Think about what that does for a dilettante. They write a twenty-line Flask app. Normally it lives on `localhost:5000` and dies there, because sharing it means a box, a domain, a cert, and accounts — and accounts are where every house project dies. The chore rotation needs to know who you are. The grocery list needs to know who added the oat milk. The door camera needs to know who's asking. Every one of those hits the auth wall and gets abandoned. With this, their app reads a header. No OAuth, no passwords, no user table, no session cookies, no Auth0 free tier. And because it's HTTP headers over a byte splice, it works in Flask, Express, a Go binary, or a shell script with `netcat`. That's what makes it a substrate rather than a framework — it's language-agnostic because it refuses to be clever. The sleeper feature is that your laptop is a server. For dilettantes, "deploy" is where projects go to die. If `python app.py` on the machine where you wrote it is already reachable by the whole house, the loop from idea to multiplayer is one command and zero infrastructure. That's the thing that'll get five of them building in the first week. And here's the one that'll actually land with a coliving community, which I didn't expect to find in your code: `RevocationProposal` collects votes and `has_majority` decides — a single node cannot evict a peer on its own. Removing someone is a proposal, not a command. That's not a feature, it's a *political stance*, and it's the same one the house already runs on. A home server has an admin; someone owns it, someone pays for it, someone's the asshole when it's down, and everything breaks when they move out. That's not a technical problem, it's a social one, and it's why coliving infrastructure rots. Your membership model dissolves it. For a house of cool people who are suspicious of centralization but keep accidentally building it, "no admin, and eviction is a vote" is the thing they'll repeat to each other. What not to extract, since you asked for the layer specifically. Not corpora, not enrichment, not RAPTOR — too much surface, and none of it is why they'd start. Not the mesh join ceremony as a concept they have to learn; someone sends a link, you click it, you're in. The test I'd hold it to: can someone build their first house app without learning a single new noun beyond "the house" and "expose"? If they have to know what a node or a peer or an endpoint is, you've extracted too much. Don't lead with the model server, even though it's your strongest technology. With one GPU the mesh version is identical to their plan with extra steps, and they'll notice. It becomes compelling the moment there are two, and the honest wedge isn't "decentralized" — it's the queue. Twenty-five people sharing one 4090 is a waiting room. The other half is social: someone can contribute their gaming PC while they're asleep without handing anyone root on it. Let that arrive in month two, after the service bus has already made five of them productive. The five-minute demo I'd build, because this audience buys with their hands: someone writes a stupid app — who's home, what's in the fridge, whose turn for dishes — types one command, and everyone's phone opens it at a stable name and it already knows who they are. Then unplug the WAN and show it still works. That last beat is the whole argument, made in four seconds, with no slide. Two traps worth naming before you pitch it. The membership question has real teeth in a house: if anyone can invite anyone, someone's ex has a key, and the revocation vote is the answer but only if it's actually wired and they know about it — lead with it rather than discovering it later. And their instinct will be to run one always-on box anyway, for the things that must be up when laptops are closed. That's fine and you shouldn't fight it. Just make sure it joins as a peer rather than a hub, because the moment it becomes the place everything lives, you've built their home server with extra steps and the mesh is decoration. Want me to fold this into the design note as its own section? It's a different audience than the lightning-mesh engineering piece, so it might deserve a separate file — something like a house-substrate brief you could actually hand to the collaboration.
