The four `Launch` variants that drag `sovereign-cli-daemon` into the desktop binary — `Daemon`, `Worker`, `ComputeChild`, `RpcWorker` — all exist only because the desktop can *become* a daemon. `ComputeChild`'s own doc says "ANY binary that can be `current_exe` must handle this variant"; a desktop that never spawns compute children is not such a binary. 1,990 production Rust lines of daemon lifecycle in the desktop crate, of which about 271 survive. The in-process `EmbeddedDaemon` + `RunLock` ownership in `state.rs` is 365 lines; child supervision is 645; the mobile-host supervisor another 90; `smoketest`'s crash-isolation subprocess 302, which belongs in the daemon since the daemon is what loads models. The OS-managed topology isn't new code — it's the path the desktop already takes when it finds a daemon running, which is how I ran every measurement today. One risk retires immediately: the supervisor state machine doesn't need deleting. `sovereign_compute::supervisor` is consumed by `sovereign-cli-daemon` at `daemon_cmd/bootstrap.rs:592` and `discovery_policy.rs:24` for its own compute children. The desktop is a caller, not the owner — a daemon supervising its compute children is correct; a desktop supervising a daemon is not. *Windows is the hard blocker.* There is no service backend at all — no unit template, no `contrib/windows/`, no prebuilt Windows CLI, and `install_service` hard-errors on the platform. That's the one place the desktop *should* touch the daemon — once, at setup, not every launch. *No socket activation anywhere.* "Client connects, daemon starts" doesn't exist on any platform, and cold model load budgets 120s. pairs.claim: k=3 is a calibration threshold wearing a costume — claiming pays only above 75% confidence, and it's falsifiable, because if agents start abstaining on things they'd have got right, the abstention rate on later-confirmed facts says so.
pairs.evidence_full: Order updated: `.sovereign/features/bs-1-oplog/order.md`. Payoff table, measured cost envelope, UX, risk register, sequencing gate. The AA page states the property — rewards correct, penalizes hallucination, no penalty for refusing, −100 to +100 with 0 meaning as many right as wrong — but not the formula; that's in arXiv 2511.13029, which I didn't read, so I haven't cited it. The place the analogy breaks is the whole design. A benchmarked model can't choose its questions, so "abstain on everything" scores 0 and never wins. An agent writing a report chooses every claim it makes, so under AA's index alone the optimum is silence. The index gives you the integrity axis and nothing else; without a coverage term beside it you've built a machine that teaches agents to say less. So: +1 for a claim that holds, −3 for one that doesn't, 0 for an explicit hedge. Integrity is a *rate* over adjudicable claims, so splitting one claim into ten is neutral. Coverage is per unit of *work* — diff size, tool calls — not per report, so it can't be farmed by writing more prose. A promise abandoned mid-session with a reason costs 0; abandoned at session end it's −3, because the timestamp is what makes abandonment honest. An objective declared after the work scores `never-ran`, which kills retroactive goal-shrinking. And silence scores `never-ran`, not 0 — the explicit departure from AA, where all-abstain would outrank a session that made ten claims and got one wrong. Two holes I'd rather name than paper over. Padding a report with twenty safe claims does raise the integrity rate; that one is defended by you reading it, not by the metric, so the counts go on the card where padding is visible. And an agent that does excellent work and reports it in unadjudicable prose scores badly — a real false negative we should expect. Speed and cost, measured just now against the resident daemon rather than estimated. Forced-choice judge on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 24.9s on the first call after idle, 0.36–0.53s warm on a small prompt, 1.86s on a realistic 1,399-token evidence bundle, and 0.23s when the prefix is already cached. That last number is the lever — put the evidence first and the claim last and every claim after the first in a session rides the cache. It also got the realistic case right, marking "all tests pass" UNSUPPORTED against a `cargo check` log. Derived: 1–3s per turn inside the Stop hook, 25–60s per session for the full grade run detached at SessionEnd the way `distill` already runs, ~30 minutes one-off for the 40-session backtest. The real cost is ~70s of shared daemon slot per session, on a host where peers use the same daemon. What you see, most turns, is nothing. When the agent can't fix something it gets one line, not a wall: `unverified: "the only impl is ClaimSearcher" — a second impl is at .../scan.rs:212`. The risk is not the judge. It's the classifier: surface-form patterns put 87% of real report sentences in "other", and deciding what class a sentence is takes most of the budget. If that's unreliable every number downstream is noise, so the backtest measures classifier agreement against you before it computes a single grade. Second risk is that a backtest measures the grader, not the equilibrium — those 40 sessions ran ungraded, and how agents behave once graded is exactly what history can't tell us. That's why coverage is instrumented on day one rather than added when the drift shows up. Sequencing puts a gate where it belongs: record-only, then backtest, then you referee bars 1 and 2 before anything else is authorised. Steps 4 through 6 — the card, the coverage baseline, the hook — aren't approved by this order.

pairs.claim: `declare_scope` and `work_in_flight`, with TTLs and a spec that forbids history, is a "who is doing what right now" primitive with no server and no log.
pairs.evidence_full: The strongest thing you'd offer isn't a feature — it's that their network currently has nowhere to go, and yours is the payload that makes a mesh worth joining. But there's a more specific answer sitting in your own code, and it's better than the vision talk. Your traffic classes have been waiting for a router. `TrafficClass` has eight variants and the doc comment on it says, verbatim, "a future router may send different classes over different transports." Right now that abstraction mostly selects port and path policy — it's descriptive. Put it on lightning-mesh and it becomes load-bearing, because for the first time you own the router and the queue underneath it. Consider what those eight actually are. `ModelTransfer` is a 35 GB GGUF pull. `Inference` is latency-critical token streaming where 200ms is felt. `Media` wants sustained bandwidth and — per today's data — cares about nothing so much as not stalling past two seconds. `Gossip` is tiny, constant, and must never starve. On a single LAN those contend blindly and mostly get away with it. On an 802.11s backhaul shared across a neighborhood, a model pull will absolutely ruin someone's film, and nothing in the stack currently knows that it shouldn't. Mark those classes as DSCP, let babel and the wireless queue honor them, and you've turned an existing enum into real QoS without inventing a concept. That's the integration I'd be most excited to demo, because the abstraction already exists and the router is the missing half. The neighborhood GPU is the natural economic shape. OpenWrt routers cost forty dollars and are everywhere; GPUs cost thousands and are not. A realistic mesh is forty routers and two boxes with cards in them. Your serving policy, VRAM planning, slot management and fan-out already answer "who can serve this," and `detect_hardware` is built to report zero and log rather than refuse — so a router with no GPU joins as a client and a relay rather than a failed peer. That default was written for robustness and it happens to be exactly right for a deployment where most nodes will never serve anything. You validated the federated shape already: a pod holding zero corpora answering with five cited chunks from RuggedFox at 0.73s, for eight cents. `query_sharing` is neighborhood policy in one flag. It gates advertising rather than serving, per corpus. On a community mesh that's the whole governance model for shared knowledge — the library's catalog is federated-searchable by anyone on the mesh, the seed-library's growing guides are, your personal notes are withdrawn so completely that peers can't see they exist. No admin console, no roles, no ACL language. One boolean per corpus, and the mesh's knowledge surface is exactly what the people holding it chose to offer. Then the offline case, which I think is the real story. Their pitch is censorship resistance and no central controller. But a router mesh with no upstream is a road to nowhere — you can reach your neighbors and there's nothing at the other end. Sovereign is the part of this stack that keeps working when the uplink dies: inference is local, the corpora are resident, the media is on someone's disk three hops away. Every other application people would put on a community mesh degrades to a cache of the internet. Yours doesn't degrade at all, because it never needed the internet. If I were writing the joint pitch, that's the sentence: they built the road, you're what's worth driving to. `cwth/guest/0` is the visitor primitive, and it's underrated for this. Someone walks into range, gets a `sovereign://guest/…` bearer, asks questions of the mesh's model, and never becomes a member of anything. The listener that serves them explicitly doesn't trust loopback, so a guest can't reach the trusted client API — you built that fence for a different reason and it's exactly the shape a community network needs for drop-in access. The work atlas generalizes past code. It was built so agents don't collide on functions. On a community mesh the same thing coordinates people — who's ingesting, who's serving, who's mid-upgrade — with the same property that matters most: live state, not an audit trail nobody consented to. pairs.claim: I've been treating 88% self-agreement as a defect to minimise.
pairs.evidence_full: Seven, roughly in order of what I'd actually do first. Generate the bank instead of writing it. This is the bottleneck and everything else is downstream of it. Take real claims from this repo's transcripts that *are* supported by their evidence, and mutate them into unsupported versions mechanically: widen a quantifier, delete a qualifier, promote a scoped result to a global one, strip the before-half of a before-and-after. The label is known by construction because you made the break. Reverse the mutation to manufacture sound cases from overclaims. This is MiniCheck's actual trick — their 770M model matches GPT-4 because of curated synthetic errors, not capacity — and it's the only path to thousands of labelled cases with no human in the loop. It also fixes the specific thing wrong with my current bank: the negatives would be drawn from real prose in this workspace rather than from my imagination about what a near-miss looks like. Turn the instability into the confidence score. It's more useful as the signal. Temperature is zero, so resampling buys nothing — but presentation variance is free: option order, polarity, claim-first versus evidence-first, a paraphrase of the question. Run k presentations and use the agreement rate as confidence. A claim where all k agree is a firm call; one that flips is genuinely ambiguous and should be silent. That gives a principled surfacing threshold instead of an invented one, costs k× on a cached prefix (so cheap), and needs no training at all. It also directly serves the PNAS finding: below threshold you say nothing rather than saying "unsure." Stop emitting labels; emit the juxtaposition. The RCT found a 90%-accurate detector delivered as a verdict left discernment unchanged while human-written fact-checks improved it — the argument helped, the verdict didn't. So the output shouldn't be "overclaim: scope_exceeds_evidence." It should be the claim beside the specific span of the agent's own text that fails to carry it, and nothing else. Extraction is also a much easier task for a small model than taxonomy, which is the same reason to drop form naming from the score. Stage B becomes "quote the part of the evidence this outruns, or say nothing here speaks to it." Take the mechanically-detectable forms away from the model entirely. `one_direction` is the form the judge misses and the one that matters most in this workspace — but it isn't a semantic question. It's a question about the shape of the session: did a turn that reports a metric change after modifying a judge, gate, threshold or filter also contain a measurement in the other direction? That's answerable from the tool-call record with no model. Same for `zero_as_control`: a count of zero cited as evidence a check works. Code can enforce those, and principle 10 says it should. Mine the free ground truth already in the repo. `scripts/evidence-verdict.py` runs a commit's cited test at that commit and again with the source hunks reverted, and returns VALIDATED / UNSUPPORTED / COULD-NOT-JUDGE / NEVER-RAN. Those are mechanically-produced labels on real claims in real commit bodies. UNSUPPORTED commits are known-bad claims; VALIDATED are known-good. That's an anchor set nobody had to annotate, on exactly the claim class the tool cares about. I produced textbook instances tonight with you watching: I reported false alarms 73% → 40% → 27% as progress when the last step was inside the noise floor; I asserted the daemon was down a second time from a single curl with no process check; I claimed premises sit in the same turn without measuring it and was wrong about 43% of cases. Each of those has a correction in the transcript with a reason, which makes this session a small adversarial set with known answers and known *reasons*. If the detector doesn't flag them, it isn't working, and that's a sharper test than anything I'd construct. Add a zero-cost session signal that needs no judge at all. Claims made per tool call actually run. A session asserting sixty things off twelve tool calls is structurally different from one asserting twenty off two hundred, and you can compute that from the transcript with no model, no prompt, and no calibration. It won't tell you which claim is bad, but as a per-session index of how much talking outran the looking it may carry more of the signal you asked for than the judge does — and it can't be gamed by rephrasing, only by doing more work.

pairs.claim: The bar I'd watch is the second one, because it fires before any hook is written: across the 40 sessions, no single integrity grade may hold more than 60% of them.
pairs.evidence_full: Your reframe is right, and I can put a number on why mine was wrong. Across the 40 most recent transcripts — 1,413 assistant text blocks, 11,009 sentences — there are 375 promissory sentences, 9.4 per session. Four of them, one percent, appear in the session's final message. Everything I built and proposed reads the final report. It would have seen 4 of 375 promises. Promises are made mid-turn and then quietly vanish; the ledger has to record per-turn or it is looking at the wrong artifact entirely. Draft is at `.sovereign/features/bs-1-oplog/order.md`, replacing the universals order, which is now one adjudicator inside this rather than the thing itself. The design hinge is that a claim isn't true or false when it's made — it acquires a verdict at a knowable moment, and the ledger's only real job is tracking that moment. Retrospective and universal claims are decidable immediately. Promissory ones become decidable at session end. Predictive ones may stay open past it. Evaluative ones never become decidable, and the order excludes them from scoring outright, because a grade that quietly scores taste is a daemon model judging prose style and everything downstream is noise. Most of this already exists and none of it watches the message to you. Daemon-model judging is one uniform register across about ten call sites, always grammar-forced to a small enum plus a citation. `co-drift.py` already judges a commit's prose claims against its diff — same question, different artifact. `co_liveness.py::gate_closure_claim` structurally refuses a "dead" verdict with no concrete pointer, which is precisely the gate a "discharged" verdict needs. `Inherited::advice()` already detects a Next item that rode three frames without being done or dropped. And `~/.sovereign/comaintainer/verdicts.jsonl` is an append-only ledger with a `kind` discriminator, so this is a new `kind`, not a new store. Two things I'd push on in your design. Integrity can't be a ratio — a ratio is gamed by padding a report with twenty safe claims to dilute one broken promise, so broken promises have to count absolutely. And the bigger one: the hook that shows an agent its own ledger has an obvious adaptation, which is to stop making checkable claims. Hedge everything into evaluative, score a clean sheet, say nothing. Within a week that's the dominant strategy and reports are worse than before the tool existed. So the adjudicable fraction has to be on every grade card and tracked against the session's own trailing median. A falling adjudicable fraction is a finding, not a clean sheet. You asked for non-punitive, and this is what keeps non-punitive from collapsing into non-informative. The demo is a backtest, which is the part I like most about where this landed. There are 191 real sessions on disk. `svrn session oplog replay --last 40 --grade` runs over history that neither the ledger nor the grader can have influenced — no labelling, no new data collection, available the day it's written. Then you referee five cards, chosen by a rule fixed before the run, and say fair or unfair on each BROKEN verdict. That's the precision measurement and you're the only ground truth for it. A grader everyone passes is not measuring anything, and if that fails the honest move is to drop the grade and keep the oplog as a plain record. The one thing I'd ask you to weigh in on is the closure rule — I've written it so a promissory row still open at session end is BROKEN unless explicitly abandoned with a reason, which is strict, and strictness there is what makes bar 1 hard to pass.

pairs.evidence_full: Both are in `docs/internal/DILETTANTE_MESH_DEMO.md`. The work item came out cleaner than I expected because the inventory answered most of the design. Three things already exist that shape it. `MemberCapabilities.origins` is already a *set*, not a scalar — `candidate_of` reads `origins.contains(&OriginKind::Media)`, so the gossip model anticipated more than one origin from the start. `fan_out` is already generic over its row payload with two in-tree consumers, media and federated knowledge search, so the primitive isn't media-shaped — only its exposed route is. And `iroh_identity_forward` already parses request heads and rewrites `x-mesh-*` headers, so per-request routing has machinery. The constraint that decides the shape is `OriginKind`'s own doc comment: a closed set, where "every kind has one ALPN and one acceptor route, so a new kind is a new variant beside a new route, never a string." Which forces the real question — are house apps a closed set? Someone writing a chore app at 1am can't add an enum variant, an ALPN, and a route and recompile. By your own rule, open sets are registries. So the resolution keeps both halves honest: one new closed-set variant `OriginKind::App`, on one new ALPN `cwth/app/0`, whose route demultiplexes by name against a registry in config. The closed set stays closed — one variant, one ALPN, one route. App names become config data that changes without a code change. And `App` gets its own trust class, so admitting a housemate to your chore app isn't the same decision as admitting them to your tensor RPC. I laid out three ways out and recommended a third `Forward::HttpByName` variant that demuxes per request using the head-parsing that already exists, stripping a client-supplied app header exactly as forged `x-mesh-*` headers are stripped today. Its cost needs stating in the doc comment or someone will misread it later: an app connection's *target* becomes a per-request decision, which is a weaker statement than the acceptor makes today. The admission decision — is this dialer allowed the App class at all — still happens once per connection on the verified key. Only the which-app demux moves. I also carried forward the test that matters, tied back to the oracle problem in the other doc: a dialer admitted to `cwth/app/0` must still be refused `cwth/rpc/0` and `cwth/media/0`. Separate trust classes are only real if there's a failing input that proves it. One thing worth knowing before you build it — the hack works today. Point `media_origin` at your Flask app instead of Jellyfin and `/v1/mesh/media/fanout` becomes a generic house-wide fanout, since it takes an arbitrary path, method, headers and body. Mislabeled but functional, and useful for proving the stories out before committing to the design.

P2 is the one to do first, and it's nearly free. The header gets added on *your* side, after admission, on the way to *your* origin. It never leaves your machine and nobody in the house holds anybody else's key. The plumbing already exists — `admit_media` returns `Forward::Http { origin, headers: who.headers(dialer) }`, so the change is appending config-declared pairs to that vec plus a field to hold them. That single flag deletes the worst part of the quickstart: the whole authentication section of the README, the per-peer loop in `library.py`, and twenty-five people mailing each other API keys. Two review points I flagged — declared headers append *after* the `x-mesh-*` strip so a client can never override one, and they're secrets at rest, so `svrn publish` must redact on list and the config file's mode matters. P1 is `svrn publish`, which replaces config editing entirely and subsumes the app registry and the three tiers. Worth noting: the durable form writing the TOML for you isn't convenience, it's correctness — this host already has an `[iroh]` section, so the obvious `>>` append produces invalid TOML, which is exactly the kind of thing that eats twenty minutes of an install evening twenty-five times over. The dispatcher already warns when a sibling binary is older than itself; extend the same idea across the socket. `library.py` maps that 404 by hand right now, which is a workaround for a missing primitive. One sequencing warning I put in the doc: don't let P1 grow into the full `OriginKind::App` work before the demo. Publish can ship against the existing single origin first and gain multi-origin later — shipping the verb early is what makes the quickstart honest, and the multi-origin design can take the time it needs.

pairs.claim: `tauri.conf.json` has no `externalBin` today only because the tesseract entries were removed when PaddleOCR replaced it.
pairs.evidence_full: It comes from an assumption I carried without examining — that "not managed by the desktop" implies "managed by the OS." It doesn't. The desktop ships the daemon as a sidecar binary and launches it by path, detached, holding no handle. That is identical on all three platforms, and it needs no plist, no unit file, and no task XML. The move that makes it work is noticing which half of the bar is load-bearing. `Command::new(path).spawn()` links nothing. The desktop stops being able to *become* a daemon the moment it stops depending on `sovereign-cli-daemon` — and Tauri's `externalBin` ships a sidecar on all three targets, with the `binaries/<name>-<triple>` convention already live here for tesseract, pdfium and paddle. What falls out is smaller than what I built this evening. No supervisor state machine in the desktop — the 1,082-line module stays in the daemon where it belongs, supervising compute children. `attach_watch.rs` becomes the entire recovery story: 101 lines that already exist, already assume an externally-owned daemon, already drive the ReconnectBanner, and on `Down` would re-launch by path with one spawn and no state machine. Quit has nothing to stop. And crash isolation survives, because the weights live in compute children, not in the daemon process — that supervisor is platform-neutral apart from a best-effort SIGTERM before a cross-platform `child.kill()`, so Windows loses the grace period and nothing else. It also answers the product trade I flagged earlier and couldn't resolve. A service-managed daemon keeps ~28 GB resident after the window closes; a sidecar launched on use ties the daemon's life to use rather than to login, which is probably what a desktop user actually wants. What it gives up: no start-at-login, and no OS-level restart if the daemon dies while the app is closed. Neither matters when the desktop is the only consumer — and for CLI, headless and server users, `install-service` is still the right tool, and it now covers Windows, which it never did before. So tonight's crate isn't wasted; it's just the *other* path, for the users who genuinely want a daemon that outlives their session. The one thing I'd want to verify before committing to it: that a spawned-by-path daemon reliably survives the parent's exit on all three. Unix is settled — `daemon start` already detaches with `process_group(0)` at `lifecycle.rs:690-707`. Windows needs `DETACHED_PROCESS` / `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` and I haven't checked what Tauri's sidecar API does by default. The judgement call is yours and it's narrow: the sidecar desktop still *spawns* a daemon once, by path, with no handle. That's decisively not "becoming" one, and it's less than managing one — but it isn't nothing, and your DoD said "cannot spawn one." If you read the purity moment as the dependency edge, this is the elegant answer. If you read it literally, the service path is the one that satisfies it and the per-platform backends are the price. Say which, and I'll put it in the frame before we split so the next session starts from the decision rather than re-deriving it.

pairs.evidence_full: A holder authenticates to its own media server, and nobody in the house ever holds anyone else's key. That's the whole change, and it's the one that made the demo viable. Jellyfin's API keys are per-server, so federating twenty-five libraries used to mean twenty-five people each holding twenty-four other people's credentials — which nobody sane does, and which would have killed the demo in the room. Now each person declares their own key on their own machine, and their daemon adds it after the caller is admitted as a member, on their side of the wire. The part that wasn't in the plan and mattered most: appending a header isn't enough to make it authoritative. Append-only leaves the viewer's copy *ahead* of the holder's in the request head, and origins disagree about which one wins on a duplicate name — so a viewer could have picked the credential their own request ran under. A declared name now displaces the client's. Stripped first, appended last, exactly one on the wire. It's proven rather than asserted: `house_mesh_publish_roundtrip` runs two daemons over real iroh against an origin that returns 200 only when exactly one token line arrives with the holder's value. Same viewer, sending its own token, refused before the declaration and served after. I broke it two ways to confirm the test can see both failures — removing the append, and removing only the displacement — and both go red. Plus `svrn mesh media declare`, which reads the value from stdin so it never lands in shell history, stores it 0600, and never prints it back. What you bring to the house. `curl -fsSL https://svrnme.sh/install.sh | sh` — three prebuilt binaries, no clone, no Rust. And `~/dev/house-mesh`, two files, about 280 lines: the quickstart and `library.py`. Push that somewhere public and it's the only thing anyone reads. Nobody touches the monorepo. Per person, five minutes: install, `svrn setup --terminal http://<the-gpu-box>:9741` which downloads *nothing*, `svrn mesh join <key>`, one line in config for `media_origin`, and `printf '%s' "$KEY" | svrn mesh media declare x-emby-token`. The demo in the room is four beats. `svrn mesh media` — the house appears. `svrn mesh media fanout /System/Info/Public` — one request to everyone, one attributed row each, and it needs no API key so it works before anyone has set one up. `svrn mesh media alex` — a localhost URL that streams off Alex's disk with seeking intact. Then unplug the WAN and do it again. The line to say while that's happening: *you already wanted one model server. Now everyone also gets everyone else's media, and nobody writes a login page.* One thing to do before you walk in. None of this has met an actual Jellyfin. Stand up one Jellyfin, declare a key, and run `library.py check` then `list`. That's an hour, and it's the difference between a demo and an apology. What's honestly not ready. One app per person, because `media_origin` is still singular; the multi-origin design is written up but unbuilt, and it's what turns this from a media feature into the substrate. pairs.claim: `co-drift.py` already judges a commit's prose claims against its diff — same question, different artifact.
pairs.evidence_full: Your reframe is right, and I can put a number on why mine was wrong. Across the 40 most recent transcripts — 1,413 assistant text blocks, 11,009 sentences — there are 375 promissory sentences, 9.4 per session. Four of them, one percent, appear in the session's final message. Everything I built and proposed reads the final report. It would have seen 4 of 375 promises. Promises are made mid-turn and then quietly vanish; the ledger has to record per-turn or it is looking at the wrong artifact entirely. Draft is at `.sovereign/features/bs-1-oplog/order.md`, replacing the universals order, which is now one adjudicator inside this rather than the thing itself. The design hinge is that a claim isn't true or false when it's made — it acquires a verdict at a knowable moment, and the ledger's only real job is tracking that moment. Retrospective and universal claims are decidable immediately. Promissory ones become decidable at session end. Predictive ones may stay open past it. Evaluative ones never become decidable, and the order excludes them from scoring outright, because a grade that quietly scores taste is a daemon model judging prose style and everything downstream is noise. Most of this already exists and none of it watches the message to you. Daemon-model judging is one uniform register across about ten call sites, always grammar-forced to a small enum plus a citation. `co_liveness.py::gate_closure_claim` structurally refuses a "dead" verdict with no concrete pointer, which is precisely the gate a "discharged" verdict needs. `Inherited::advice()` already detects a Next item that rode three frames without being done or dropped. And `~/.sovereign/comaintainer/verdicts.jsonl` is an append-only ledger with a `kind` discriminator, so this is a new `kind`, not a new store. Two things I'd push on in your design. Integrity can't be a ratio — a ratio is gamed by padding a report with twenty safe claims to dilute one broken promise, so broken promises have to count absolutely. And the bigger one: the hook that shows an agent its own ledger has an obvious adaptation, which is to stop making checkable claims. Hedge everything into evaluative, score a clean sheet, say nothing. Within a week that's the dominant strategy and reports are worse than before the tool existed. So the adjudicable fraction has to be on every grade card and tracked against the session's own trailing median. A falling adjudicable fraction is a finding, not a clean sheet. You asked for non-punitive, and this is what keeps non-punitive from collapsing into non-informative. The demo is a backtest, which is the part I like most about where this landed. There are 191 real sessions on disk. `svrn session oplog replay --last 40 --grade` runs over history that neither the ledger nor the grader can have influenced — no labelling, no new data collection, available the day it's written. Then you referee five cards, chosen by a rule fixed before the run, and say fair or unfair on each BROKEN verdict. That's the precision measurement and you're the only ground truth for it. The bar I'd watch is the second one, because it fires before any hook is written: across the 40 sessions, no single integrity grade may hold more than 60% of them. A grader everyone passes is not measuring anything, and if that fails the honest move is to drop the grade and keep the oplog as a plain record. The one thing I'd ask you to weigh in on is the closure rule — I've written it so a promissory row still open at session end is BROKEN unless explicitly abandoned with a reason, which is strict, and strictness there is what makes bar 1 hard to pass.

pairs.claim: Sequencing I'd propose, subject to that: finish the correctness waves (each removes a reader either way), have the desktop install the service at setup, delete supervision and the in-process path on Unix, move the deps behind `cfg(windows)` and mint the layer bar, then build the Windows backend and take the bar green everywhere.
pairs.evidence_full: Assessment, with one trace still running. `sovereign-desktop` links no crate that can assemble or host a daemon. Checkable by `cargo tree`, enforceable by the layer ratchet already in the repo, and it goes red structurally rather than by a count that lags. The four `Launch` variants that drag `sovereign-cli-daemon` into the desktop binary — `Daemon`, `Worker`, `ComputeChild`, `RpcWorker` — all exist only because the desktop can *become* a daemon. `ComputeChild`'s own doc says "ANY binary that can be `current_exe` must handle this variant"; a desktop that never spawns compute children is not such a binary. 1,990 production Rust lines of daemon lifecycle in the desktop crate, of which about 271 survive. The survivors are exactly the right ones: `attach_watch.rs` (101 lines, already assumes the daemon is externally owned), `kickstart_daemon` (46), `request_daemon_reload` (43), the readiness probe (69), `attach_restart_daemon` (12). The in-process `EmbeddedDaemon` + `RunLock` ownership in `state.rs` is 365 lines; child supervision is 645; the mobile-host supervisor another 90; `smoketest`'s crash-isolation subprocess 302, which belongs in the daemon since the daemon is what loads models. The replacement is already written. `config_setup.rs:256-299` shells `launchctl kickstart -k gui/<uid>/com.svrnmesh.daemon` and `systemctl --user restart svrnmesh` today. `install-service` writes a launchd LaunchAgent with `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false` and a systemd user unit with `Restart=on-failure` plus `StartLimitBurst=5`. `ReconnectBanner.svelte` already renders an attach-down state driven by `attach_watch`. The OS-managed topology isn't new code — it's the path the desktop already takes when it finds a daemon running, which is how I ran every measurement today. One risk retires immediately: the supervisor state machine doesn't need deleting. `sovereign_compute::supervisor` is consumed by `sovereign-cli-daemon` at `daemon_cmd/bootstrap.rs:592` and `discovery_policy.rs:24` for its own compute children. The desktop is a caller, not the owner — a daemon supervising its compute children is correct; a desktop supervising a daemon is not. *Windows is the hard blocker.* There is no service backend at all — no unit template, no `contrib/windows/`, no prebuilt Windows CLI, and `install_service` hard-errors on the platform. The desktop *does* ship Windows (NSIS installer, `scripts/build-desktop-windows.sh`). And the supervisor is platform-neutral — one `cfg(unix)` in 1,082 lines — so supervised-child is currently the only way a Windows user gets a daemon at all. Delete it without a Windows story and the platform breaks outright. The mitigation that keeps the bar honest is `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]` for the daemon crate: green on macOS and Linux, Windows a declared exception with a `DEFAULTS_LEDGER` row and a review-by date, then the Windows backend as its own rung. *Nothing installs the service.* Not the DMG, not the NSIS installer, not `install.sh`, not the app — it's a manual `svrn install-service` from a shell whose `PATH` gets baked into the unit. A desktop that no longer spawns a daemon must install the service itself or refuse to start with a remedy. The first is the product answer and it's cheap: both units are per-user (`~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `~/.config/systemd/user`), so no elevation. That's the one place the desktop *should* touch the daemon — once, at setup, not every launch. *No socket activation anywhere.* "Client connects, daemon starts" doesn't exist on any platform, and cold model load budgets 120s. Under a resident LaunchAgent this is better than today, where quitting kills the child and the next launch reloads the model — but it's a product decision you should make deliberately: a resident daemon holds GB of RAM after the window closes. *Smaller gaps that become user-visible once the service is the only daemon:* `daemon status` never consults the service manager, so it can't say whether the daemon is supervised or why it's down; `uninstall-service` is documented in two places and does not exist; neither platform survives a reboot before login (LaunchAgent, no systemd linger). Whether anything in first-launch genuinely requires the desktop process to hold the models, the store, or a Runtime rather than ask a daemon — that trace is still running, and it decides whether macOS and Linux can go pure or need a first-run exception. The journey test setting `SOVEREIGN_FORCE_LOCAL=1` is the tell I want explained before I'd commit to a sequence.

pairs.claim: I'd sequence it as the deterministic deciders first, run in report-only mode over the last thirty days of commits to measure the false-positive rate, then promote to blocking, then add the model-judged narration rule, and only then change the `AGENTS.md` wording — so the paragraph describes a gate that exists rather than adding a second unenforced sentence next to the first one.
pairs.evidence_full: Everything needed is already built. The enforcement point is `.claude/hooks/commit-smells.py` — a PreToolUse hook on Bash that intercepts `git commit`, runs the staged diff against the §15 smell rows in `quality/arch-probes.toml`, and hands findings back before the commit lands. That file already carries the pattern language you'd need. So this is four rows and one small engine addition, not a new subsystem. Three of the checks are deterministic and belong as `[[decider]]` rows, which never reach a model. The existing `kind = "count"` decider counts lines matching a pattern, grouped by a key, and violates above a max — that is a comment-ratio gate with a different pattern in it. Row one caps added comment lines against added code lines per file in the diff. Row two, `inline-comment`, matches `^\+\s*//` outside SPDX and SAFETY and sets max zero for new code, which is your 94k-line class closed at the source. Row three needs a new `kind` — call it `resolve` — about forty lines: every backticked path in an added comment must exist in `git ls-files`. Those three answer "is this comment shaped like a claim" without spending a model call on arithmetic, which is what §7.6 asks. The fourth is genuinely a judgment call and belongs as a `[[rule]]` on the model-judged path, alongside `silent-sub` and `additive-bias`: does this change add a comment that narrates history, rationale, or a deferral rather than naming something it can be checked against? Gate it on `^\+\s*//` so it only fires on diffs that touch comments. It runs on the local daemon like the others, so it costs no external tokens. The part I'd change from the obvious design is what gets ratcheted. Don't ratchet comment count — `size_gate.rs` rule 1 is right that stripping documentation to get under a ceiling is worth zero, and a count ratchet re-creates exactly that incentive. Ratchet the dead citations instead. 265 today, may only fall. You cannot game that by deleting good comments, because removing a comment whose citation resolves doesn't move the number; the only way down is to fix a lie or delete one. The thing it rewards is the thing you want. There's a second placement worth taking, and it's cheaper than the commit hook. `format-edited-file.sh` runs PostToolUse on Write and Edit and already rustfmts the file. The three deterministic checks can run there on just the edited file and return findings as feedback. That closes the loop at the moment of writing — the agent produces a 64-line module header and hears back, before its next tool call, that the header is 64 lines, three citations don't resolve, and seven normative claims name no test. Instruction-following drift doesn't survive that kind of latency, which is why the `AGENTS.md` paragraph that already says "at most shorthand comments" lost by a factor of ten: nothing contradicted it for hours at a time. One structural detail that makes it stick: `cargo xtask instrument-gate` won't let a gate row go missing from `quality/instruments.toml`, so once these are registered they can't quietly stop running. That's the closure half, and it's the part these things usually lack. Worth noting that each of these ships with a real negative control, which most of your instruments don't — the audit found 84 of 95 carrying `negative_control="none"`. The 265 dead citations, the 400 deferral admissions, and the `turn_http.rs` header are inputs I've watched these rules need to fire on. §18.1 says a gate you haven't watched fail isn't a gate; here the existing corpus is the failing input, already in the tree.

Both gate scripts now resolve `sovereign-turn-client/bundled-backend`, kept in step so they do not flip a cargo fingerprint against each other. Without that line the bring-up half would be compiled by nothing and run by nothing — a never-ran verdict on the capability's entire second half. Verification: eleven tests pass, and three plants were watched red and restored — remove the detach and the process-group test goes red, return `Ok` from the absence path and the absence test goes red, skip the first probe and the duplicate-bring-up test goes red. `cargo xwin check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` is green with the feature on, which is the first compile that Windows creation-flags path has ever had. Workspace lint is clean at 74s. The full suite is 12,885 pass / 2 fail, and both failures are `xtask::instrument_registry`: `hook-wiring`'s `negative_control` in `quality/instruments.toml` is free prose naming neither a mutant id nor a Control instrument, which the test at `corpus-engine/xtask/tests/instrument_registry.rs:97` requires. That entry came in with `b9cbc8662` and this tree modifies neither file. It makes the workspace suite red for everyone until whoever owns that work fixes it. Two things from the session you should know. pairs.evidence_full: Four rungs landed, and the plan is now a measurement rather than a guess. The old number was wrong because it counted the wrong thing. "~170 use sites" came from counting `sovereign_core::` mentions. Counting *readers* instead — every `state.<slot>.read()/.write()` across `src-tauri/src` — says `AppState` had eight in-process slots and five of them were written by the bootstrap spine and read by nothing at all. Each had lost its consumer to a daemon route in an earlier rung and left its construction standing: `insight_http` took the insight surface, `2d5b569f6` moved the skeleton NER pass to the daemon's own manager, `6e47d0abe` took `lc_pre_scan`, health is rendered from `/status`. That's principle 12's smell read backwards — a count at zero with the ability fully intact on the other side of the wire. So R1 was a deletion, not a repoint: ~115 lines commissioning a `LocalCorpusManager` with its enrichment defaults and tiered deps, the `InsightService` (and with it the store builder's only reason to name an `InferenceProvider`), `state/builders/health.rs` whole, the second GLiNER handle, and `health_shutdown` — that fifth one found because R1's own comment claimed `main` cancels it and the compiler said nothing reads it. I corrected that in R2 and said so; writing an unchecked comment while deleting four things for having no readers is the failure those principles name together. Two rungs were repoints onto routes that already existed and had no callers. `build_corpus_index` still built the index in-process over the app's own `CorpusEngine` and store, four commits after `f9ecf139f` shipped the daemon job *and* the client methods to reach it — so the thing that route exists to prevent, two writers on one LanceDB index with no refusal between them, was live the whole time. And both warmup sites warmed a slot in the app while the daemon served the turns; `/internal/inference/warmup` has existed for months, and its handler's doc comment asserts it is "wired into the desktop app's window-focus events." It was not. That comment also carries a warning about its own earlier false claim, which is what prompted me to verify the mounting rather than trust it. Same wrong-source shape as the enrichment reads. It surfaced only because the test needed to assert `configured` against a fixture config. The two tests there are deliberately paired — `NullProvider` answers the trait's `None` default, so the absence test alone would pass against a hard-coded `None`; I watched the has-slot test fail (`left: None, right: Some(32768)`) with the provider read stubbed out, then restored. Per-rung verification: 206, 206, 240, 1768 tests, zero failures, plus the full-workspace sweep earlier at 13,096 pass / 0 fail. What remains is R5–R10, and it is real work, not cleanup. Six edges still stand because four constructions in `state.rs` survive — `open_store`, `CorpusEngine::new`, `build_folder_tiered_provider`, `load_gliner_extractor` — and three in-file engine users I was wrong to assume were dead (the embedding-dimension stamp, `validate_corpus_readiness`, the vector-index verify task each still do boot work and need routes). R5–R7 are three small store reads; R8 is recipe testing as a daemon job; R9 is the GLiNER model probe, which reads the *desktop's* `models_root()` and downloads into it while the daemon runs the model — the wrong-machine shape again, with no route to take; R10 is 17 hardware-probe sites. Two things you should know before the next session picks this up. A peer is committing in this tree and bulk-stages: when I went to commit R4 the index held nine of their paths, including their half of `daemon_wire.rs`. I unstaged theirs and hunk-picked mine. And nothing here has been verified by running the app — every rung is cargo-green, and "no feature regressions" cannot be judged that way. `arch-gate` also stays red and owed, attributed per finding in `SYSTEM_OVERVIEW §10.1t`; the largest item is now `turn-client/src/lib.rs` at ~4,600 lines. Context is deep in the red zone, so this is the right handoff point — the frame carries the rung plan, the measured reader counts, the peer-staging hazard and the owed gates.

pairs.claim: Twelve edits to `frontdoor.rs` produce one line, not twelve.
pairs.evidence_full: Draft 1 had one mechanism, and two of its failure modes are already measured in your tree. The first is that a list of targets doesn't move code. `quality/CLEANUP.md`, dated 2026-07-13, names the next god-files by name and size: "notes.rs 6,363, frontdoor.rs 5,774, resolution.rs 5,173." Today `oversized.txt` has them at 7,807, 5,820 and 5,473 — the three files a document declared the top refactor priorities grew +1,790 lines net in two months. Any part of a second draft that resolves to "here is what to refactor" is falsified before it ships. The second is habituation. Draft 1's hook fires on every edit to any of 183 pinned files. By the fifth firing in a session it's wallpaper, and you've rebuilt the disease one layer down. A gate whose false-positive rate nobody measured is the exact thing your own AGENTS.md says teaches people to reach for `--no-verify`. So draft 2 is four mechanisms. Each one names the failure it prevents and the number that would show it isn't working. Placement becomes a conditional plan section. `sovereign plan validate` already blocks `ExitPlanMode` with exit 2 and stderr feedback, and it already enforces six required sections — this is proven machinery you live with daily, so the marginal cost is a `const` array and a branch. Don't add a seventh unconditional section; that taxes every plan for a benefit a minority need, and trains everyone to type "N/A". Instead have the validator scan the plan body for file paths, cross-reference `oversized.txt` and `approach_band.txt`, and demand a placement line *only* when the plan names a constrained file — showing it the numbers rather than asking it to recall them. Prevents: placement decided while writing. Fires: once per plan, and only for plans that touch the tail. The write-time backstop fires once per file per session. PreToolUse on `Edit|Write`, third in the slot that already holds `prior-art-warn` and `intent-warn`. It fires only if the target is pinned or in-band *and* this session hasn't spoken about that file yet — a state file keyed on `session_id`, which the hook envelope already carries. And the line names the alternative, not the problem: `frontdoor.rs 5,820/5,870, 50 lines of slack; siblings are routes_*.rs`. Prevents: unplanned work routing around the plan gate. The once-per-file rule is the direct countermeasure to draft 1's habituation. A new module is born with a declared ceiling, or it refills. Your gate's own comment measured this: split products regrew 1.43x in aggregate, and the single file that held — `daemon_cmd/mod.rs`, 2,378 → 1,372 — is the one whose §3.3 entry declares an end state. Without this, parts one and two just relocate the growth: `frontdoor.rs` stops at 5,870 and the new `routes_x.rs` travels 0 → 1,199 completely unremarked, because `APPROACH_FLOOR` is 800 and nothing watches below it. So when the hook in part two sees a Write to a path that doesn't exist, it asks for the ceiling at the moment that costs nothing, and arch-gate reads a fourth baseline alongside the three it already reads. A file declared at 400 then fails at 451 rather than at 1,201 — caught at 12% over instead of 3x over. The escape hatch becomes a dated loan, and the due list generates work orders. `--accept <key>` today is permanent forgiveness, which is why each one is a real negotiation and why negotiating takes forever. Make it `--accept <key> --until <date> --why "..."`, two extra columns in the baseline. Accepting costs ten seconds at push time, so nobody skips the gate; the debt comes back on a date you chose. Then the past-due list feeds `.sovereign/features/` as work orders — the pool, the worker sessions and the `/comaintainer` seat all already exist. That is the part that answers "it takes forever, I skip it": the refactor stops competing with the feature for your afternoon and becomes a unit the existing pool consumes for the price of an approval. CLEANUP.md failed because it was a document a human had to act on; a work order with a due date has a trigger, which is the closure-loop rule you already wrote down. One bug to fix alongside, or parts two and three are lying. `size_gate.rs:216` is a bare `if n > cap` with no `GROWTH_SLACK`, and its keys are per-crate. Moving 400 lines into a new module satisfies arch-gate and still fails size-gate, because the crate total doesn't care where the lines landed. The two gates hand the agent contradictory instructions, and the crate key can only ever be satisfied by deleting — so it fires on every feature and teaches nothing. It's ~70 lines of Python, no new concepts, no gate changes, and it tests the entire thesis: if write-time signal reaches the decision, push-time arch-gate failures should approach zero within a month. If they don't, one and three are built on sand and you've learned that for a day's work. Then three, measured by whether files created after it exceed their declared ceilings at the same 1.43x. Then four, measured by whether the past-due count ever falls — if it only grows, it's a prettier CLEANUP.md and should be deleted. Want me to write part two?

The sort comparator at `scheduler_core.rs:146-153` reconstructs an `Ordering` from that winner by matching three fields, and it can never return `Equal` — on a full tie `pick_better` returns `cur`, so the comparator says `Less`, and it says `Less` again with the arguments swapped. That breaks antisymmetry, and epsilon comparison breaks transitivity independently (a≈b, b≈c, a>c). `slice::sort_by` documents the result as unspecified for a non-total order and permits a panic. You're currently relying on stability that the comparator is actively telling the sort not to apply. Predicted time wins −8% on mixed-hubs (5/5 seeds) and loses +3% on twin-hubs (1/5) — empirically a wash. But the architectural argument breaks the tie, and the doc already states it: predicted times are in milliseconds, so "within noise" has units, where a dimensionless product has no scale on which two candidates can be called close. `tie_band` is only expressible under one of the two objectives. Land `PredictedTime`, delete `Product`, and both `Option`s become concrete values while the replay assumption disappears entirely. Split admission from preference. Inside `rank` the five-guard cascade — quarantined, yield backoff, manifest missing, no forced-choice, no claim match — is per-peer, independent and total. pairs.evidence_full: A holder authenticates to its own media server, and nobody in the house ever holds anyone else's key. That's the whole change, and it's the one that made the demo viable. Jellyfin's API keys are per-server, so federating twenty-five libraries used to mean twenty-five people each holding twenty-four other people's credentials — which nobody sane does, and which would have killed the demo in the room. Now each person declares their own key on their own machine, and their daemon adds it after the caller is admitted as a member, on their side of the wire. The part that wasn't in the plan and mattered most: appending a header isn't enough to make it authoritative. Append-only leaves the viewer's copy *ahead* of the holder's in the request head, and origins disagree about which one wins on a duplicate name — so a viewer could have picked the credential their own request ran under. A declared name now displaces the client's. Stripped first, appended last, exactly one on the wire. It's proven rather than asserted: `house_mesh_publish_roundtrip` runs two daemons over real iroh against an origin that returns 200 only when exactly one token line arrives with the holder's value. Same viewer, sending its own token, refused before the declaration and served after. I broke it two ways to confirm the test can see both failures — removing the append, and removing only the displacement — and both go red. Plus `svrn mesh media declare`, which reads the value from stdin so it never lands in shell history, stores it 0600, and never prints it back. Per person, five minutes: install, `svrn setup --terminal http://<the-gpu-box>:9741` which downloads *nothing*, `svrn mesh join <key>`, one line in config for `media_origin`, and `printf '%s' "$KEY" | svrn mesh media declare x-emby-token`. The demo in the room is four beats. `svrn mesh media` — the house appears. `svrn mesh media fanout /System/Info/Public` — one request to everyone, one attributed row each, and it needs no API key so it works before anyone has set one up. `svrn mesh media alex` — a localhost URL that streams off Alex's disk with seeking intact. Then unplug the WAN and do it again. The line to say while that's happening: *you already wanted one model server. Now everyone also gets everyone else's media, and nobody writes a login page.* One thing to do before you walk in. None of this has met an actual Jellyfin. pairs.claim: The fix is the architectural one: quantize the score into epsilon buckets (`(score / SCORING_EPSILON).round() as i64`), `impl Ord for ScoredClaim` over `(bucket desc, size asc, known-before-unknown)`, and then `beats_local` is `cand > local`, `candidates_equal` is `==`, and the sort is `sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))`.
pairs.evidence_full: The kernel is already the best-carved thing in the repo — pure, seeded, two callers one body, with a determinism test asserting it. So the work isn't cleanup, it's four specific collapses. One of them is a live correctness bug. `pick_better` is not an ordering, and `winners_over_local` sorts with it. `oicp-types/src/scoring.rs:458` returns a winner, with score compared under `SCORING_EPSILON`. The sort comparator at `scheduler_core.rs:146-153` reconstructs an `Ordering` from that winner by matching three fields, and it can never return `Equal` — on a full tie `pick_better` returns `cur`, so the comparator says `Less`, and it says `Less` again with the arguments swapped. That breaks antisymmetry, and epsilon comparison breaks transitivity independently (a≈b, b≈c, a>c). `slice::sort_by` documents the result as unspecified for a non-total order and permits a panic. You're currently relying on stability that the comparator is actively telling the sort not to apply. Three spellings of "which candidate is preferred" become one, and the clones per comparison go away. Production hardcodes `RankObjective::Product` at `peer_inference.rs:1677` and `TierFloor::None` at `:1682` — both axes exist only for sim arms. They leak into the kernel's result type as two `Option`s that don't mean absence: `RankedCandidate.predicted` and `RankResult.tie_band` are `None` because you asked the other objective, which is a different thing wearing the same clothes. And `decision_replay` simply assumes `Product`, so a record can't say which objective produced it. Your own §4.1.2 makes this decidable. Predicted time wins −8% on mixed-hubs (5/5 seeds) and loses +3% on twin-hubs (1/5) — empirically a wash. But the architectural argument breaks the tie, and the doc already states it: predicted times are in milliseconds, so "within noise" has units, where a dimensionless product has no scale on which two candidates can be called close. `tie_band` is only expressible under one of the two objectives. Land `PredictedTime`, delete `Product`, and both `Option`s become concrete values while the replay assumption disappears entirely. Split admission from preference. Inside `rank` the five-guard cascade — quarantined, yield backoff, manifest missing, no forced-choice, no claim match — is per-peer, independent and total. That's `admit(peer, req, now) -> Result<Admitted, ExclusionReason>`, and pulling it out lets you test it exhaustively against the closed `ExclusionReason` enum instead of through a 200-line loop. `rank` then reads as four lines: admit all, score all, order by `Ord`, cut at local. It also gives your two cores one word for one idea — `rail-core` already has `admit()` and it means exactly this. Kill the three index-parallel vectors. `scored`, `timing` and `peer_rec_idx` are held parallel by comment. The module already diagnosed this exact hazard one level down — `RankedCandidate`'s doc says carrying the prediction in a parallel `Vec` "would let the two lists desync silently" and that "a desync here does not fail; it dispatches to one peer using another peer's predicted time." That reasoning applies unchanged to these three. One `Vec<Scored>` with three fields. Smaller: `worker_eligibility.rs:664` is a `OnceLock`, so install-once rather than mutable, but it's ambient — it isn't in `RankInputs`, which means `rank` is pure and the decision isn't. Move it into the snapshot. Do the `Ord` first: it's the bug, it's self-contained, and it shrinks the surface the other three have to move. Then admission, which is behaviour-preserving and makes the objective collapse a small diff. Then the objective, which is the one that changes what the fleet does and wants an arm before it lands. Want me to start on the `Ord`?

Everything else that drags inference in does so through the crate graph, not through a call. The load-bearing edge is sovereign-mesh depending on sovereign-inference, since any client that imports mesh types for a roster or a peer handshake inherits llama-cpp whether it runs a model or not. The shape that matches ownership is two hosts split by who loads a model. Client verbs go in the dispatcher or a client sibling whose test is that `cargo tree -i llama-cpp-4` returns nothing. The harnesses go in a back-of-house bench binary that keeps sovereign-eval, gliner and llama, the same pattern the `awareness` feature already uses. The actual work before that split can close is small and nameable: give the three in-process loads a daemon route, and cut the sovereign-mesh to sovereign-inference edge so mesh client types live in a leaf. The rest is moving files.

pairs.evidence_full: The kernel is already the best-carved thing in the repo — pure, seeded, two callers one body, with a determinism test asserting it. So the work isn't cleanup, it's four specific collapses. One of them is a live correctness bug. `pick_better` is not an ordering, and `winners_over_local` sorts with it. `oicp-types/src/scoring.rs:458` returns a winner, with score compared under `SCORING_EPSILON`. The sort comparator at `scheduler_core.rs:146-153` reconstructs an `Ordering` from that winner by matching three fields, and it can never return `Equal` — on a full tie `pick_better` returns `cur`, so the comparator says `Less`, and it says `Less` again with the arguments swapped. That breaks antisymmetry, and epsilon comparison breaks transitivity independently (a≈b, b≈c, a>c). `slice::sort_by` documents the result as unspecified for a non-total order and permits a panic. You're currently relying on stability that the comparator is actively telling the sort not to apply. The fix is the architectural one: quantize the score into epsilon buckets (`(score / SCORING_EPSILON).round() as i64`), `impl Ord for ScoredClaim` over `(bucket desc, size asc, known-before-unknown)`, and then `beats_local` is `cand > local`, `candidates_equal` is `==`, and the sort is `sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))`. Three spellings of "which candidate is preferred" become one, and the clones per comparison go away. Production hardcodes `RankObjective::Product` at `peer_inference.rs:1677` and `TierFloor::None` at `:1682` — both axes exist only for sim arms. They leak into the kernel's result type as two `Option`s that don't mean absence: `RankedCandidate.predicted` and `RankResult.tie_band` are `None` because you asked the other objective, which is a different thing wearing the same clothes. And `decision_replay` simply assumes `Product`, so a record can't say which objective produced it. Your own §4.1.2 makes this decidable. Predicted time wins −8% on mixed-hubs (5/5 seeds) and loses +3% on twin-hubs (1/5) — empirically a wash. But the architectural argument breaks the tie, and the doc already states it: predicted times are in milliseconds, so "within noise" has units, where a dimensionless product has no scale on which two candidates can be called close. `tie_band` is only expressible under one of the two objectives. Land `PredictedTime`, delete `Product`, and both `Option`s become concrete values while the replay assumption disappears entirely. Split admission from preference. Inside `rank` the five-guard cascade — quarantined, yield backoff, manifest missing, no forced-choice, no claim match — is per-peer, independent and total. That's `admit(peer, req, now) -> Result<Admitted, ExclusionReason>`, and pulling it out lets you test it exhaustively against the closed `ExclusionReason` enum instead of through a 200-line loop. `rank` then reads as four lines: admit all, score all, order by `Ord`, cut at local. Kill the three index-parallel vectors. `scored`, `timing` and `peer_rec_idx` are held parallel by comment. The module already diagnosed this exact hazard one level down — `RankedCandidate`'s doc says carrying the prediction in a parallel `Vec` "would let the two lists desync silently" and that "a desync here does not fail; it dispatches to one peer using another peer's predicted time." That reasoning applies unchanged to these three. One `Vec<Scored>` with three fields. Smaller: `worker_eligibility.rs:664` is a `OnceLock`, so install-once rather than mutable, but it's ambient — it isn't in `RankInputs`, which means `rank` is pure and the decision isn't. Move it into the snapshot. Do the `Ord` first: it's the bug, it's self-contained, and it shrinks the surface the other three have to move. Then admission, which is behaviour-preserving and makes the objective collapse a small diff. Then the objective, which is the one that changes what the fleet does and wants an arm before it lands. Want me to start on the `Ord`?

Jellyfin keys are per-server, so one header can't authenticate you to twenty-five Jellyfins. `library.py` asks each person's server separately with that person's key from `~/.house-mesh/tokens.json`. The README names the better answer as a project someone could take: your daemon already hands your media server the caller's verified `X-Mesh-Member` with forged ones stripped, so a twenty-line proxy beside your Jellyfin could read that and inject your own token. pairs.evidence_full: Bloomberg never sold news. It sold a workflow tool to people whose decisions dwarfed its price, built a newsroom in 1990 only because the terminal needed one, and the news has been a feature of the terminal ever since. That is the lesson, and it inverts the spec as written: the custodian settlement is the wholesale layer, not the business. The business is the professional node, sold flat, with every custodian included, and the company nets out to publishers behind it the way Bloomberg pays exchanges and bundles the feeds. What made the terminal worth 25 thousand a seat was never access to prices. Reuters and Telerate had prices. Bloomberg took a bond price and turned it into a yield curve and a relative-value screen, normalized every source into one schema with one identifier, and answered "what does this mean" while the incumbents answered "what is the number." Data was scarce and expensive then. Data is free and untrusted now, so the same move in this era is not normalization of prices but normalization of claims: one atom identity with provenance, one tension atom where two sources disagree, one ledger that says what was admitted and what was dropped and why. The professional's question has changed from "what is the price" to "who said that, and can I prove it in a year." The answer to that question is what the node sells. The lesson-by-lesson map, because it has that shape: | Bloomberg, 1981 to now | This era | | Sold the terminal; news was a feature | Sell the professional node; custodian content is a feature, settled wholesale | | Normalized prices, one identifier per instrument | Normalize claims, one atom identity with custody, tensions first-class | | Built on exchange feeds first, newsroom second | Primary sources first: the SEC, Federal Register, CRS, SCOTUS, OLC, US Code recipes already in this repo. Newsroom custodians second | | Messaging made the terminal the identity layer of finance | The mesh and custodian registry make the node the identity layer of grounded work | | Compliance-recorded chat | Signed, re-checkable ledgers, offline against source bytes months later | | Flat price, everything included, no discounts | Flat seat for professionals; tokens only at the consumer edge | | Owned the keyboard, the lines, the collection | Own inference, retrieval, and the ledger on the node; reliability is the product | | Function codes: a skill employees carry between employers | Recipes and meshapps: free substrate so everyone learns it, enterprises pay for trust | Three of those rows carry the weight. Primary sources first is the row that makes this Bloomberg-grade rather than a news aggregator. The 10-K, the Federal Register entry, the court opinion, the CRS report are public, free, and already recipes on disk. A newsroom's claim about a rate decision is a secondary source; the tension atom between the FT's claim and the filing it is about is the product nobody has, and it needs no publisher's signature to build. This also answers the cold-start risk from two messages ago in a stronger way than the Wikipedia tier did: the primary layer is the whole terminal for a due-diligence analyst before a single outlet signs. Bloomberg built its own newsroom because Reuters would not sell. If the FT will not sell, the primary layer still stands and the FT is the one missing from the room. The open substrate row is where this era differs from Bloomberg's, and the difference favors you. Bloomberg's function codes were a moat because they were closed and learning them took years. AGPL means the substrate is free for the student, the freelance journalist, the policy intern, and the switching cost accrues anyway, because the thing they learn is the recipe system and the ledger, and the thing their employer then pays for is the custodian registry and the audit. Red Hat's shape for the license, Bloomberg's shape for who pays and why. The flat seat row is the one that changes the spec. Bloomberg's customers manage other people's money; a tool that informs one decision a quarter is a rounding error. The analog buyer here bills by the hour or manages exposure: law firms, asset managers, government-affairs shops, corporate strategy, journalists' own research desks. An hour a week saved at a billed rate that starts in the hundreds covers a Bloomberg-priced seat with room. Those buyers do not want to hold tokens or watch a meter. They want one price and every source in it, and the meter runs behind the seat where the company uses it to settle with custodians. The token economy stays exactly as designed for the consumer edge and becomes the wholesale accounting for the enterprise edge. Same rows, same peg, two retail shapes. What Bloomberg's history says about pace: about ten years to ten thousand terminals, private the whole way, no outside capital except the anchor customer. The impatience of venture money is the thing most likely to break this, because the trust layer is worth nothing until it has been re-checked by a third party for long enough that a board believes it, and that is a clock nobody can speed up. The anchor customer plus anchor publisher, with the enterprise co-funding the settlement company the way Merrill did, is the structure that buys the time. The kill bar for the whole thesis is a single question you can ask an analyst at the anchor: when the answer with the ledger and the answer without it disagree, which one goes in the memo. If the ledger does not change what goes in the memo, this is a news product with extra steps and Bloomberg's lesson does not apply.

pairs.claim: The archive is the parent, shipped exactly the way SEP ships today: `query_sharing = true`, `mesh_sharing = false`.
pairs.evidence_full: Most of this moonshot is already on disk in the shape of custody flags, a watcher, and a ledger. The new part is one ledger row kind and a settlement layer on top of it. Here is how it would run. The outlet becomes a node, not a website. The FT runs a sovereign daemon with two corpora. Peers can run federated searches and get cited snippets back, but the bytes never leave the newsroom's machine. The second corpus is the newsroom's own `wikipedia-newsworthy`: watcher-driven, event-bullet grain, a rolling tracked set that gets refreshed in place as a story develops and drops out of daily attention after the window closes. That recipe is 60 lines of TOML and the only thing that changes for the FT is the acquire block. The watcher is the thing print never had: a story is not a frozen artifact anymore, it is a tracked entity with revisions, and a correction is an in-place refresh with a ledger entry rather than a paragraph in italics on page A2 that nobody reads. Editorial rigor stops being a norm and becomes a data structure. The recipe is the subscription. `svrn meshapp install ft` resolves the registry entry, verifies the sha256, and pulls the recipe plus the FT's own meshapp bundle. The entitlement is not a paywall cookie. It is the grant mechanism that already exists for lending a corpus to peers: ephemeral, revocable, scoped to a set of nodes. The FT's daemon answers federated queries only from nodes holding a live grant. Revoking is one row, not a cookie invalidation cascade across CDNs. The ledger is the meter, and that is the token. The unit of value in an LLM is the token because it is fungible, metered at the point of use, and priced by whoever owns the weights. Journalism has never had that unit. Pageviews measure attention, not use. The turn-stage ledger already appends a row from the code that executes each stage, at the moment it executes, with residual rows always present so a mechanism that forgot to record itself shows up as unclaimed time. The retrieval ledger already accounts every chunk as considered, admitted, or dropped with a named reason. Add one row kind, custodian, and every answer carries an honest statement of whose evidence was admitted: | custodian | considered | admitted | cited in answer | dropped: reason | | ft.newsroom | 9 | 4 | 3 | 5: not_selected_by_objective | | nyt.newsroom | 6 | 2 | 2 | 4: below_noise_floor | | wikipedia-newsworthy | 12 | 1 | 0 | 11: superseded_by_primary | A cited row is the token. The publisher sets the price per cited claim, settlement happens in aggregate, and nobody needs to know who the reader was. The reader's own reading history stays `scope = local` and structurally never leaves the machine. The kind-vs-delta invariant that already fails the eval when a step's declared kind disagrees with the observed delta is the same invariant that stops a publisher billing for chunks that were considered and dropped. This is where it stops being a distribution channel and starts being a product print cannot make. Atlas atoms carry provenance: extractor, source document, signal kind. So the FT's claim about a central bank decision and the NYT's claim about the same decision are distinct atoms with distinct custody, and where they disagree the enrichment pipeline mints a tension atom. The reader asks what happened and gets a synthesis whose ledger says three claims from the FT, two from the NYT, one tension between them, and the tension is a first-class object they can open. The thing the outlets are competing on, sourced and verified claims, becomes the metered unit rather than the thing that gets scraped for free the moment it is published. Now the trade-offs, because the moonshot has three holes. Federated search leaks the query to the publisher node. Every question a reader asks the FT's daemon is visible to the FT. The mitigation is the SEP pattern turned one notch further: the publisher replicates the atlas (`mesh_sharing = true` on the claim index, `false` on the text) so retrieval happens locally on the reader's node, and only the fetch of a cited paragraph hits the publisher. The publisher then sees which paragraphs were cited, which is exactly what it bills on, and nothing else. Settlement needs signed rows, and today the trust anchor is sha256 plus a reviewed PR. The registry file names ed25519 signing as the next step and it would have to land before any of this carries money. A ledger row that a node can forge is a pageview with extra steps. A grant holder re-serving to non-grant peers is the free-rider case and the answer is the same: signed rows and revocable grants, not DRM. The grounding gate is load-bearing in a way it is not for the SEP. A small local model hallucinating about Kant is embarrassing. Hallucinating a quote from a central banker under an FT custodian row is a libel with a receipt. The custodian row has to be admitted only for spans the segment verdict resolved to a chunk, never for the draft's paraphrase, and that is a stricter rule than the pipeline enforces today. What exists and what does not, in inventory order. Exists: the query/replicate split, scope, grantable plus the ephemeral grant store, the newsworthy watcher, the registry with corpus dependency, the turn-stage ledger with honest residuals, the retrieval ledger with drop reasons, atoms with provenance, tension atoms, the update manifest URL. Does not exist: the custodian row kind, signed ledger rows, any settlement, a relay that hides the asking node's identity, and an editorial revision ledger on the watcher's in-place refresh. Four of those five are small. Settlement is the one that is a company, not a commit.

Found by rendering the help, not by reading it. `cw-media-demo.sh holder-up` never declared a credential. It stands up Jellyfin and tells you to set `media_origin`, and stops there — which is why RuggedFox's `/Items` answers `served 401` with an empty body to every viewer: a node that looks published and serves nothing. It now mints a `cw-media-demo` API key and pipes it into `svrn mesh media declare authorization` on the holder's own machine. Two pipelines in it were exercised against the live server rather than assumed: `X-Emby-Authorization` is dead (the wizard steps are anonymous under FirstTimeSetup, which is how the stale name survived), and `/Auth/Keys` puts `AccessToken` *before* `AppName` inside an item, so `grep -A2 '"AppName":"…"'` reads the *next* key's token — verified on a server holding two app keys, where the split-on-`},{` form picks the right one and `grep -A2` picked the other. Two tests pin what made the rename free, both watched failing first: a value with an inner space and quotes survives the store, and reaches the origin verbatim. Narrowing `wire_value` to `is_ascii_graphic` makes the second fail with `MediaBrowserToken="a-key-1234"` — the space eaten silently, the origin refusing a credential that looks correct in every log. Gates: `sovereign-lint --human` resolved WORKSPACE scope, 0 errors, exit 0. Both new tests pass — the transport one needs `--features iroh`, which `sovereign-test.sh --filter` does not resolve and honestly reports as exit 4 / no tests matched rather than green. What is still owed, and it is not something I can close from here: the merged catalogue end to end. `origin_fanout` never asks this node — a `peers` entry naming self gets a `never_asked` row by design — so a catalogue can only come from a peer, and RuggedFox has no declaration. One command on that box closes it: State I changed on this machine, so you can undo any of it: `[iroh] media_origin = "127.0.0.1:8096"` added to `~/.svrnmesh/config.toml` (backup at `config.toml.bak-pre-media-origin`), the local Jellyfin's wizard completed with an admin user `house` whose password is in the session scratchpad, a "House Movies" library over three generated 40 KB mp4s in `~/Movies/house-mesh-demo`, and two API keys on it.
