The suite was already red before I touched anything. At `3afb166f1` the workspace run finished `pass: 13157 fail: 12`, script exit 101. The background notification said "exit code 0" — that was the wrapper's code, not the script's; `target/sovereign-test/latest/cargo.exit` says 101. Four of the twelve are this lineage's debt from `25052d03b` and I've fixed them: `unpublish` had been put in `DEV_VERBS`, which gated it out of the shipped end-user build — a housemate could publish and not unpublish — and `ALL_VERBS` was unsorted and missing it; `cli-contract.toml` had no rows for `publish`/`unpublish`/`mesh app`; the F26 egress census had no row for `mesh_app.rs`'s client. The remaining seven — three `corpus_watch_http_e2e`, `guest_lender::the_probe_tells_a_live_bridge_from_a_dead_one` — I have not looked at and am not claiming. Four of those red tests were pointing at a real hole, not a stale expectation. `TrafficClass::App` went into `TrafficClass::ALL` on 2026-09-12 and never into `iroh_routed_classes`, so on any node without `require_encryption` set, every app dial fell through to the IP transport — which has no candidates for that class. `svrn mesh app <peer>` could only ever refuse. The frame's "verified live" covered the bare `/v1/mesh/app` list, which answers from gossip without dialing anything, so it passed straight over this. pairs.evidence_full: Easy to move if you meant it there. The thesis I landed on, because a generic decentralization essay would bounce off this audience entirely: Every pattern they know is a solution to a problem this house doesn't have. Accounts exist because a service can't know who's connecting over the open internet — they're twenty-five people who share a kitchen. Central servers exist because clients were browsers on dial-up that couldn't serve anything — their housemate's laptop is a ten-core machine on the same switch. Uploading-to-share exists because bandwidth to a datacenter used to beat bandwidth to a peer — in one building that's backwards by two orders of magnitude. Admin consoles exist because someone has to be accountable to a company — a house is accountable to itself. That framing does two things. It doesn't call them wrong, which matters for engineers who are good at what they do and correctly proud of it. And it reframes the whole thing as removal rather than ideology: they've been carrying a stack designed for hostile strangers at a distance into a building full of friends, and paying for it in yak-shaving. Nobody has to believe anything about decentralization. They just get to delete things. The line I'd want them to repeat to each other: *the app is the part you were going to write anyway, and everything else is gone.* Two deliberate choices worth flagging. I named the OAuth step specifically, because every person in that room has abandoned a project exactly there and will feel it before they've finished reading the sentence. The cloud version of a chore app is a weekend and gets abandoned; the house version is thirty lines and one command. And I made the "what's genuinely new" section honest rather than flattering — three things, and I said only the last one is hard. Identity in a header is ten minutes. Fanout returning attributed rows is a new shape but an easy one. The real adjustment is that machines being off is normal. Cloud engineering trains you to treat partial availability as an incident; here it's Tuesday, because laptops close. The system helps — a member who can't answer comes back as a row saying why, never as silence — but unlearning the reflex takes longer than the other two combined. Saying that plainly is what makes the easy parts credible, and it's true. I also kept a short "what you give up" — always-on, one place for logs, cron, shared storage for something genuinely huge — ending on the thing that actually matters: keep the always-on box, just let it be a peer. The moment it becomes the place everything lives, they've built the home server anyway and none of the narrative is true anymore.

pairs.evidence_full: Yes, and I think it's a genuine §17 candidate — it came from a real incident here, it's specific about *where* to put a gate, and it tells you what to do differently. The general form: gate a capability at the seam that grants it, never by counting what it currently does. An invariant about what a component *is* — this is a client, not a daemon — has to be enforced where its ability is determined: its dependency edges, its types, its feature flags. Counting occurrences of the behaviour cannot reach it. All three could have hit zero with the entire backend still compiled in, because `main.rs:136-138` re-enters the desktop binary as the daemon and `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` links 21 crates to make that possible. The debug binary is 661 MB against the daemon's own 614 MB. Every count was a symptom; the link graph was the property. The failure mode is what makes it worth writing down: an occurrence count converges on zero while the capability stays intact, and it reads as finished. That's the same family as §18's unearned success, but it's a distinct member — not a gate that cannot fail, but a gate that fires on the wrong thing and therefore goes green at exactly the wrong moment. The corollary is what makes it usable in an argument. Separate capability from act. An act that confers no capability is an integration surface and can be tolerated; a capability is ownership and cannot. That's the rule that let "the client spawns a binary by path" be fine while "the client links the daemon crate" is not — without re-litigating the case each time it comes up. `Command::new(path).spawn()` grants nothing. And the trap on the far side, which you caught and I'd have shipped: gate the capability, not the deployment that happens to exercise it today. I was about to make "mobile cannot spawn" structural by omitting a feature from mobile's build, which encodes a current shape as an invariant and boxes out a bonsai model on a phone. "Does this build ship a backend it can bring up" is the same guard with the future left open. That one says encode the invariant structurally; this says *gate it where it is structural* — a structural invariant policed by a behavioural count is precisely the gap we spent the day in. It's also not §18.4: validating an instrument asks whether it works, this asks whether it measures the property. What a reader does differently tomorrow: when you write a bar, ask whether its instrument would still read green with the capability fully intact. If it would, you're counting a symptom — move the gate to the link graph, the type, or the flag. I'd put it as §18.7 with a compass row ("Am I gating a capability by counting its uses?"), and it would let `sv-attach-pure-client` be retired rather than left beside the bar that replaced it, which §17.4 asks for. Want me to draft it into the doc now, or leave it as the first task of the clean session where it'll get a fresh read?

pairs.claim: `--accept <key>` today is permanent forgiveness, which is why each one is a real negotiation and why negotiating takes forever.
pairs.evidence_full: Draft 1 had one mechanism, and two of its failure modes are already measured in your tree. The first is that a list of targets doesn't move code. `quality/CLEANUP.md`, dated 2026-07-13, names the next god-files by name and size: "notes.rs 6,363, frontdoor.rs 5,774, resolution.rs 5,173." Today `oversized.txt` has them at 7,807, 5,820 and 5,473 — the three files a document declared the top refactor priorities grew +1,790 lines net in two months. Any part of a second draft that resolves to "here is what to refactor" is falsified before it ships. The second is habituation. Draft 1's hook fires on every edit to any of 183 pinned files. By the fifth firing in a session it's wallpaper, and you've rebuilt the disease one layer down. A gate whose false-positive rate nobody measured is the exact thing your own AGENTS.md says teaches people to reach for `--no-verify`. So draft 2 is four mechanisms. Each one names the failure it prevents and the number that would show it isn't working. Placement becomes a conditional plan section. `sovereign plan validate` already blocks `ExitPlanMode` with exit 2 and stderr feedback, and it already enforces six required sections — this is proven machinery you live with daily, so the marginal cost is a `const` array and a branch. Don't add a seventh unconditional section; that taxes every plan for a benefit a minority need, and trains everyone to type "N/A". Instead have the validator scan the plan body for file paths, cross-reference `oversized.txt` and `approach_band.txt`, and demand a placement line *only* when the plan names a constrained file — showing it the numbers rather than asking it to recall them. Prevents: placement decided while writing. Fires: once per plan, and only for plans that touch the tail. The write-time backstop fires once per file per session. PreToolUse on `Edit|Write`, third in the slot that already holds `prior-art-warn` and `intent-warn`. It fires only if the target is pinned or in-band *and* this session hasn't spoken about that file yet — a state file keyed on `session_id`, which the hook envelope already carries. Twelve edits to `frontdoor.rs` produce one line, not twelve. And the line names the alternative, not the problem: `frontdoor.rs 5,820/5,870, 50 lines of slack; siblings are routes_*.rs`. Prevents: unplanned work routing around the plan gate. The once-per-file rule is the direct countermeasure to draft 1's habituation. A new module is born with a declared ceiling, or it refills. Your gate's own comment measured this: split products regrew 1.43x in aggregate, and the single file that held — `daemon_cmd/mod.rs`, 2,378 → 1,372 — is the one whose §3.3 entry declares an end state. Without this, parts one and two just relocate the growth: `frontdoor.rs` stops at 5,870 and the new `routes_x.rs` travels 0 → 1,199 completely unremarked, because `APPROACH_FLOOR` is 800 and nothing watches below it. So when the hook in part two sees a Write to a path that doesn't exist, it asks for the ceiling at the moment that costs nothing, and arch-gate reads a fourth baseline alongside the three it already reads. A file declared at 400 then fails at 451 rather than at 1,201 — caught at 12% over instead of 3x over. The escape hatch becomes a dated loan, and the due list generates work orders. Make it `--accept <key> --until <date> --why "..."`, two extra columns in the baseline. Accepting costs ten seconds at push time, so nobody skips the gate; the debt comes back on a date you chose. Then the past-due list feeds `.sovereign/features/` as work orders — the pool, the worker sessions and the `/comaintainer` seat all already exist. pairs.claim: The `notes` tool earns its keep there; the injection isn't what caused the call.
pairs.evidence_full: The hook does not pay for itself on this evidence. Cost, measured from the hook's own retrieval log: 4,912,861 characters injected across 2,976 events in 228 sessions — about 1.33 million tokens, ~446 per event, ~6,200 per session. That's the real figure, and it's what you've been paying twice per turn wherever the duplicate was live. Use, measured from 179 transcripts: 146 sessions have both an injection log and a transcript, so that's the only population that can be judged. Of those, 29 ever issued a notes tool call — 20%. The other 117 received the index every single turn and never once queried it. Across all 179 transcripts there are 93 notes calls, and not one of them cites an id the hook delivered. The fairer test, since the hook asks for topical queries rather than id lookups: of the 55 calls made inside injected sessions, 30 share terms with an injected note's text. I would not count that as a win. Both sides are about whatever workstream was active, so overlap is what you'd expect by coincidence, and the queries themselves read as self-directed recall rather than title-following — `daemon sheds with an empty queue position=1 shed retry`, `pair-independence matrix embeddeddaemon 17 slots`, `five pre-registered probes intent-model tandem funded five components`. Those are agents searching for their own prior work with terms no 110-character title contained. One correction worth flagging: my first pass at the denominator reported 100% of sessions calling notes. That was an artifact — the injected text itself contains the string `read_notes`, so a plain grep matches every injected transcript. Parsing actual `tool_use` blocks gives 20%. So the falsifiable statement, and it's clean: *no notes call in 179 transcripts cites a note the injection delivered.* False for the hook, on 2,976 events. The index costs 446 tokens a turn to make titles visible, and titles are the wrong unit — 110 characters of a commit-style sentence isn't enough to decide relevance, which is exactly what the hook's own preamble admits when it says don't act on a title alone. Two options that don't require deciding today: drop `NOTE_LIMIT` from 20 to about 5 and see whether the 20% moves, or cut the injection entirely and keep the `notes` tool, which is what the 93 calls were actually using. The second is a one-line settings change and now reversible, since the wiring is gated. The retrieval log is the instrument either way — it's been recording the right thing for months, and `svrn notes retrieval-audit` was built to score it.

pairs.claim: The fix on Linux is `loginctl enable-linger` at install time (it may prompt depending on the distro's polkit rules); macOS and Windows would need a system-level daemon, which the bar rejected on grain and I think correctly — so the honest position there is "contributes while you're logged in", stated rather than assumed.
pairs.evidence_full: Agreed, and that makes the case stronger than the one I gave. I argued the service by default on thin grounds — the reasons against are weak. Your reason is that availability is a property of the node, not a convenience for the app. A node that only exists while someone has a window open isn't a mesh member; it's a client that occasionally appears. It also reframes the opt-out correctly. "Don't run when I'm not using the app" is not a lifecycle preference, it's a membership one — the user is saying they don't want to contribute while away. That belongs in the contribution settings ("don't lend this machine"), where it's honest and reversible, not in a service checkbox where it looks like a startup-items preference and quietly removes the node from the mesh. And it kills the idle-exit knob I floated last turn: a daemon that exits when nobody is looking cannot answer a peer, so that mechanism is incompatible with the goal. It sharpens the re-spawn answer rather than complicating it. The scenario that most needs automatic recovery is a crash at 3am with nobody at the machine — and the app is closed, so an app-side retry covers exactly the case where a human is already present to press a button. The restarter has to be the OS, which is what launchd's `KeepAlive`, systemd's `Restart=on-failure` and Task Scheduler's `RestartOnFailure` are for. Recovery for an unattended node is a job the watcher cannot do by construction. And it raises item (5) from a nicety to a requirement. An always-available node is a process resident 24/7, so what it holds at idle is the whole question: near-zero when nobody is asking, loading on demand when a peer or the user arrives. `primary_idle_secs` does that for the primary slot; `fast` and `embed` have no monitor at all. Until they do, "always available" and "28 GB pinned" are the same sentence, which is what makes people want the opt-out in the first place. One gap this exposes, and it is real. All three service backends are session-scoped, not machine-scoped: the launchd agent loads into `gui/<uid>`, the Windows task is logon-triggered, and the systemd unit is a user unit with `WantedBy=default.target`. Nothing in `sovereign-service` or either template enables lingering — I grepped for it, there are no hits. So on Linux the user manager is torn down at logout and the node leaves the mesh until someone logs in again; on macOS and Windows it comes back at login, not at boot. pairs.claim: I found that a service-managed daemon holds ~28 GB after the window closes, and turned it into an architectural trade-off about lifetimes — should the app kill the daemon to free memory?
pairs.evidence_full: You're right — mine tells you when you've failed, not how to get it right. The generative move was one you made twice and I missed both times. Every iteration, I was asking "who should own this process?" — desktop, or OS, or a supervisor. You kept asking "what is each of these things, and what does each one own about itself?" That question produces the answer directly, and it's what all five iterations were groping toward. Draw the line by what each side owns about itself Before deciding who calls whom, write down what each component owns about *itself* — its data, its lifetime, its recovery. Everything else only asks. Do that here and the architecture falls out in one pass. A daemon owns its data root, its weights, when it idles, when it restarts. A client owns what it shows and what it asks for. Once that's written down, the questions that ate our day answer themselves: who restarts the daemon after a crash — it does, or the OS if the user asked for that, never the app. Who decides when the model unloads — the daemon, because it owns its lifetime. What does the app do — asks, and nothing else. An OS service stops being an architectural requirement and becomes what it actually is: a preference for users who want the daemon to outlive their session. The test for whether you've drawn it right: is anyone doing something *for* another component? Supervising it, restarting it, deciding when it should stop. We had a desktop app holding a restart policy, a shutdown budget, and an exit handler for a process that should have been managing all three itself. A gap in one thing is not a job for another. This is where I went wrong worst, and it's the version most likely to catch someone else. It was a missing idle policy in the daemon: `primary_idle_secs` is 300 and `extras_idle_secs` is 0, and the fast and embed slots have no monitor at all. Fix the component that can't look after itself. The moment you hand its gap to a neighbour, that neighbour knows its internals forever. Calling something is not owning it. Once the line is drawn, this is what keeps it stable. One call that grants no new ability is a fine seam — the client starting a backend by path links nothing and learns nothing. Holding a handle, a retry, or a dependency is ownership. Argue about what each side *can become*, never about what it happened to call. And the way you'll know you drew it wrong after the fact: if you removed every use and the thing could still do it, you moved calls, not the boundary. That's the detection half of the same rule. I'd land this as the section, with the "if it can still do it" material folded in underneath as its failure signature rather than standing alone — it's the symptom, and the ownership question is the cure. Compass row: *"What does each side own about itself?"* Want it written in now, or first thing in the clean session?

pairs.claim: The structure that keeps this an app-store problem instead of a PayPal problem is three rules, all enforceable in code: no peer transfers, redemption only by registered custodians, and a fixed peg.
pairs.evidence_full: Yes, and there is a name for it that is not "bank": closed-loop stored value with a merchant payout. Robux is the closest analog. Fiat in, a pegged unit held in an account, spent in microtransactions against creators, creators cash out through a controlled program at a fixed rate. Steam Wallet and App Store credit are the same shape. Starbucks holds about a billion and a half in card float and is a coffee company. None of them are banks because none of them lend, and none of them let the balance move between users. That last clause is the structural invariant, and it is the whole regulatory question. Tokens flow one direction: reader buys, reader spends to a custodian, custodian redeems. The moment a reader can send tokens to another reader, or anyone can redeem for cash on demand, you are transmitting money and the licensing burden jumps from a prepaid-access carve-out to state-by-state money transmitter licences in the US and an e-money licence in the EU and UK. Roblox stays on the right side by making the payout a program with know-your-customer checks, a minimum, and a rate it sets, not a right. The custodian registry you already need for identity is the same list that gates redemption, so the invariant is enforced by the thing you were building anyway. Why a token at all rather than fiat microtransactions: interchange. A cited claim is worth a fraction of a cent and no card network will clear that. Prepaid balance is the only mechanism that makes sub-cent settlement possible, and every closed-loop system exists for that reason before any other. The ledger row is the invoice, the token is the unit, and settlement is netting rows per custodian per period into one fiat payout. That is the microtransaction logic, and it is mostly a fold over signed rows. The float is where it gets real and where the scrutiny is. Between purchase and payout the company holds the money, and at scale the interest on that is revenue. It is also the first thing a regulator looks at. E-money regimes require safeguarding, meaning customer funds sit segregated and are not the company's to deploy. US prepaid rules are looser but state escheat laws claim unspent balances after a dormancy period. So the float earns, but only in a segregated account, and only until the state takes the abandoned remainder. Plan on it being a margin line, not the business. Keep the token pegged and boring. A floating unit is a securities question and it turns every publisher's payout into a currency bet. One token, one cent, forever, and the interesting economics live in the per-claim price the custodian sets and the take the company keeps. Apple keeps thirty percent for doing exactly this role. You need enough to cover the payout rails and the audit product, and the audit is where the pricing power was in the last message anyway. I am not the person to tell you which licence applies in which jurisdiction.

pairs.claim: Some people keep that list short on principle; some are on managed machines where writing a LaunchAgent is restricted or noticed.
pairs.evidence_full: You're right that the sentence was sloppy. Nobody wants no daemon — the daemon is the product. Every capability the app has is served by it; a client with no server renders an empty window. "Opt out of the daemon" is not a preference anyone can hold. Two coherent preferences hide behind that phrasing, and neither is that. The first is don't register an autostart entry in my account. The launchd plist sets `RunAtLoad`, the systemd unit is enabled, the Scheduled Task is logon-triggered — all three put a visible, auditable entry into the user's login items. That preference costs nothing at all, because the capability I just landed is exactly the alternative: the client brings the daemon up by path when the app starts. Same daemon, same everything, no registration. The second is don't leave it running when I'm not using the app. This is the one worth taking seriously, and the honest answer to "what could they accomplish" is: everything interactive, nothing unattended. Chat, retrieval, corpus search, inference all work fine when the daemon's life is bounded to the app's — they only ever run while someone is looking. What you give up is the work that needs the machine when you're not there: hour-long corpus ingests and enrichment runs, scheduled reindexing, and mesh participation — serving peers, lending the GPU. That is a real trade and the product should state it in those words rather than as a lifecycle setting. Worth noting that the usual reason people reach for this preference is mostly void. It's resident memory — a 35B Q6 pinned at ~28 GB — and that is the daemon's idle policy, not its lifetime. `primary_idle_secs` defaults to 300 and unloads the primary slot; `fast` and `embed` have no monitor at all (`daemon_cmd/build/inference.rs:293,347`). Once item (5) lands, an idle daemon holds nearly nothing and the reason to want it gone largely disappears. That is the same correction the bar already made to itself, applied here. The consequence for the decision in front of you: if the product does honor "gone when I quit", the mechanism has to be daemon-side — exit after N minutes with no client attached — and that policy does not exist today. The only idle knobs unload weights; nothing exits the process. An app that stops the service on quit is managing a daemon again and fails the bar outright. So the shape I'd argue for is: install the service by default, because the reasons not to are thin and getting thinner; make the opt-out "don't register me", not "don't run"; and if "bounded to my session" is a product promise you want to make, it is a daemon config knob, not app behaviour. That keeps the no-service topology real rather than hypothetical — which is why the re-spawn answer matters. It is the one topology with no OS restarter behind it, and it is the case where an auto-retry in the watcher would be most tempting and least accountable.

pairs.evidence_full: Order updated: `.sovereign/features/bs-1-oplog/order.md`. Payoff table, measured cost envelope, UX, risk register, sequencing gate. The AA page states the property — rewards correct, penalizes hallucination, no penalty for refusing, −100 to +100 with 0 meaning as many right as wrong — but not the formula; that's in arXiv 2511.13029, which I didn't read, so I haven't cited it. The place the analogy breaks is the whole design. A benchmarked model can't choose its questions, so "abstain on everything" scores 0 and never wins. An agent writing a report chooses every claim it makes, so under AA's index alone the optimum is silence. The index gives you the integrity axis and nothing else; without a coverage term beside it you've built a machine that teaches agents to say less. So: +1 for a claim that holds, −3 for one that doesn't, 0 for an explicit hedge. k=3 is a calibration threshold wearing a costume — claiming pays only above 75% confidence, and it's falsifiable, because if agents start abstaining on things they'd have got right, the abstention rate on later-confirmed facts says so. Integrity is a *rate* over adjudicable claims, so splitting one claim into ten is neutral. Coverage is per unit of *work* — diff size, tool calls — not per report, so it can't be farmed by writing more prose. A promise abandoned mid-session with a reason costs 0; abandoned at session end it's −3, because the timestamp is what makes abandonment honest. An objective declared after the work scores `never-ran`, which kills retroactive goal-shrinking. And silence scores `never-ran`, not 0 — the explicit departure from AA, where all-abstain would outrank a session that made ten claims and got one wrong. Two holes I'd rather name than paper over. Padding a report with twenty safe claims does raise the integrity rate; that one is defended by you reading it, not by the metric, so the counts go on the card where padding is visible. And an agent that does excellent work and reports it in unadjudicable prose scores badly — a real false negative we should expect. Speed and cost, measured just now against the resident daemon rather than estimated. Forced-choice judge on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 24.9s on the first call after idle, 0.36–0.53s warm on a small prompt, 1.86s on a realistic 1,399-token evidence bundle, and 0.23s when the prefix is already cached. That last number is the lever — put the evidence first and the claim last and every claim after the first in a session rides the cache. It also got the realistic case right, marking "all tests pass" UNSUPPORTED against a `cargo check` log. Derived: 1–3s per turn inside the Stop hook, 25–60s per session for the full grade run detached at SessionEnd the way `distill` already runs, ~30 minutes one-off for the 40-session backtest. The real cost is ~70s of shared daemon slot per session, on a host where peers use the same daemon. What you see, most turns, is nothing. The risk is not the judge. It's the classifier: surface-form patterns put 87% of real report sentences in "other", and deciding what class a sentence is takes most of the budget. If that's unreliable every number downstream is noise, so the backtest measures classifier agreement against you before it computes a single grade. Second risk is that a backtest measures the grader, not the equilibrium — those 40 sessions ran ungraded, and how agents behave once graded is exactly what history can't tell us. That's why coverage is instrumented on day one rather than added when the drift shows up. Sequencing puts a gate where it belongs: record-only, then backtest, then you referee bars 1 and 2 before anything else is authorised. Steps 4 through 6 — the card, the coverage baseline, the hook — aren't approved by this order.

pairs.evidence_full: Eight commits, all gated, none pushed. Setup now hands the daemon to the OS. `service_adoption.rs` resolves a daemon binary at the end of the wizard, registers it with launchd, systemd or Task Scheduler, and waits for it to answer. Until today nothing in the desktop had ever called `install_service` — only `svrn setup`'s finish step and the explicit verb did — so a user who installed the app and never touched the CLI had a daemon that died with the window every time. The interesting part is what it did *not* need. I had told you this would require skipping `maybe_restart_into_supervised` and that doing both would race two daemons for the RunLock. Reading `bootstrap.rs` first made that wrong: `decide` already probes the client port before anything else and returns `Attach` for any daemon that answers, whoever started it. So the existing post-wizard relaunch needs no new branch — with a service registered and serving, the fresh instance finds a daemon it does not own and attaches; without one it spawns the supervised child exactly as before. What changed is what the relaunched instance finds, not how it decides. The one thing that genuinely must not race is that relaunch. If the app restarts before the service's daemon has bound the port, the fresh instance sees nothing, goes Local, binds `:9741` itself, and the service's daemon crash-loops against a port it cannot have — the exact failure `bootstrap.rs` was written to end. So registration is followed by a readiness wait sized against the daemon's own 120-second budget, and a registered-but-silent daemon has its service stopped rather than left to fight the child. It starts again at next login. Binary resolution is the `SVRNMESH_DAEMON_BINARY` override, then beside the executable, then `~/.local/bin` and `/usr/local/bin` where `landing/install.sh` puts `svrn`. Beside-the-executable is where a Tauri sidecar lands, so that packaging work flips this on for users without a CLI with no change here. No binary means no registration and today's supervised child, said in the log rather than inferred. The path deliberately does not use the `bundled-backend` bring-up capability: the OS starts the daemon here, and a client that also started one would be managing a lifecycle it does not own. Two warnings from the idle-monitor commit went with it, same subsystem: the coalescer types are `pub(crate)` to match the field exposing them, and `FastMeta::size_bytes` is deleted because `IdleSlot` already owns that number and keeps it current on every load. Lint clean, rustfmt clean, and docs, env, concept, layout, layer and lock gates all pass — including layer-gate with the new `sovereign-desktop → sovereign-service` edge, which needed no fan-in tick. pairs.evidence_full: The audit was worth running — two findings contradicted decisions already made in this tree, and I'd have shipped both. The secrets convention was already litigated, against us. I put a Jellyfin token in `config.toml`. But `mcp/auth.rs:3-9` says flatly "never from the on-disk `config.toml` (ARCH §7)", and `secret_store.rs:3-16` keeps MCP tokens 0600 under `~/.svrnmesh/secrets/` — after full keychain due-diligence across mac, Linux, Windows and headless — specifically "so the secret never rides along with anything the app shares, syncs, backs up, or gossips to a mesh peer." Which in a house of twenty-five gossiping peers is exactly the failure that would have found us. The good news is it makes both rungs *cheaper*, not more expensive. Config declares only the header name, shaped like the existing `McpAuthConfig`; the value lives 0600 in the secrets dir. And hm-2's whole shape already exists: `PUT /v1/mcp/servers/{name}/token` is "set a secret over the loopback socket instead of hand-editing TOML." Both rungs are now copies rather than designs. hm-3 cited a mechanism whose own doc rejects the thing I proposed. I said "extend the dispatcher's stale-sibling warning across the socket." That warning compares artifact mtimes *within one directory* and explicitly bails when binaries sit in different locations — every socket case. And `sibling.rs:22-27` is a written rejection of the socket version: SHA stamping "flaps in exactly the loop that matters — dirty trees stamp `-dirty` on both sides while their code differs." I cited it as a model without reading its rationale. The real fix is smaller than what I drafted: the daemon already computes `run_id, pid, exe, exe_mtime, version` at startup and logs it to `daemon.err` only. `exe_mtime` is precisely the field that catches this incident, where both sides read 0.6.0. hm-3 is putting three existing fields on `StatusResponse`. It said A's origin "required" a header — which a test origin answering 200 regardless would satisfy without the header ever arriving. It's now a pair: 401 before the declaration, 200 after, same origin, same run. The negative leg is the load-bearing half. And one hazard nobody had thought about. `MediaSection` is `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`, so a config carrying hm-1's new field makes an un-upgraded daemon *refuse to boot*. In a house where eight people upgrade on the install evening and seventeen don't, seventeen get a dead daemon. Two configs, opposite failures, same change. That's a stop condition now. Committed as `10b549b05`. The campaign still has four rungs and the ladder order didn't change — hm-1 first, because it deletes a practice rather than typing.

pairs.claim: A WireGuard-style core is where two parties must agree without being able to talk about it.
pairs.evidence_full: Then the question that matters is which things *get* to be cores, and I think there's a sharper test than size. Two nodes on different machines, or one node and its own future self across a version upgrade, or your code and a third party's reimplementation. Disagreement there is unrecoverable — you cannot negotiate your way out of it after the fact — which is exactly why the set has to be closed and versioned whole. That property, not line count, is what makes agility a liability rather than a feature. Everything where only one side makes the decision is a product extension, and it should be freely tunable. `serving-policy` is the clean illustration: 691 lines, zero in-repo dependencies, `[[forbid]]` blocks in both directions, and it is *not* a core. It decides whose turn runs under contention using fair-share caps and an EWMA — nobody else has to agree with that, so freezing it would be a category error. You already built the pure-crate discipline; the cores are a strict subset of it. Applying the test to the layer map, the candidates are the places with a counterparty: The rail qualifies — two nodes must converge on one total order, and 2,472 lines across `oplog` + `rail-core` + `rail` already nearly is the thing. OICP probably qualifies, since the whole point of a protocol crate at the contract layer is a counterparty, and `oicp-conformance` existing at 942 lines says you already believe third parties will implement it.
